teile.einleitung: The Terracotta Army is a huge army of clay figures in China. It was made for the tomb of the first emperor of China and was meant to protect him after death. Farmers discovered it in 1974 while digging a well.
wichtigste: The figures are made of baked clay, which is what terracotta means.
Most of the figures are soldiers, and there are also horses and chariots.
Farmers discovered the army in 1974 while digging a well.
It is estimated that there are around 8000 figures.
Almost every figure has a different face.
The figures were originally painted in bright colours.
The army lies near Lintong, east of Xi'an.

abschnitte.text: In **221 BC**, **Qin Shihuangdi** united several kingdoms into one large country. He became the **first emperor of China**. During his lifetime he had a huge tomb complex built. The clay army was meant to protect him after his death. It stands in several underground **pits** close to his burial mound.

**Terracotta** means “baked earth”. The figures were shaped from **clay** and then baked in a kiln. This made them hard. Most of them are **soldiers**: archers, foot soldiers and officers. There are also **horses** made of clay, some of which pull chariots. Some of the soldiers carried real weapons made of **bronze**.

The craftsmen gave the soldiers different **faces**, hairstyles and beards. That is why almost every figure looks different. It is not known exactly whether real people served as models. Originally all the figures were **painted in bright colours**. Over time the paint has almost completely flaked off. When figures are dug up, the remaining paint often fades very quickly in the air.

In **1974**, **farmers** near the city of **Xi'an** wanted to dig a well. They came across pieces of pottery and parts of figures. Large **excavations** then began. Researchers estimate the number of figures at around **8000**. Many of them have not even been dug up yet. The pits lie near Lintong in the province of **Shaanxi**.

The Terracotta Army has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since **1987**. Today very many people visit the excavations every year. Large halls stand over the pits so that the figures can be seen. The emperor's actual **burial mound** has still not been opened. The researchers want to wait until they can protect the treasures inside properly.

gewusst: Some of the clay soldiers have already been shown in exhibitions all over the world, including in Switzerland.
Among the figures there are also kneeling archers, which are especially well preserved.

teile.einleitung: Medusa is a monster from Greek legend. Instead of hair she had snakes on her head, and whoever looked at her was turned to stone. She was defeated by the hero Perseus.
wichtigste: Medusa had living snakes instead of hair on her head.
Whoever looked directly at Medusa was turned to stone.
She was one of the three Gorgons: Stheno, Euryale and Medusa.
Only Medusa was mortal.
The hero Perseus defeated her with the help of the goddess Athena.
Perseus looked at Medusa only in the reflection of his shield.

abschnitte.text: Medusa was a **Gorgon**. That is what monsters with a terrible gaze were called in Greek legend. On her head, instead of hair, grew living **snakes** that hissed and writhed. There were **three Gorgon sisters**: **Stheno**, **Euryale** and **Medusa**. The other two were immortal, and only Medusa could be killed. According to the legend the Gorgons lived far away at the edge of the world.

The gaze of Medusa was so terrible that anyone who looked at her directly at once turned **to stone**. That is why she was so feared, and nobody dared to come near her. In the legend many petrified people and animals that had met her stand around her cave.

The hero **Perseus** was sent out to fetch the head of Medusa. The gods helped him. The goddess **Athena** gave him a brightly polished **shield**. From Hermes, according to the legend, he received winged sandals, and also a cap of invisibility and a bag. Perseus looked only at the **reflection** in the shining shield. In this way he never looked at Medusa directly and could defeat her while she slept.

Even when cut off, the head kept its power: it turned to stone anyone who looked at it. Perseus held it up to his **enemies** and so turned them to stone. According to the legend the winged horse **Pegasus** sprang from Medusa. In the end Perseus gave the head to the goddess Athena. From then on she wore it on her protective breastplate, the **aegis**.

The face of Medusa with the snake hair is called the **Gorgoneion**. The ancient Greeks and Romans painted or carved it on shields, temples, coins and mosaics. It was meant to ward off evil and frighten enemies. To this day Medusa is a popular motif in art, films and books.

gewusst: The winged horse Pegasus, according to the legend, sprang from Medusa.
In biology, jellyfish are also called medusae, because their tentacles recall snake hair.

teile.einleitung: The Neo-Babylonian Empire existed from 626 to 539 BC in Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq. In this short time Babylon became one of the largest and most magnificent cities in the world.
wichtigste: The Neo-Babylonian Empire existed from 626 to 539 BC, that is, 87 years.
The royal family probably descended from the Chaldeans.
The best-known king was Nebuchadnezzar II.
The ziggurat Etemenanki is often linked with the Tower of Babel.
The last king, Nabonidus, lived for about ten years in the oasis of Tayma.
In 539 BC the Persians conquered Babylon.

abschnitte.text: The **Neo-Babylonian Empire** began in **626 BC** with King Nabopolassar, who freed Babylon from the Assyrians. It ended in **539 BC**. With years BC one subtracts the smaller number from the larger: 626 minus 539 gives **87 years**. The ruling family probably descended from the **Chaldeans** in the south of Mesopotamia. That is why people also speak of the **Chaldean Empire**.

The most powerful king was **Nebuchadnezzar II**. He conquered large areas in Syria and Palestine. The Phoenician island city of **Tyre** he besieged, according to ancient reports, for about **13 years**, until it recognised Babylonian overlordship. In **597 BC** he captured Jerusalem for the first time and installed **Zedekiah** as a dependent king, a **vassal**. When he rebelled, the destruction of Jerusalem followed.

In Babylon huge buildings arose. The stepped tower **Etemenanki** means roughly “House of the Foundation of Heaven and Earth”. It belonged to the sanctuary of the city god **Marduk** and is often linked with the biblical **Tower of Babel**. Through the blue **Ishtar Gate** led a processional way. Numerous bricks bear a **stamp** with the names and titles of Nebuchadnezzar. They show how much he had built.

The last king, **Nabonidus**, promoted especially the moon god **Sin**. He stayed for about **ten years** in the Arabian oasis of **Tayma**. In Babylon meanwhile his son **Belshazzar** conducted the business of government. In the **Book of Daniel** Belshazzar sees the mysterious writing “Mene mene tekel” on the wall. Daniel interprets it as an announcement of the end of his rule. From this comes the expression “writing on the wall” for a warning sign.

In **539 BC** the Persian king **Cyrus II** conquered Babylon. The Neo-Babylonian Empire became part of the Persian Empire. Cyrus allowed the people of Judah who had been brought to Babylon to return to their homeland. With that the Babylonian Exile ended. But Babylon remained an important city for a long time. Its ruins lie about 90 kilometres south of Baghdad and have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2019.

gewusst: The word “Menetekel” for a warning sign comes from the story of Belshazzar.
On many bricks from Babylon the name of Nebuchadnezzar can still be read today.

teile.einleitung: The Middle Kingdom is a golden age of ancient Egypt, roughly from 2000 to 1700 BC. After a period of fragmentation the land was reunited, and art, literature and agriculture flourished.
wichtigste: Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt from Thebes around 2000 BC.
Amenemhat I founded the 12th Dynasty and moved the residence to Itjtawy.
Senusret III built fortresses at the second Nile cataract and conquered Nubia.
Under Amenemhat III the Faiyum became fertile farmland.
The Story of Sinuhe is regarded as a classic of Egyptian literature.
Texts about the afterlife were written on wooden coffins, the Coffin Texts.

abschnitte.text: Before the Middle Kingdom Egypt had broken up into several spheres of power in the **First Intermediate Period**. Around **2000 BC** King **Mentuhotep II** of the 11th Dynasty reunited the land from **Thebes**. His mortuary temple lies at **Deir el-Bahari** on the west side of the Nile. After that **Amenemhat I**, probably formerly vizier, that is, chief official, founded the **12th Dynasty**. He moved the residence to **Itjtawy** near present-day Lisht.

The kings protected the borders with fortresses. Amenemhat I had the **Walls of the Ruler** laid out on the eastern edge of the Nile Delta to keep out nomads from the east. In the south **Senusret III** led several campaigns into **Nubia**. He greatly strengthened the chain of fortresses at the **second Nile cataract**, a set of rapids of the Nile. Fortresses such as **Semna** secured the southern border and the trade in gold and other goods.

The **Faiyum** is a large depression west of the Nile with a lake. The kings of the 12th Dynasty had it opened up with **canals and dykes**, above all under **Amenemhat III**. In this way fertile farmland arose. At Hawara Amenemhat III had a pyramid built. Beside it stood a huge temple complex that Greek travellers later called the **Labyrinth**. Many pyramids of this period consisted inside of mud bricks.

In the Middle Kingdom works arose that the Egyptians themselves read as **model works**. Most famous is the **Story of Sinuhe**: a court official flees to Western Asia after the death of Amenemhat I, lives there for a long time and returns to Egypt in old age. The language of this period, **Middle Egyptian**, was later regarded as classical. Sayings about the afterlife were written on the inner walls of wooden coffins. They are called **Coffin Texts**, and now high officials also used them.

gewusst: Egyptian pupils were still copying out the Story of Sinuhe for practice centuries later.
The language of the Middle Kingdom is still the first thing Egyptologists learn today.

teile.einleitung: The Western Schism was a split in the Catholic Church in the late Middle Ages. For around 40 years there were several popes at the same time, who did not recognise each other.
wichtigste: “Schism” means **split**.
The schism began in **1378**.
At first there were popes in **Rome** and in **Avignon**.
In Rome **Urban VI** was elected, and in Avignon **Clement VII** resided.
After the Council of Pisa in 1409, there were even **three** popes.
The schism lasted **around 40 years**.
The Council of Constance ended it.

abschnitte.text: In the 14th century, the popes did not live in Rome for a long time, but in **Avignon** in southern France. Only in 1377 did a pope return to Rome. When he died shortly afterwards, the cardinals elected a new pope in Rome in 1378: **Urban VI**. The election took place under great pressure from the Romans, who wanted a pope from Italy.

Soon many cardinals were dissatisfied with Urban VI. **French cardinals** declared his election invalid. Still in **1378** they elected another pope, **Clement VII**. He resided in **Avignon**. Now there were two popes. The word **“schism”** means **“split”**, and that is exactly what happened to the Church.

The countries of Europe also had to decide. **France** supported the pope in Avignon. **England** sided with the pope in Rome. Other countries chose according to their interests. Many believers were unsettled, because both popes said they were the only right one.

In **1409**, bishops gathered for the **Council of Pisa**. They deposed both popes and elected a new one. But the other two did not step down. Now there were even **three popes** at the same time. Scholars such as **Jean Gerson**, chancellor of the University of Paris, kept looking for a solution.

The solution came at the **Council of Constance**, near the Swiss border on Lake Constance. It began in 1414. The popes were persuaded to resign or were deposed. In **1417**, **Martin V** was elected as the only pope. This ended the schism after **around 40 years**. Only the antipope **Benedict XIII** of the Avignon line refused to resign until his death.

gewusst: The election of Martin V in Constance is the only papal election ever held on what is now German soil.
Benedict XIII withdrew to a castle in Spain and went on regarding himself there as the rightful pope until his death.

teile.einleitung: A Roman villa was a large country house that belonged to rich families. Often a farm was attached that supplied grain, wine or oil. In Switzerland too, remains of such villas with magnificent mosaics have been found.
wichtigste: A villa was a large country house of rich Romans.
To many villas a farm belonged.
The atrium was the entrance hall with an opening in the roof.
In the basin of the atrium rainwater was collected.
The peristyle was a garden with a colonnade all around.
Mosaics adorned mainly the floors.
Near Orbe in the canton of Vaud one can see large Roman mosaics.

abschnitte.titel: A country house with a farm
abschnitte.text: The Latin word **villa** means country house. Rich families owned villas in the countryside, often with fields, stables and workshops. Many people worked there, including slaves. The farm supplied grain, wine, oil or meat. The living quarters for the owners were often furnished very beautifully.

Behind the entrance lay the **atrium**, a large hall. In the roof was an opening through which light and rain came in. Beneath it stood a basin, the **impluvium**, for the rainwater. Further back there was often the **peristyle**. This was a garden inside the house around which ran a passage with columns. There one could stroll in the shade.

Many floors were decorated with **mosaics**. A mosaic consists of many small stones that together make a picture. Because they lie on the floor, they last a very long time. In Pompeii a famous mosaic at an entrance shows a dog on a chain. Beneath it is written “Cave canem”, which means “Beware of the dog”.

Some villas had **underfloor heating**, which is called a **hypocaust**. Hot air flowed from a furnace through the space beneath the floor. Larger villas even had their own baths with warm and cold rooms. So life was pleasant even in winter. For the heating, however, one needed a lot of wood and a lot of work.

In the area of present-day **Switzerland** too there were many Roman villas. Near **Orbe** in the canton of Vaud the remains of a very large villa were found. Its beautiful mosaics can still be seen there today. Many other villas have been discovered on the Swiss Plateau. They show that the Romans lived here for centuries and practised agriculture.

gewusst: We still use the word villa today for a large, beautiful house.
A single small stone of a mosaic is called a tessera.
The mosaics of Orbe are among the largest Roman mosaics north of the Alps.

teile.einleitung: Vindonissa was a large camp of the Roman army at present-day Windisch in the canton of Aargau. Almost 2000 years ago, thousands of legionaries, that is, Roman professional soldiers, lived here. Today you can still discover walls, roads and even an amphitheatre in many places.
wichtigste: Vindonissa was a camp for legionaries at present-day Windisch in Aargau.
It was the only legionary camp of the Romans in the area of present-day Switzerland.
At Vindonissa, the three rivers Aare, Reuss and Limmat meet.
The camp was built around AD 15 and remained a legionary camp until about AD 101.
At times about 6000 soldiers lived in the camp.
The camp included an amphitheatre, whose remains can still be visited today.
The Museum Aargau shows the life of the soldiers on the Legionaries' Trail and in the Vindonissa Museum in Brugg.

abschnitte.text: Vindonissa was a **legionary camp**, that is, a permanently built camp for a whole legion. A legion was a unit of about 5000 to 6000 soldiers. The Romans built the camp around AD 15, in the time of Emperor Tiberius. It was the only legionary camp in the area of present-day Switzerland.

The camp lay on a plateau above the confluence of the **Aare, Reuss and Limmat**. This area is now called the **Wasserschloss (“water castle”) of Switzerland**. The position was ideal: the rivers protected the camp, and goods could be transported on them. In addition, important Roman roads crossed here, for example towards the Rhine and towards the Alps.

First the 13th Legion was stationed at Vindonissa. Later the 21st Legion followed, and after it the 11th Legion. The soldiers were to secure the border on the Rhine against the Germanic peoples. Around AD 101, the last legion left, because the border had been moved further north.

In the camp there were **barracks**, workshops, storehouses, a hospital and baths. A water pipe brought fresh water into the camp, and part of it still carries water today. In front of the camp stood an **amphitheatre** for thousands of spectators, in which fights and shows took place. Around the camp, traders, craftsmen and families lived in a village.

The Romans threw their rubbish onto a large **rubbish mound** at the edge of the camp. For archaeologists this is a treasure today. Because the ground there was damp, even things made of wood and leather were preserved. Shoes, tools and wooden writing tablets with letters from the soldiers were found.

After the legion left, Vindonissa remained a place for traders and veterans. In late Roman times the Romans built a fortress here again, and in the early Middle Ages Windisch was the seat of a bishop. Today the site is among the most important Roman sites in Switzerland. On the **Legionaries' Trail**, children can try out how the soldiers lived, ate and slept.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large unit of the Roman army with about 5000 to 6000 soldiers.
A Roman professional soldier who served for around 20 to 25 years.
A round or oval building with rows of seats for spectators of fights and games.
The science that digs up and studies ancient things from the ground.

gewusst: The name Vindonissa is Celtic, because before the Romans, Celtic Helvetii lived here.
A Roman water pipe from Vindonissa has been carrying water for almost 2000 years.
In the rubbish mound, wooden tablets were found on which soldiers had written letters and notes.

teile.einleitung: Mount Olympus is the highest mountain in Greece. In the Greek legends it was the home of the most important gods, who ate ambrosia and drank nectar there.
wichtigste: Olympus is a mountain range in the north of Greece.
Its highest peak, Mytikas, is about 2,918 metres high.
It lies between Thessaly and Macedonia, not far from the sea.
According to the legend the gods around Zeus lived there.
The gods ate ambrosia and drank nectar.
Since 1938 the area has been the first national park of Greece.

abschnitte.text: **Olympus** is a **mountain range** in **northern Greece**. It lies between the regions of **Thessaly** and **Macedonia**, not far from the sea. Its highest peak is called **Mytikas** and is about **2,918 metres** high. That is the highest point of the country. For comparison: the Säntis in eastern Switzerland is 2,502 metres high, so about 400 metres lower. In winter snow often lies on Olympus for a long time.

In the Greek legends Olympus was the **home of the gods**. There lived **Zeus**, the father of the gods, and other important gods such as Hera, Athena, Apollo and Poseidon. So they are also called the **Olympian gods**. The summit was often wrapped in clouds. For people it was therefore a mysterious place that one should not enter.

According to the legend the gods ate **ambrosia** and drank **nectar**. This special food and drink was meant to keep them **immortal** and forever young. Humans were normally not allowed to taste them. Today the sweet juice in flowers, from which bees make honey, is also called **nectar**. The word comes from Greek legend.

For a long time nobody stood on the highest peak. Only in **1913** was **Mytikas** climbed for the first time. Taking part were two **Swiss from Geneva**, the photographer **Fred Boissonnas** and **Daniel Baud-Bovy**, together with a local guide. Today Olympus is a popular goal for walkers. The last part to the summit, however, is steep and rocky and requires climbing skills.

The area around Olympus became in **1938** the **first national park of Greece**. Rare **plants** and **animals** are protected there. Many plants grow only here and nowhere else in the world. In the forests live, for example, chamois, roe deer and many species of birds. On the way up the landscape changes from deciduous forest through coniferous forest to bare rock.

gewusst: The highest peak of Olympus was first climbed in 1913 by two Swiss from Geneva with a Greek guide.
The ancient Olympic Games did not take place on Olympus but at Olympia on the Peloponnese.

teile.einleitung: Already the early Egyptians built boats of reed, more exactly of papyrus. These light boats were very useful on the Nile. Thousands of years later a researcher showed that with such boats one can even cross the sea.
wichtigste: Early Egyptians built simple boats from bundles of papyrus.
Papyrus stalks are light and float well.
The Nile flows north into the Mediterranean.
Without wind the boats were moved with oars.
Thor Heyerdahl crossed the Atlantic in 1970 with the papyrus boat Ra II.

abschnitte.text: On the Nile much **papyrus** grew, a tall reed plant. People cut off the long stalks and tied many of them firmly together into bundles. From several bundles a boat with upturned ends was made. Because the stalks are light and contain air, the boat floated well. Such boats were used for fishing, for hunting and for crossing the river.

The **Nile** flows from Africa **north** into the Mediterranean. With the current boats travelled easily northwards. In Egypt, however, the wind mostly blows from the north. So with a sail one could sail well southwards. When no wind blew, men rowed the boat. Large ships had many **rowers**, and later they were also built of wood.

The Norwegian researcher **Thor Heyerdahl** wanted to show that even ancient peoples could travel far across the sea. He had a boat made of papyrus built on an old model. The first voyage with the **Ra** he had to abandon. In 1970 he sailed with the **Ra II** from Morocco across the **Atlantic** to Barbados in the Caribbean. With that he proved that such boats can manage long journeys.

gewusst: Boats of reed are still built today, for example on Lake Titicaca in South America.
From papyrus the Egyptians also made their writing material.

teile.einleitung: A villa rustica was a Roman farm estate in the countryside. Large farms like this existed everywhere in the Roman Empire, including in the area of present-day Switzerland. Walls and mosaics have survived from many of them.
wichtigste: A **villa rustica** was a large Roman farm.
The owner lived in the **manor house**.
Rich estates had **underfloor heating**.
The estate of **Seeb near Winkel** in the canton of Zurich is well known.
**Orbe-Boscéaz** in the canton of Vaud is famous for its mosaics.
The Romans spread the **grapevine** in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: The Latin name **villa rustica** means roughly “country house”. It refers to a large **estate** with fields, pastures and several buildings. Grain, fruit and vegetables were grown there and animals were kept. The estates supplied the cities and the soldiers with food.

An estate had two parts. In the **manor house** lived the owner with his family. It was often handsomely built, with columns, painted walls and a bath of its own. In the **farm part** there were stables, barns, workshops and houses for the workers. A wall often surrounded the whole site.

Rich manor houses were heated in winter with **underfloor heating**. It is called a **hypocaust**. The floor rested on small columns made of bricks. A fire heated the air underneath, and the warm air flowed under the floor and through the walls. In this way the rooms stayed pleasantly warm.

In grand rooms, **mosaics** lay on the floor. A mosaic is made of many **small stones** in different colours, put together to form pictures and patterns. The estate of **Orbe-Boscéaz** in the canton of Vaud is famous for its magnificent mosaics. You can visit them there today.

In the area of present-day Switzerland there were very many Roman estates. The estate of **Seeb near Winkel** in the canton of Zurich is well known, where you can visit remains of walls. The Romans brought new plants with them. They spread, for example, the **grapevine**, in order to make wine.

gewusst: Some present-day place names in Switzerland probably go back to the names of Roman estates.
For underfloor heating an estate needed a lot of wood, so slaves or workers had to tend the fire constantly.

teile.einleitung: The Law of the Twelve Tables was the first collection of laws in ancient Rome to be written down. It was created around 450 BC and was set up in public so that everyone could know the law.
wichtigste: The Law of the Twelve Tables was written down **around 450 BC**.
A committee of **ten men** wrote it down.
The tables stood in public in the **Roman Forum**.
For the **plebeians** it was important because the law could now be read by everyone.
Roman envoys are said to have visited **Athens** beforehand.
According to Cicero, children had to **learn it by heart**.

abschnitte.text: In early Rome there were rules, but they were not written down. Only the noble **patricians** knew them exactly, because they provided the judges and priests. The ordinary citizens, the **plebeians**, often felt unfairly treated. They therefore demanded that the law be **written down**. Then anyone could check what was allowed and what was not.

According to tradition, a committee of **ten men** was formed, a **board of ten**. In Latin they were called decemviri. They were to collect and write down the laws. Before that, Roman envoys are said to have travelled to **Athens** to learn about the laws of the Greeks. Whether this journey really took place is uncertain.

The laws were written **around 450 BC** on **twelve tables**. That is how the law got its name. The tables were set up in the **Roman Forum**, the most important square in Rome. There anyone could read them. The laws regulated, for example, debts, inheritances, land and punishments.

The original tables have not survived. They were probably lost **when the Gauls invaded** Rome around **387 BC**. Even so, we know some of the content. Later Roman writers quoted individual sentences from the law. Researchers have collected and arranged these fragments.

The Law of the Twelve Tables remained important for centuries. The Roman orator **Cicero** reports that in his youth children still had to **learn it by heart**. Roman law later shaped many laws in Europe, including the law in **Switzerland**. That is why the Law of the Twelve Tables is regarded as an early foundation of our law.

gewusst: One principle of the Law of the Twelve Tables was that a law should apply equally to all citizens.
Cicero wrote that in his time the law was no longer learnt by heart at school, but had been when he was a child.

teile.einleitung: The Persian Royal Road was a long road through the Persian Empire. It linked the city of Sardis in the west with the residential city of Susa in the east. On it messengers travelled as fast as nowhere else in the ancient world.
wichtigste: The Royal Road was built in the Persian Empire.
King Darius I had it expanded.
It was about 2,700 kilometres long.
It began in the west at Sardis and in the east at Susa.
At regular intervals there were stations with fresh horses.
Riding messengers needed about a week, and on foot it took about three months.
The historian Herodotus described the road.

abschnitte.titel: A road right across the empire
abschnitte.text: The **Persian Empire** was huge about 2,500 years ago. To be able to govern it well, the king needed fast connections. King **Darius I** therefore had a long road expanded, the **Royal Road**. It led from **Sardis** in the west, in present-day Turkey, to **Susa** in the east, in present-day Iran. The route was about **2,700 kilometres** long.

Along the road there were **stations** at regular intervals. There **fresh horses** and riders waited. A messenger rode to the next station and passed the message on there. The next rider galloped off at once. In this way the message was on its way day and night, almost like a relay race.

The **riding messengers** needed for the whole route only **about a week**. A person **on foot**, by contrast, was on the road for about **three months**. For that time it was an incredibly fast postal system. Merchants, soldiers and officials also used the road. It helped the king to hold his great empire together.

The Greek historian **Herodotus** described the Royal Road. He admired the Persian messengers, who let nothing hold them up, neither snow nor rain, heat nor darkness. A sentence that goes back to this description stands today on a large **post office building in New York**. There it is regarded as the unofficial motto of letter carriers.

gewusst: The idea of passing messages on from station to station was later also used by mail coaches in Europe.
Herodotus counted over a hundred resting places along the Royal Road.

teile.einleitung: The Roman army was one of the strongest and best organised armies of antiquity. With it the Romans conquered an empire that stretched from Britain to Egypt. Its soldiers, the legionaries, were well trained, strictly led and uniformly equipped.
wichtigste: A Roman soldier is called a legionary.
The largest unit was the legion with several thousand soldiers.
A centurion led about 80 soldiers.
Legionaries carried a short sword and a rectangular, curved shield.
With the tortoise the soldiers protected themselves on all sides.
On the most important standard of a legion was an eagle.
On the march the soldiers built a camp every evening.
In the imperial period a legionary served about 20 to 25 years.

abschnitte.text: The largest unit was the **legion** with about 5,000 to 6,000 soldiers. It consisted of ten cohorts, which in turn were divided into smaller groups, the centuries. A century of about 80 men was led by a **centurion**. At the very top stood the legate as commander of the legion.

A **legionary** wore at his side a short sword, the **gladius**, and usually two throwing spears as well. His large shield, the **scutum**, was rectangular and curved so that it covered the body well. In addition there were a metal helmet and armour of metal strips or chain mail. On his feet he wore hobnailed sandals, the caligae.

The Romans fought in a disciplined way in orderly ranks. Famous is the **tortoise** formation, Latin testudo: the soldiers held their shields close together in front, at the sides and over their heads. In this way they were protected against arrows and stones. On the most important standard of every legion was an **eagle**, and it was considered a great disgrace to lose it to the enemy.

On a campaign the soldiers marched with heavy baggage, often 30 kilometres a day. Every evening they built a fortified **camp** with a ditch, a rampart and a palisade. The tents always stood according to the same plan, so that everyone knew his place. From permanent camps on the frontier towns often later grew.

In the imperial period the army was a professional army, and a legionary served about **20 to 25 years**. He received a fixed pay and after service money or land. Besides the legions there were **auxiliary troops** of non-Romans, who received Roman citizenship after their period of service. Discipline was very strict, and harsh punishments were usual.

In present-day Windisch in the canton of Aargau lay the legionary camp **Vindonissa**, the only legionary camp on the territory of present-day Switzerland. In the 1st century AD several thousand soldiers were stationed there. Archaeologists found remains of an amphitheatre, of barracks and many everyday objects. In the Vindonissa Museum in Brugg one can view these finds.

begriffe.erklaerung: The largest unit of the Roman army, with several thousand soldiers.
A Roman soldier in a legion.
An officer who led a unit of about 80 soldiers.
Latin for tortoise, a formation with shields on all sides.

gewusst: The word “salary” probably comes from the Latin word for salt, sal.
Roman soldiers also had to build roads, bridges and canals, not just fight.

teile.einleitung: Vesuvius is a volcano in southern Italy, right next to the city of Naples. It is famous for its eruption in AD 79, which buried the Roman city of Pompeii under ash.
wichtigste: Vesuvius is a **volcano** in Italy.
It lies next to the big city of **Naples**.
In AD 79 it buried the cities of **Pompeii** and Herculaneum.
The Roman **Pliny the Younger** described the eruption in letters.
Vesuvius is still active today and can erupt again.

abschnitte.text: Vesuvius lies on the Bay of Naples, only a few kilometres from the city of **Naples**. It is a **volcano**. When it erupts, **glowing lava**, ash and rock come out of its interior. On its slopes, vines and vegetables grow well, because the volcanic soil is very fertile.

In **AD 79**, Vesuvius erupted violently. A huge cloud of ash and pumice rose into the sky. The Roman cities of **Pompeii** and **Herculaneum** were buried under a thick layer. Many inhabitants managed to flee, but for others rescue came too late.

The young Roman **Pliny the Younger** saw the eruption from a distance. Later he described in **letters** to the historian Tacitus what he had experienced. His uncle, the scholar Pliny the Elder, had set out with ships to help people, and lost his life doing so. The letters are an important source for research.

For many centuries, Pompeii and Herculaneum lay hidden. In the 18th century, excavations began. Under the ash, houses, streets, wall paintings and everyday objects were well preserved. So today we can see exactly how the Romans lived. Pompeii is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

Vesuvius is **still active today**. It has erupted again and again since Roman times, most recently in **1944**. Today very many people live near it. Experts therefore watch it closely with measuring instruments. For emergencies there are plans for how the inhabitants can be brought to safety quickly.

gewusst: After the letters of Pliny the Younger, a particular type of violent volcanic eruption is now called a “Plinian eruption”.
The observatory on Vesuvius is regarded as the oldest volcano observatory in the world.

teile.einleitung: Roman roads were the paved long-distance roads that the Romans built throughout their empire. They ran as straight as possible across plains, through forests and over Alpine passes. The saying “All roads lead to Rome” recalls this huge road network.
wichtigste: The Romans built a huge road network throughout their empire.
The most famous road is the Via Appia, which leads south from Rome.
Important roads were covered with stone slabs.
Roman roads ran quite straight whenever possible.
The surface was raised in the middle so that rainwater ran off.
Milestones at the roadside showed the distance.
Soldiers often built the roads.
An important Roman road led over the Great St Bernard in the canton of Valais.

abschnitte.text: The Roman roads were important above all for the **army**, for soldiers could march along them quickly into any province. Merchants, messengers and travellers also used them for **trade**. With the state postal service, the **cursus publicus**, news and orders were carried throughout the empire. In all, the Romans are estimated to have built over 80,000 kilometres of well-made long-distance roads.

The **Via Appia** is the most famous Roman road. Its construction began in 312 BC under the official Appius Claudius, after whom it is named. It led from Rome south to Capua and later to Brundisium, present-day Brindisi. The Romans called it the “Queen of Roads”, and parts of it can still be walked today.

For an important road the builders first dug a trench. Then they filled in several layers of coarse stones, gravel and sand. On top, important roads got large **stone slabs**, others tamped-down gravel. The surface was slightly **arched** in the middle so that rainwater ran off into the ditches at the side.

Surveyors planned the roads as **straight** as possible, even if they had to cut through hills or build bridges to do so. At the roadside stood **milestones**, stone pillars that gave the distance to the next town. A Roman mile corresponded to 1,000 double paces, that is, just under 1.5 kilometres. At regular intervals there were **staging posts** where travellers could spend the night and change horses.

Often **soldiers** built the roads when there was no war on. Slaves and hired workers also took part. For their tools and plans the Romans needed good **engineers**. Many bridges and roads were built so solidly that they were used for centuries.

Important Roman roads also ran through present-day Switzerland. One of them went over the **Great St Bernard** in the canton of Valais from Italy to Martigny and on to Lake Geneva. In Graubünden the Romans used the **Julier Pass**, where remains of pillars have been found. At the Pierre Pertuis pass in the Bernese Jura a road runs through a gap in the rock where a Roman inscription is preserved.

begriffe.erklaerung: A stone pillar at the roadside that gives the distance.
Latin word for road or way.
A place on the road for spending the night and changing horses.
An expert in planning and building roads, bridges and machines.

gewusst: Our word “street” comes from the Latin “via strata”, which means “paved way”.
Many of today's main roads and motorways in Europe still follow roughly the course of old Roman roads.

teile.einleitung: Amerigo Vespucci was a merchant and navigator from Florence. The continent of America was named after him.
wichtigste: Vespucci first worked for a trading house of the Medici and so came to Seville.
In 1499 he took part in a Spanish voyage, and in 1501 to 1502 he sailed on behalf of Portugal.
On the Portuguese voyage, the coast of present-day Brazil was explored.
The name Venezuela, “Little Venice”, is said to have arisen on a voyage in 1499.
Around 1503, the account “Mundus Novus”, “New World”, appeared under his name.
In 1508 he became Chief Pilot in Spain.

abschnitte.text: Amerigo Vespucci was born in **Florence** in 1454. He worked for a trading house of the famous **Medici** family. On their behalf he came to **Seville** in Spain. There he helped, among other things, to equip ships for voyages of discovery. Soon he wanted to sail across the Atlantic himself.

Vespucci sailed for **Spain and Portugal**, which were then leading the voyages of discovery. In 1499 he took part in a Spanish expedition to the north coast of South America. There the sailors saw houses on stilts in the water, which reminded them of Venice. That is where the name **Venezuela** is said to come from, which means “Little Venice”. In 1501 to 1502 he sailed on behalf of Portugal far to the south along the coast of present-day **Brazil**.

Around 1503, a short travel account with the Latin title **“Mundus Novus”**, which means **“New World”**, appeared under Vespucci's name. It says that the newly discovered lands do not belong to Asia, but are a continent of their own. The account was translated into many languages and made Vespucci famous in Europe. Whether he wrote all the texts himself is disputed among researchers.

In 1507, the cartographer **Martin Waldseemüller** drew a map of the world. On it he named the new continent after Amerigo Vespucci **“America”**. The name caught on. Vespucci himself became **Chief Pilot** in Spain in 1508, in Spanish “Piloto Mayor”. He trained navigators, examined them and collected new maps. He died in Seville in 1512.

gewusst: The map by Waldseemüller on which “America” appears for the first time is kept in Washington today.
Columbus believed until his death that he had landed in Asia.

teile.einleitung: A polis was a Greek city-state of antiquity, that is, a city with its surrounding land that governed itself. Instead of one great empire there were hundreds of such small states in Greece. From the word “polis” also comes our word “politics”.
wichtigste: A polis was an independent Greek city-state.
Mountains and sea separated the small plains of Greece from one another.
In the classical period there were about 700 city-states.
The word politics derives from polis.
The agora was the central marketplace and assembly place.
Acropolis literally means upper city.
All city-states shared language, gods and festivals such as the Olympic Games.

abschnitte.text: A **polis** consisted of a city and the land around it with villages, fields and pastures. It had its own laws, its own coins, its own army and often its own patron god. Most city-states were small and had only a few thousand inhabitants. The largest and best known were **Athens** and **Sparta**.

Greece is full of **mountains**, bays and islands. The small plains were separated from one another by mountains and sea, and travelling was arduous. So many independent communities developed instead of one great empire. In the classical period, roughly the 5th and 4th centuries BC, there were about **700 city-states**.

The centre of a polis was the **agora**, a marketplace and assembly place with shops, public buildings and colonnades. There the citizens met to trade and discuss. On a hill there often lay the **acropolis**, the upper city, with temples and a citadel for protection. The most famous is the Acropolis of Athens with the temple of the Parthenon.

The city-states had very different forms of government. In an **oligarchy** a small group of rich or distinguished citizens ruled. A **tyrant** was a sole ruler who had seized power without a right of inheritance. In Athens in the 5th century BC **democracy** arose, in which all citizens could take part in decisions, though only free men and not women, foreigners or slaves.

Each polis defended itself with its own citizens. The heavily armed foot soldiers were called **hoplites** and fought in a dense line, the phalanx. When land became scarce, many cities founded **colonies** on distant coasts between about 750 and 550 BC. In this way arose, for example, Massalia, present-day Marseille, and Neapolis, present-day Naples.

Although the city-states often fought one another, all felt themselves to be **Hellenes**. They spoke the same language, worshipped the same gods and visited the same sanctuaries such as Delphi. Every four years they met for the **Olympic Games**. Against common enemies such as the Persians they sometimes joined together.

begriffe.erklaerung: A Greek city-state of antiquity.
The marketplace and assembly place of a Greek city.
The fortified upper city on a hill.
Rule by a small group of rich or distinguished people.
A heavily armed Greek foot soldier.

gewusst: The words police and metropolis also go back to the Greek word polis.
The name Naples comes from the Greek Neapolis and simply means “new city”.

teile.einleitung: Odoacer was a Germanic general who deposed the last western Roman emperor in the year 476. After that he ruled as king over Italy until Theodoric the Great defeated him in 493.
wichtigste: Odoacer deposed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus in 476.
The year 476 is often regarded as the end of the Western Roman Empire.
Odoacer ruled as king, in Latin “Rex”, and not as emperor.
He sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople.
Romulus Augustulus afterwards lived with a pension near Naples.
In 493 Theodoric the Great defeated and killed Odoacer in Ravenna.

abschnitte.text: **Odoacer** came from a Germanic people and served as an officer in the army of the **Western Roman Empire**. In the 5th century this army consisted to a large extent of Germanic warriors. Real power often lay not with the emperor but with the army commanders. In **475** the army commander **Orestes** raised his young son **Romulus Augustulus** to emperor and drove out the previous emperor **Julius Nepos**.

The Germanic soldiers demanded land in Italy. When Orestes refused, they stood behind Odoacer. His troops defeated Orestes, who was killed in **476**. After that Odoacer deposed the young emperor **Romulus Augustulus**. He sent him into retirement with a **pension**, to the **Castellum Lucullanum near Naples**. The year of his death is unknown. The year **476** is therefore often regarded as the **end of the Western Roman Empire**.

Odoacer gave up the imperial title. He ruled as king, in Latin **Rex**, over Italy. The imperial **regalia** of the west, the insignia, he sent to **Constantinople** to Emperor **Zeno**. This was meant to show that the west no longer needed an emperor of its own. Formally Odoacer recognised the emperor in the east. For Constantinople, however, **Julius Nepos** in Dalmatia remained the lawful emperor of the west until his murder in **480**.

Odoacer ruled Italy for about 17 years and left the Roman administration largely in place. But he became too powerful for the emperor in Constantinople. On the emperor's commission the Ostrogothic king **Theodoric the Great** marched to Italy. After several battles Odoacer withdrew to **Ravenna**. After a long siege the two made a treaty. Shortly afterwards, in **493**, Theodoric killed Odoacer with his own hand and became ruler of Italy himself.

gewusst: The name Romulus Augustulus combines the founder of Rome and the first emperor Augustus, and “Augustulus” means “little Augustus”.
Many historians today see 476 rather as a symbolic date, because life in Italy hardly changed at once.

teile.einleitung: In 480 BC a small Greek army tried to hold up the Persians at a narrow pass. This pass is called Thermopylae. The Greeks lost, but their resistance became famous.
wichtigste: The Battle of Thermopylae took place in 480 BC.
The Spartan king Leonidas I led the Greeks.
According to tradition 300 Spartiates and several thousand other Greeks fought.
The Persian Great King Xerxes I led a huge army.
“Thermopylae” means “hot gates”.
A traitor showed the Persians a path over the mountains.
At the same time the Greek fleet fought at Cape Artemisium.

abschnitte.text: Ten years after the defeat at Marathon the Persian king **Xerxes I** marched against Greece. He was the son of Darius I and wanted to avenge his father's defeat. He came with a huge army and a large fleet. Many Greek cities joined together to defend themselves. They wanted to stop the Persians at a narrow point in central Greece.

**Thermopylae** was a narrow passage between mountains and sea. The name means **“hot gates”**. It comes from hot sulphur springs nearby, and “pylai” means “gates” in Greek. At this narrow spot the great Persian army could hardly use its superior numbers. At the same time the Greek fleet fought at **Cape Artemisium** in the north of the island of Euboea.

The Spartan king **Leonidas I** led the Greek army. According to tradition **300 Spartiates** fought, that is, full Spartan citizens. In addition there were several thousand warriors from other cities. When the Persians demanded that they hand over their weapons, Leonidas is said to have answered “Molon labe”. That means roughly “Come and take them!” and is handed down by the writer **Plutarch**.

For two days the Greeks held the pass. Then a Greek named **Ephialtes** showed the Persians a path over the mountains. In this way they could outflank the defenders from behind. Leonidas sent most of the Greeks away and stayed behind with a **rearguard**. This was completely defeated, and Leonidas fell. After the fall of the pass the fleet also withdrew.

The battle ended with a **defeat** for the Greeks. Nevertheless their resistance became a model of **bravery**. It gave the other Greeks time to prepare. In the same year the Greek fleet won at **Salamis**. Today a monument at the old pass recalls Leonidas and his men.

gewusst: A famous inscription on a memorial stone begins “Stranger, if you come to Sparta”. Friedrich Schiller rendered it into German.
Because the sea has withdrawn, the once narrow pass is today a broad plain.
The hot springs at Thermopylae still exist today.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Marathon took place in 490 BC in Greece. There the Athenians, with a little help, defeated a larger Persian army. The victory became a sign of hope for the Greeks.
wichtigste: The Battle of Marathon took place in 490 BC.
The Persian Great King Darius I had sent the army.
Persia wanted to punish Athens because it had supported the Ionian revolt.
Only the small city of Plataea sent troops to help.
The general Miltiades is regarded as the victor of Marathon.
According to Herodotus 192 Athenians and about 6,400 Persians fell.
The Spartans arrived too late because of a religious festival.

abschnitte.text: Around 500 BC Greek cities in **Ionia**, on the coast of Asia Minor, rose against Persian rule. **Athens** sent ships to help them. The revolt failed, but the Persian king **Darius I** wanted to punish Athens for it. He stayed in Persia himself and sent an army with ships across the Aegean. It landed on the plain of **Marathon**, north-east of Athens.

Athens fought with **hoplites**, heavily armed foot soldiers. They wore a helmet, armour, a large round shield and carried a spear. In a dense line, the **phalanx**, they stood shoulder to shoulder. From the small city of **Plataea** about 1,000 men came to help. Athens never forgot this loyalty.

The Athenians also asked **Sparta** for help. The Spartans, however, were just celebrating a sacred festival. They wanted to set out only after the **full moon**. When they arrived at Marathon, the battle was already over. They looked at the battlefield and praised the Athenians.

The general **Miltiades** persuaded the Athenians to attack instead of waiting. He made the centre of his line weak and the two **wings** strong. The Persians pushed the centre back, but the wings enclosed them from both sides. According to the historian **Herodotus** 192 Athenians and about 6,400 Persians fell. The fallen Athenians were buried in a burial mound on the battlefield, which can still be seen today.

A later **legend** tells of a messenger who ran to Athens after the battle to announce the victory. The **marathon race**, introduced at the first modern Olympic Games in 1896, recalls this. Today the distance is exactly 42.195 kilometres. Whether the run to Athens really happened is uncertain. In Switzerland too many marathons take place every year.

gewusst: The burial mound of the Athenians at Marathon is about nine metres high.
Herodotus reports a runner named Pheidippides who ran to Sparta to fetch help.
Ten years after Marathon the Persians attacked again under Xerxes.

teile.einleitung: The Albigensian Crusade was a war in the south of France from 1209 to 1229. It was directed against the Cathars, a Christian religious community that the Catholic Church regarded as heresy.
wichtigste: The crusade was directed against the **Cathars**, also called **Albigensians**.
The occasion was the **murder of a papal legate** in 1208.
In 1209 there was a massacre of the population in the city of **Béziers**.
The military leader was **Simon de Montfort**.
In 1244 the mountain fortress of **Montségur** fell.
The **Languedoc** afterwards passed to the French crown.

abschnitte.text: In the south of France, in the **Languedoc**, many **Cathars** lived in the 12th century. They were Christians, but believed differently from the Catholic Church. They lived very simply and rejected the wealth of the Church. Because many of them lived around the city of **Albi**, they were also called **Albigensians**. The Church saw their faith as **heresy**, that is, as false teaching.

The pope sent envoys, so-called **legates**, to bring the Cathars back to the Catholic faith. In **1208**, one of these papal legates was murdered. Pope Innocent III then called for a **crusade**. For the first time, a war of this kind was directed against Christians in Europe.

In **1209**, a large army from northern France marched south. In the city of **Béziers**, the crusaders killed almost the entire population, Cathars and Catholics alike. The military command was soon taken over by the northern French nobleman **Simon de Montfort**. The war lasted many years, and many towns and castles were captured.

Many Cathars fled to castles on mountains. An important refuge was the mountain fortress of **Montségur**. It fell in **1244** after a long siege. More than 200 people who would not renounce their faith were executed afterwards. After that the Cathars gradually disappeared.

The most important political consequence was that the **Languedoc passed to the French crown**. Before that, counts of its own had ruled there, above all the counts of Toulouse. In addition, the Church set up the **Inquisition**, a court that searched for people with different beliefs. Today many castle ruins in the south of France recall this time.

gewusst: The castle ruins of the Cathars in southern France are popular destinations today and are called “Cathar castles”.
The Cathars called their most important members “the Perfect”.

teile.einleitung: The toga was the garment of Roman citizens. It consisted of a large woollen cloth that was wrapped skilfully around the body. From a toga you could tell who someone was and what office they held.
wichtigste: The toga was a long, large cloth made of wool.
Only Roman citizens were allowed to wear it.
The ordinary toga was white or the colour of undyed wool.
Underneath, people wore a tunic.
Boys and high officials wore a toga with purple stripes, the toga praetexta.
Married Roman women wore a stola instead of the toga.
The word candidate comes from the white toga of those standing for office.

abschnitte.text: The **toga** was a long, semicircular cloth of **wool**. It was several metres long. You laid it over the left shoulder, took it round the back and under the right arm, and threw it over the shoulder again. To make it hang in nice **folds**, a slave often helped with putting it on. You could not run quickly or do heavy work in a toga.

The toga was the sign of **Roman citizens**. Slaves and foreigners were not allowed to wear it. Citizens put it on for official occasions, in court or at meetings in the Forum. Under the toga they wore a **tunic**, a simple shirt-like dress. At work and at home, many people wore only the tunic, because the toga was impractical.

The ordinary toga was **white** or had the pale colour of undyed wool. Boys and high **officials** wore the **toga praetexta**. Its edge was decorated with a reddish **purple stripe**. Purple was a very expensive dye. When a boy became an adult, he received a completely white toga in a ceremony, the **toga of manhood**. A victorious general wore a magnificent embroidered toga in the triumphal procession.

abschnitte.titel: Where the word candidate comes from
abschnitte.text: Anyone who stood for an office wore an especially **white toga**. It was rubbed with chalk so that it shone. The Latin word **candidus** means “gleaming white”. Our word **candidate** comes from it. When someone stands in an election today, in the municipality or for the National Council, the Roman toga is still hidden in that word.

**Married Roman women** did not wear a toga. They wore a long dress, the **stola**. Over it they often laid a large cloak, the **palla**, which they could also pull over the head. In time the toga also became rarer among men. Later it was worn almost only on solemn occasions.

gewusst: Emperor Augustus is said to have demanded that citizens appear in the Forum only in the toga.
The Romans sometimes called themselves “the people in the toga”.

teile.einleitung: Over 4,000 years ago Mohenjo-Daro was one of the largest cities in the world. It belonged to the Indus Civilisation and was astonishingly well planned, with straight streets, baths and drains.
wichtigste: The ruins of Mohenjo-Daro lie in the south of Pakistan on the Indus.
The city was one of the largest of the Indus Civilisation.
The streets were straight and crossed at right angles.
Many houses had a bathroom, and the waste water flowed into covered drains.
The Great Bath is a water tank of brick.
The script of the Indus Civilisation has still not been deciphered.

abschnitte.text: **Mohenjo-Daro** lies in Sindh Province in the south of **Pakistan**, close to the river **Indus**. The whole **Indus Civilisation** is named after this river. The city flourished over 4,000 years ago. It was very well **planned**: the main streets ran straight and crossed at **right angles**, rather like a grid. It was built of fired **bricks** that were almost everywhere the same size. On a raised part, the citadel, stood large buildings.

Many houses had a **bathroom** and a toilet. The dirty water flowed into covered **drains** under the streets. Many cities did not have anything like this for thousands of years afterwards. Especially well known is the **Great Bath**: a tank of brick, about 12 metres long and 7 metres wide, with steps. It was sealed with **bitumen**, a kind of natural tar. Perhaps it was used for religious washing.

In Mohenjo-Daro many small **seals** of stone were found. On them animals and short inscriptions can be seen. Often they show an animal with only one horn. Researchers call it a **unicorn**, even if it may show a bull in side view. The inscriptions are very short. To this day nobody has been able to decipher the **Indus script** with certainty. So little is known about the language, the rulers and the beliefs of the people.

A small figure of **bronze** is especially well known: the **Dancing Girl**. She is only about 10 centimetres high and stands there very lively. Also well known is the stone figure of a bearded man whom people call the “Priest-King”. Excavations began in the **1920s**, after the Indian archaeologist **R. D. Banerji** recognised the importance of the mound in 1922. Since 1980 the ruins have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The name **Mohenjo-Daro** means “**Mound of the Dead**”. It comes from the Sindhi language and is much younger than the city. What the city was called in the past nobody knows. Around 1900 BC the city lost importance, and the people moved away. Why is not certainly known. Today salt in the ground and damp threaten the old brick walls.

gewusst: The bricks of the Indus cities often had the same proportions, as if there had been a standard.
Another great city of the Indus Civilisation is Harappa, after which the civilisation is also called the Harappan Civilisation.

teile.einleitung: A ziggurat is a stepped temple tower from ancient Mesopotamia. Buildings like this stood in many cities between the Euphrates and the Tigris. On top of the ziggurat stood a temple for a god.
wichtigste: Ziggurats are stepped temple towers from **Mesopotamia**.
They were built of **mud bricks**.
Sometimes **reed mats** were laid between the layers.
Baked bricks were stuck together with **bitumen**.
At the very top stood a **temple**.
The ziggurat of Ur was dedicated to the **moon god**.
The **Tower of Babel** was perhaps a ziggurat.

abschnitte.text: In Mesopotamia there was little stone and wood, but a lot of **mud**. That is why people built their ziggurats from **mud bricks**. The core often consisted of unbaked bricks. On the outside lay a layer of **baked bricks**, which were harder and more weatherproof. These were stuck together with **bitumen**, a black, sticky substance from the ground.

In some ziggurats, the builders laid **reed mats** between the layers of mud bricks. The reeds grew in the marshes by the rivers. The mats helped to keep the heavy building stable. In addition, moisture could escape better this way.

A ziggurat had several steps that became smaller towards the top. You went up **by broad staircases**. **At the very top** stood a **temple**. It was dedicated to a god of the city. The ziggurat of **Ur**, for example, was dedicated to the **moon god**. Probably only priests were allowed to climb all the way to the top.

Ziggurats are often compared with the **pyramids** in Egypt, because both are huge buildings with sloping sides. But there are differences. Pyramids were tombs for kings. Ziggurats were not tombs, but the base for a temple. In addition, ziggurats have flat steps and no point.

The Bible tells of the **Tower of Babel**. Many researchers think that the great ziggurat of **Babylon** was the model for this story. Today, of most ziggurats **only ruins** remain. Wind and rain have worn away the mud bricks over thousands of years.

gewusst: The ziggurat of Babylon was called Etemenanki, which roughly means “house of the foundation of heaven and earth”.
One of the best-preserved ziggurats is not in Iraq, but at Chogha Zanbil in present-day Iran.

teile.einleitung: The Nazca Lines are huge pictures and lines in the ground of a desert in Peru. They are about 2,000 years old and so large that they are best seen from the air.
wichtigste: The Nazca Lines lie in a desert in the south of Peru.
They show animals, plants, straight lines and geometric shapes.
Famous is the hummingbird, which is almost a hundred metres long.
People cleared away dark stones, and lighter ground came to light beneath.
Because it hardly rains, the lines survived.
The German researcher Maria Reiche studied them all her life.

abschnitte.text: The **Nazca Lines** lie on a dry plateau in the south of **Peru**, between the towns of Nazca and Palpa. They are huge **drawings on the ground**: animals, plants, dead-straight lines, triangles and spirals. They were made by the **Nazca culture** about **2,000 years ago**, roughly at the time of the ancient Romans. Since 1994 they have been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

One of the best-known pictures is the **hummingbird**. It is almost a hundred metres long. Besides it there is a **monkey** with a curled tail, a **spider**, a condor and many more figures. The pictures mostly consist of a single line that is never interrupted. Because they are so large, they can hardly be recognised from the ground. They are best seen **from the air**, for example from a small aircraft or from observation towers.

The ground of the desert is covered with **dark stones**. Beneath lies **lighter soil**. People cleared the dark stones aside, and so light lines arose. To get straight lines and exact shapes they probably used stakes and cords. Why the lines were made is not certain. Researchers think of religious ceremonies, of paths for processions or of requests for water.

The desert of Nazca is one of the **driest places on Earth**. It **hardly rains**, and the wind at ground level is mostly weak. So the lines were not washed away or blown away and survived for almost 2,000 years. Today they are in danger all the same, for example from vehicles driving across the desert. That is why it is forbidden to enter the areas without permission.

The German researcher **Maria Reiche** came from Dresden and moved to Peru. She surveyed the lines for **decades**, often alone and with simple means such as brooms and a measuring tape. She also campaigned for their **protection** when people wanted to lay out fields and roads in the area. In Peru she is still greatly revered. She lived until a great age near the lines.

gewusst: Many Nazca pictures consist of a single line that crosses itself nowhere.
Maria Reiche swept lines clear with brooms so that she could survey them better.

teile.einleitung: Nefertiti was the chief wife of the Egyptian king Akhenaten and lived in the 14th century BC. She is world famous for her painted bust, which today stands in Berlin.
wichtigste: Nefertiti was the chief wife of the pharaoh Akhenaten.
Her name means “The Beautiful One Has Come”.
She lived in the 14th century BC in the city of Amarna.
Her bust was found in 1912 in an excavation under Ludwig Borchardt.
Today the bust stands in the Neues Museum in Berlin.

abschnitte.text: **Nefertiti** was the **chief wife** of the pharaoh **Akhenaten** in the New Kingdom. Her name means “**The Beautiful One Has Come**”. Akhenaten worshipped almost only the sun god **Aten** and founded the new capital **Amarna**. In many pictures of this time Nefertiti can be seen beside the king, often just as large as he. That shows how important she was. What happened to her later is not certainly known.

The German archaeologist **Ludwig Borchardt** led excavations at **Amarna**. There his team found the bust of Nefertiti on **6 December 1912** in the workshop of the sculptor **Thutmose**. It is made of limestone, covered with stucco and painted in colour. Nefertiti wears a tall blue crown. One eye is inlaid, and the other lacks its inlay. Probably the bust was a model for other works of art.

The bust came to **Berlin** and today stands in the **Neues Museum** on Museum Island. It is among the best-known works of art in the world, and very many people visit it every year. Egypt has already several times demanded the **return** of the bust. Germany points out that the find was divided at the time according to the rules then in force. The question is still discussed today.

gewusst: On the bust of Nefertiti, the inlay is missing in one eye.
The bust was found in the workshop of a sculptor, not in a tomb.

teile.einleitung: The Kingdom of Kush was a powerful kingdom in Africa, south of ancient Egypt. It lay in Nubia on the middle Nile, in the area of present-day Sudan. For many centuries Kush was a neighbour, an opponent and at times even a ruler of Egypt.
wichtigste: Kush lay in Nubia on the Nile, mostly in present-day Sudan.
Important centres were, one after another, Kerma, Napata and Meroe.
In the 8th and 7th centuries BC kings from Kush ruled over Egypt as pharaohs.
They formed the 25th Dynasty, which is often called the “black pharaohs”.
In Sudan stand over 200 pyramids, more than in the whole of Egypt.
Meroe was an important centre of iron production.
Powerful queens bore the title Kandake.

abschnitte.text: Already in the 2nd millennium BC a great culture flourished at **Kerma** by the third cataract of the Nile. A cataract is a rapid where the Nile flows over rocks. The rulers of Kerma were strong opponents of the Egyptian Middle Kingdom. From them come huge mud-brick buildings that are called **deffufa**. Later Egypt conquered the area and ruled over Nubia for a long time.

From the city of **Napata** Kush became strong again. Around 730 BC King **Piye** marched downriver and conquered Egypt. He had his victory recorded on a great stele, an inscribed stone slab. His successors ruled as the **25th Dynasty** over the whole of Egypt. They revered the Egyptian gods and built temples. In the 7th century BC they were driven back south by the Assyrians.

The kings of Kush had themselves buried in **pyramids**. In Sudan there are over 200 of them, more than in Egypt. They are smaller than the pyramids of Giza and have steeper sides. Many stand in groups at Napata and Meroe. The pyramids of Meroe are today part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

In the late period **Meroe** became the capital, from about the 4th or 3rd century BC. The city lay on the Nile north-east of present-day Khartoum. At Meroe great heaps of **iron slag** were found, that is, waste from iron production. The city was therefore an important centre of **iron smelting** in Africa. Kush traded in gold, ivory and other valuable goods.

Powerful queens and queen mothers bore the title **Kandake**. The Kandake **Amanirenas** waged war against the Romans. In Meroe a script of its own came into being, the **Meroitic script**. Since about 1909 its signs can be read. But because the language is hardly related to any known language, to this day only a few words are understood.

gewusst: Kush is one of the oldest kingdoms of Africa and lasted well over a thousand years.
The word Kandake later became the woman's name Candace.
One can read Meroitic texts aloud without knowing what they mean.

teile.einleitung: A column order is a fixed building style for columns and the parts above them. The ancient Greeks knew three main kinds: the Doric, the Ionic and the Corinthian column. They can be recognised above all by their upper end.
wichtigste: The Greeks had three column orders: Doric, Ionic and Corinthian.
The upper end of a column is called the capital.
The Doric column is plain and sturdy.
The Ionic column has two scrolls, the volutes.
The Corinthian column is decorated with acanthus leaves.
Vertical grooves on the column are called flutes.
On a temple the columns carry the heavy roof.

abschnitte.text: In Greek **temples** the columns often stand around the whole building. They carry the heavy **roof** with its stone beams. A column usually consists of three parts: at the bottom the foot, the **base**, in the middle the long **shaft** and at the top the **capital**. From the capital one recognises which order the column belongs to. Many columns have vertical grooves, the **flutes**.

The **Doric** column is the plainest. It is sturdy and stands without a foot of its own directly on the floor of the temple. Its capital consists only of a round, cushion-shaped **echinus** and a square **slab** on top. The **Parthenon** on the Acropolis in Athens has Doric columns all round the outside. That suits its sturdy, clear appearance.

The **Ionic** column is recognised by the two snail-shaped rolls on the capital, the **volutes**. It is slimmer than the Doric one and stands on a base. This order arose in **Ionia**, on the west coast of present-day Turkey. In Athens, for example, the **Erechtheion** on the Acropolis has Ionic columns.

The **Corinthian** column is the most magnificent. Its capital is decorated with the leaves of a plant called **acanthus**. It is as slim as the Ionic column. The Romans liked the Corinthian column especially and used it on many temples. They also added two forms of their own to the Greek orders, the **Tuscan** and the **Composite order**.

The column orders became very popular again in the **Renaissance** and in the 19th century. Many museums, banks, theatres and government buildings in Europe and America have columns on the Greek model. In Swiss towns too one finds such façades. Whoever looks at the capitals can often quickly say whether the column is Doric, Ionic or Corinthian.

gewusst: Some buildings combine the orders: Doric at the bottom, Ionic above and Corinthian right at the top, as at the Colosseum in Rome.
Instead of columns, at the Erechtheion in Athens figures of women carry the roof of a porch, and they are called caryatids.

teile.einleitung: In ancient Egypt only a few people could read and write. Scribes therefore had a very important profession. They wrote lists, letters and texts for the pharaoh, for temples and for the administration.
wichtigste: Only a few people in ancient Egypt could read and write.
A scribe always had a writing palette with him.
Scribes mostly used black and red ink.
For practice people wrote on pieces of pottery, because papyrus was expensive.
Many scribes sat cross-legged while working.
The name of a pharaoh was written in an oval, the cartouche.
Scribes noted, for example, how much grain was harvested.

abschnitte.text: A scribe always had a **writing palette** with him. This was a narrow board with hollows for the ink. In a slot were the **writing reeds** with which one wrote. **Black** ink was made from soot, **red** ink from red ochre. With red one picked out headings, for example.

Learning to write took many years. **Papyrus** was expensive, so people practised on other things. They wrote on **potsherds**, that is, pieces of broken vessels. Flat pieces of limestone were also well suited. Many such practice pieces have been found to this day.

Many statues show scribes sitting on the ground with crossed legs. Their kilt was stretched tight over the knees. On it they laid the papyrus as on a small table. So they could work anywhere, even in a field or in a camp.

The Egyptian **picture writing**, the hieroglyphs, consists of many small pictures. One could write it in **several directions**: from right to left, from left to right or from top to bottom. The animals and people in the script always face the beginning of the line. The name of the pharaoh was framed with an oval, the **cartouche**. So one recognised it at once in the text.

Scribes kept **lists** of harvests, taxes and supplies. So the pharaoh knew how much **grain** there was in the land. They also wrote down letters, contracts and prayers. Because only a few people could write, scribes were very **highly regarded**. Many parents wished that their son would become a scribe.

gewusst: The Egyptians used several hundred different hieroglyphs.
The word paper comes from the word papyrus.
Some scribes were buried with their writing palette.

teile.einleitung: Scribes were among the most important specialists of the state in ancient Egypt. Without them the administration of harvests, taxes and temples would not have worked. Statues, tools and teaching texts show how highly regarded this profession was.
wichtigste: The famous statue “The Seated Scribe” stands in the Louvre in Paris.
The patron god of scribes was Thoth, a god with the head of an ibis.
The most important working tool was the writing palette.
In the House of Life at temples texts were copied and scribes trained.
In daily life scribes used the fast script hieratic.
Scribes recorded harvests, taxes, cattle and supplies.
The Instruction of Kheti praises the profession of scribe.

abschnitte.text: One of the most famous figures of Egypt is **“The Seated Scribe”**. The painted limestone figure comes from **Saqqara** and from the time of the **Old Kingdom**. It shows a scribe sitting cross-legged with a papyrus roll on his knees. His eyes are inlaid with stone and look very lifelike. Today the statue stands in the **Louvre** in Paris.

The patron god of scribes was held to be **Thoth**. He was often shown with the head of an **ibis**, a bird with a long, curved beak. Thoth was the god of wisdom, of the moon and of writing. Before work scribes offered him a drop of water from their water pot. Sometimes Thoth was also shown as a baboon.

The most important working tool was the **writing palette**, an oblong wooden case. It had hollows for black and red paint and a compartment for the rushes with which one wrote. Often the palette was placed in the tomb as a sign of the profession. For letters, lists and accounts scribes did not use hieroglyphs. They wrote **hieratic**, a simplified and flowing form of picture writing.

At great temples there was a scriptorium, the **House of Life**, in Egyptian **Per-Ankh**. There sacred and scientific texts were copied and kept. It was at once a kind of **library** and **school**. Young scribes learned by copying old texts again and again. In this way much knowledge was preserved over centuries.

Scribes recorded **levies**, counted cattle and supplies and kept lists of the harvests. Without them the state would not have worked. A well-known teaching text is the **Instruction of Kheti**. In it a father advises his son to become a scribe. Other professions he describes as dirty and hard, the profession of scribe by contrast as pleasant and respected.

gewusst: Some high officials had themselves proudly portrayed as scribes, although they held much more important offices.
One reason why we know so much about Egypt today is the many surviving texts of the scribes.
Only in 1822 did Jean-François Champollion succeed in deciphering the hieroglyphs again.

teile.einleitung: A trireme was a fast warship of the ancient Greeks. It was driven mainly by rowers who sat in three rows one above another. With its triremes, Athens became the greatest sea power in Greece.
wichtigste: The trireme was a Greek warship with oars.
The rowers sat in three rows one above another.
A trireme had about 170 rowers.
At the front, just under the water, it had a bronze ram.
In a good wind it used sails, but in battle only oars.
It was built mainly of wood.
In Athens, the rowers were mostly free, poorer citizens who were paid a wage.

abschnitte.text: The name **trireme** comes from the Greek word for **three**. This is because the rowers sat in **three rows** one above another. Each rower worked his own oar. A trireme had about **170 rowers**. In addition there were sailors, some soldiers, archers and the captain. A musician with a flute often kept the **beat**, so that everyone rowed at the same time.

Triremes were built mainly of **wood**. They were long and narrow and therefore **light and fast**. In a good wind the trireme could set **sails**. In battle, however, it moved with oars only, because it could steer and accelerate better that way. Because the ships were so light, the crews often pulled them ashore at night.

At the front, just below the waterline, the trireme had a **ram** made of **bronze**. This was its most important weapon. The rowers drove at an enemy ship with full force. The ram punched a **hole** in its hull, so that water poured in. This took a lot of skill, because the trireme's own ship then had to pull free again quickly.

In the 5th century BC, **Athens** built a large fleet of triremes. The politician **Themistocles** pushed for this. In **480 BC**, the Greeks defeated the Persian fleet near the island of **Salamis**. After that, Athens was the strongest **sea power** in Greece. The ships were mostly rowed by **free, poorer citizens**, who received a wage for it.

Because the fleet was so important, the poor citizens who served as rowers also became more important. Many historians see this as one reason why they were allowed more say in the **democracy** of Athens. Rich citizens, on the other hand, had to equip and maintain a trireme. This duty was called the **trierarchy**. In this way the poor and the rich contributed to the fleet in different ways.

gewusst: In the 1980s, a trireme was rebuilt in Greece on an ancient model, and it is called “Olympias”.
The Romans took over this type of ship and called it a trireme.

teile.einleitung: The Roman Republic was the form of state of Rome after the Romans had driven out their last king. Instead of a king, two consuls elected every year now governed together with the Senate. In this time Rome grew from a small city into the mistress of the whole Mediterranean region.
wichtigste: According to tradition Rome became a republic in 509 BC.
At the head stood two consuls at the same time.
The consuls were each elected for one year.
The Senate was an assembly of experienced men with great influence.
The common people were called plebeians, the nobility patricians.
The tribune of the people protected the plebeians from the arbitrary actions of officials.
In three Punic Wars Rome fought against Carthage.
The Carthaginian general Hannibal crossed the Alps with elephants.

abschnitte.text: According to tradition the Romans drove out their last king, Tarquinius Superbus, in **509 BC**. After that they never wanted to have a king again. They founded a **republic**, a word that comes from the Latin “res publica” and means “the public matter”. The abbreviation SPQR stood for “the Senate and People of Rome”.
