At the head stood two **consuls**, who were each elected for one year. Because there were two, one could keep a check on the other. The **Senate**, an assembly of experienced men and former officials, advised them and had great influence. In great emergency a **dictator** with special powers could be appointed for at most six months.

Roman society was divided into the noble **patricians** and the common people, the **plebeians**. At first only the patricians had access to the high offices. In long struggles the plebeians won more rights, for example the office of **tribune of the people**, who protected them from the arbitrary actions of officials. Around 450 BC the laws were written down on twelve tablets so that everyone could know them.

Between 264 and 146 BC Rome fought three **Punic Wars** against Carthage in North Africa. In the second war the Carthaginian general **Hannibal** marched in 218 BC with an army and war elephants over the Alps into Italy. He defeated the Romans several times, for example in 216 BC at Cannae. In the end, however, Rome won, and in 146 BC Carthage was destroyed.

Through the conquests Rome became rich, but rich and poor drifted apart, and civil wars broke out. The general **Gaius Julius Caesar** conquered Gaul and afterwards seized power in Rome. In 44 BC he was murdered by senators who wanted to save the Republic. His adopted son Augustus became the first emperor in 27 BC, and with that the Republic ended.

The Roman Republic influenced many later states. Terms such as **senate**, republic or consul are still used today. The idea that offices are given for a limited time and that power is shared out also comes partly from here. Switzerland too is a republic, that is, a state without a king.

begriffe.erklaerung: A state without a king in which elected persons govern for a limited time.
One of the two highest officials of the Roman Republic.
An assembly of experienced men that strongly influenced politics.
The common people in ancient Rome.
An official who protected the plebeians and could block laws.

gewusst: The saying “to cross the Rubicon” for a decision with no way back goes back to Caesar, who crossed this river with his army in 49 BC.
Hannibal's route over the Alps is disputed to this day, and researchers discuss several passes.

teile.einleitung: A mummy is a dead person whose body was preserved so that it does not decay. Most famous are the mummies of ancient Egypt, which were carefully prepared thousands of years ago. The Egyptians believed that the body must be preserved for life after death.
wichtigste: A mummy is a preserved dead person.
The ancient Egyptians mummified the dead for life after death.
The body was dried with natron and wrapped in linen bandages.
The heart usually stayed in the body, other organs went into special jars.
Making a mummy took about 70 days.
The god Anubis with the jackal head protected the dead.
Animals such as cats were also mummified.

abschnitte.text: Normally a body decays after death. With a **mummy**, however, skin, hair and bones are preserved for a very long time. This can happen artificially, as in Egypt, or naturally, for example in ice, desert sand or bogs. A well-known example of a natural mummy is **Ötzi**, the Iceman, who died in the Alps over 5,000 years ago.

First the embalmers removed the brain, often through the nose, and most of the inner organs. They usually left the **heart** in the body, because people believed that the mind and the feelings are located there. Stomach, intestines, liver and lungs went into special jars, the **canopic jars**. After that the body was dried for about 40 days with **natron**, a salt-like mineral.

After drying, the body was anointed with oils and resins. Then it was wrapped in many metres of **linen bandages**, with small protective amulets laid between them. In all this took about 70 days. Distinguished dead were placed in a painted wooden coffin and then often in a large stone coffin, the **sarcophagus**.

The Egyptians believed that the soul must find the body again after death. The god **Anubis** with the jackal head was regarded as protector of the dead and of embalming. The dead were given the **Book of the Dead**, a collection of spells on papyrus that were meant to help in the afterlife. Food, furniture and jewellery were also laid in the tomb.

In ancient Egypt **animals** were also mummified, for example cats, crocodiles, ibises and falcons. Many of them were offerings to gods who were imagined in animal form. The cat, for example, was sacred to the goddess Bastet. Researchers have found millions of such animal mummies.

Today experts examine mummies with **X-rays** and computed tomography, without unwrapping them. In this way they learn how old the people became, what diseases they had and what they ate. DNA from mummies can sometimes also be studied. There are mummies in other parts of the world too, for example in South America among the Inca.

begriffe.erklaerung: Preserving a dead body.
A salt-like mineral that draws the water out of the body.
A jar in which the removed organs were kept.
A large, often decorated stone coffin.
Spells on papyrus that were meant to help the dead in the afterlife.

gewusst: The ancient Egyptians thought the brain unimportant, so they mostly threw it away during mummification.
Ötzi, the famous glacier mummy from the Alps, is over 5,000 years old and was found in 1991 in the Ötztal Alps.

teile.einleitung: Alcuin was an English scholar and teacher. He worked at the court of Charlemagne and helped to improve education and writing in the Frankish Empire.
wichtigste: Alcuin first headed the famous cathedral school of York in England.
Charlemagne met him in Italy in 781 and brought him to his court.
From 796 Alcuin was abbot of the monastery of Saint-Martin in Tours.
He revised the Latin Bible, the Vulgate.
In the circle of scholars at court, Charlemagne was called “David” and Alcuin called himself “Flaccus”.
Alcuin died in Tours in 804.

abschnitte.text: Alcuin was born in England around the year 735. He attended the **cathedral school of York**, which was among the best schools in Europe, and later became its head. There was a large library there with many old books. In 781, Alcuin met **Charlemagne** in Italy. The king asked him to come to his court.

Charlemagne wanted more people in the Frankish Empire to learn to read and write. Alcuin became one of his most important **advisers** and ran the **court school**. He taught Charlemagne himself and his family. At court, the scholars gave themselves names from the Bible and antiquity. Charlemagne was called after the biblical king **David**, and Alcuin called himself **Flaccus**.

In 796, Alcuin became **abbot** of the monastery of **Saint-Martin in Tours**. There he built up an important **writing school**. Monks there copied many books carefully by hand. In this way many texts from antiquity were also preserved. Alcuin died in Tours in 804.

Because the Bible was copied by hand again and again, many mistakes had crept in. Alcuin revised the Latin Bible, the **Vulgate**, so that it had a uniform wording. This version is called the **Alcuin Bible**. It was copied many times in Tours and spread throughout the empire.

gewusst: Alcuin wrote many letters, of which over 200 survive.
The educational movement under Charlemagne is today called the “Carolingian Renaissance”.

teile.einleitung: The Punic Wars were three wars between Rome and Carthage. With pauses they lasted from 264 to 146 BC. At the end Carthage was destroyed and Rome was the strongest power in the Mediterranean.
wichtigste: “Punic” comes from the Latin name for the Phoenicians, who had founded Carthage.
The First Punic War began in 264 BC and was mainly about Sicily.
With the boarding bridge Corvus, Roman ships held enemy ships fast.
In 241 BC the First War ended with the naval battle at the Aegates Islands.
The Second Punic War is also called the Hannibalic War.
After the peace of 201 Carthage was no longer allowed to wage war without Rome's permission.
In 146 BC Carthage and also the Greek city of Corinth were destroyed.

abschnitte.text: **Carthage** was a rich trading city in present-day **Tunisia**. It had been founded by the **Phoenicians**. The Romans called the Phoenicians “Poeni”, which is where the word **Punic** comes from. Carthage had a strong fleet and controlled many coasts. As Rome became ever more powerful, the two cities came into conflict.

The First Punic War began in **264 BC**. It was mainly about the island of **Sicily**. At first Rome had hardly any experience at sea. So the Romans invented the **Corvus**, a boarding bridge with an iron hook. With it they held enemy ships fast and fought as if on land. In **241** Rome won the naval battle **at the Aegates Islands**, and Sicily became Roman.

The **Second Punic War** began in 218 BC and is also called the **Hannibalic War**. The Carthaginian general **Hannibal** marched with an army and war elephants over the **Alps** into Italy. He defeated the Romans several times, for example at Cannae. The Roman general **Fabius Maximus** avoided great battles and slowly weakened Hannibal. For this he received the epithet **Cunctator, the Delayer**.

Finally the Roman **Scipio** attacked Carthage in Africa. In 202 BC he defeated Hannibal at Zama. In the **peace of 201** Carthage had to hand over almost all its ships and pay a great deal of money. Above all it was **no longer allowed to wage war without Rome's permission**. With that Carthage was no longer a great power.

Nevertheless many Romans continued to fear Carthage. In the **Third Punic War** the Romans besieged the city for three years. In **146 BC** Carthage was captured and destroyed. In the same year the general **Lucius Mummius** had the city of **Corinth** destroyed in Greece. Rome was now the dominant power in the whole Mediterranean.

gewusst: Over which Alpine pass Hannibal actually crossed is still not certain to this day.
Most of Hannibal's elephants did not survive the hard winter after the crossing of the Alps.

teile.einleitung: Pegasus is a winged horse from Greek legend. He is among the best-known mythical creatures of all. With the hero Bellerophon he had a great adventure.
wichtigste: Pegasus, in Greek Pegasos, is a horse with wings.
According to the legend he sprang from Medusa when the hero Perseus defeated her.
The hero Bellerophon tamed him with a golden bridle.
Together they defeated the monster Chimera.
Where Pegasus stamped his hoof on a mountain, a spring arose.
In the end Pegasus became a constellation.

abschnitte.text: In Greek legend **Pegasus** is a white horse with great **wings**. He could fly faster than any bird. According to the legend he arose from the monster **Medusa**. When the hero **Perseus** cut off her head, Pegasus sprang out of her. His father was held to be the sea god **Poseidon**.

For a long time nobody could catch Pegasus. The young hero **Bellerophon** wanted at all costs to ride him. The goddess **Athena** gave him a **golden bridle**. With it he could tame the wild horse. From then on the two flew through the air together.

Bellerophon was given a dangerous task: he was to defeat the **Chimera**. This monster had the head of a lion, the body of a goat and the tail of a snake and breathed fire. On the back of Pegasus Bellerophon attacked from the air. In this way he could defeat the monster without coming too close to it.

After many victories Bellerophon became **overconfident**. He wanted to fly with Pegasus to **Olympus**, the mountain of the gods. But no human was allowed to do that. Zeus sent a gadfly that stung Pegasus. The horse reared up, and Bellerophon fell to the earth. So the legend warns against thinking oneself as powerful as the gods.

Once Pegasus stamped his **hoof** on a mountain. At this spot a **spring** gushed forth. Pegasus himself was allowed to stay on Olympus and there carried the thunderbolts of Zeus. In the end he was set in the sky as a **constellation**. The constellation Pegasus can be seen well in the evening sky in autumn.

gewusst: Four bright stars in the constellation Pegasus form a large square that is called the “Square of Pegasus”.
Many companies and clubs use a winged horse as their symbol.

teile.einleitung: Qin Shihuangdi was the first emperor of China. In 221 BC he united the Chinese states into one empire. He is famous for his strict rules and his huge tomb.
wichtigste: Qin Shihuangdi was the first emperor of China.
In 221 BC he unified China and called himself emperor.
The title “Shihuangdi” means roughly “First Emperor”.
He had script, coins and measures made the same throughout the empire.
He had many books burned because he would not tolerate other opinions.
He searched for a means of eternal life and had a huge tomb built.
His imperial dynasty lasted only about 15 years.

abschnitte.text: About 2,200 years ago China was divided into several states that often waged war. The king of the state of **Qin** conquered all the other states. By **221 BC** he had **united the whole of China**. He called himself **Qin Shihuangdi**. The title means roughly **First Emperor**. The name **China** probably comes from the kingdom of **Qin**.

Formerly every state had its own rules. So Qin Shihuangdi had the **script**, the **coins** and the **measures** made the same throughout the empire. In this way officials and merchants could calculate and write in the same way everywhere. He also had roads built and old walls in the north joined up. That helped to hold the great empire together.

Qin Shihuangdi ruled very **strictly**. Anyone who broke the laws was harshly punished. He tolerated no **other opinions**. So he had **many books burned**, especially those about old teachings and earlier times. Scholars who criticised him were persecuted.

The emperor was afraid of death. He searched for a **means of eternal life** and sent people out to find it. At the same time he had a **huge tomb** built for the time after his death. Very many people worked on it for many years. In **1974** farmers near the city of Xi'an found parts of the **Terracotta Army**, thousands of warriors made of clay that guard his tomb.

Qin Shihuangdi died in 210 BC. His successors could not hold the empire together. Soon after his death there were uprisings everywhere. The **imperial dynasty** he had founded therefore lasted **only about 15 years**. But the idea of a united China with an emperor endured for over 2,000 years.

gewusst: The warriors of the Terracotta Army were once painted in bright colours.
The actual burial mound of the emperor has still not been opened to this day.

teile.einleitung: Teotihuacan is a huge ruined city in the Valley of Mexico. Around AD 450 it was one of the biggest cities in the world. It is famous for its mighty pyramids and the long Avenue of the Dead.
wichtigste: Teotihuacan lies about 40 kilometres north-east of Mexico City.
The Aztecs gave it its name centuries later.
The biggest pyramid is the Pyramid of the Sun, about 65 metres high.
The main axis is called the Avenue of the Dead.
Around AD 450, about 100,000 or more people lived there.
In the 6th century, large parts of the centre burnt down.
Since 1987, Teotihuacan has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.titel: A city in a high valley
abschnitte.text: Teotihuacan lies in the **Valley of Mexico**, about **40 kilometres** north-east of the present-day capital, Mexico City. The city arose in the centuries around the birth of Christ and grew quickly. What its inhabitants called it themselves and which language they spoke is **unknown**. The city was carefully planned: streets and buildings follow a fixed grid.

The biggest pyramid is the **Pyramid of the Sun**. It is about **65 metres** high and is one of the biggest pyramids in the Americas. At the northern end of the main axis stands the somewhat smaller **Pyramid of the Moon**. Unlike the Egyptian pyramids, these buildings had a flat platform at the top with a **temple**. Another important building is the temple of the **Feathered Serpent**.

A broad main axis several kilometres long leads through the city. It is called the **Avenue of the Dead**, in Spanish Calzada de los Muertos. It was named by the **Aztecs**, who came to the abandoned city many centuries later. They thought the buildings at the edge were tombs. The name Teotihuacan also comes from them, from the **Nahuatl** language. It is often interpreted as “the place where one becomes a god”.

At its height around **AD 450**, an estimated **100,000 to 125,000** people lived in Teotihuacan. That made it one of the biggest cities in the world at the time. Many people lived in large stone housing compounds. The city traded with far-away regions. Its influence reached as far as the **Maya**: inscriptions report that in AD 378 the general Siyaj K'ak' arrived in the Maya city of **Tikal**. Soon afterwards, a new line of rulers linked to Teotihuacan came to power there.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the golden age
abschnitte.text: In the **6th century**, mainly temples and palaces along the Avenue of the Dead burnt down. Archaeologists have found the traces of these **fires**. Whether an uprising by the city's own inhabitants or an attack from outside lay behind it is **disputed**. After that, the city lost its importance. Since **1987**, Teotihuacan has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and is today one of the most visited excavation sites in Mexico.

gewusst: When the Aztecs discovered the city, it had already been abandoned for centuries.
From the Pyramid of the Sun you have a wide view over the whole Avenue of the Dead.

teile.einleitung: The Senate in ancient Rome was an assembly of important and experienced men. They advised on policy and had great influence over many centuries. The abbreviation SPQR shows how important the Senate was for Rome.
wichtigste: The word senate comes from the Latin “senex”, old man.
SPQR means “Senatus Populusque Romanus”, the Senate and People of Rome.
Senators wore a toga and a tunic with a broad purple stripe.
The Senate mostly met in the Curia in the Roman Forum.
One mostly remained a senator for life.
According to legend the first Senate under Romulus had 100 members.
Sulla enlarged the Senate around 81 BC to about 600 members.

abschnitte.text: The word **senate** comes from the Latin **“senex”**, which means old man. For in the Senate sat mainly older, experienced men. According to legend King Romulus already chose 100 men for the first Senate. In the Republic the Senate consisted mainly of former office holders. Whoever had once been admitted mostly remained a senator until death.

The Senate advised on war and peace, money and relations with other peoples. Formally it gave only advice, but this was almost always followed. The highest officials were the two **consuls**, who were newly elected every year. They held the **“imperium”**, the supreme power of command, and led the army in war. The abbreviation **SPQR** for “the Senate and People of Rome” appeared on standards and buildings.

On official occasions senators wore the **toga**, a large cloth of wool. Beneath it they wore a tunic with a broad **purple stripe**. Purple was a very expensive colour that was obtained from sea snails. So everyone saw at once that someone belonged to the Senate. Special shoes also showed the rank of a senator.

Mostly the Senate met in the **Curia** in the **Roman Forum**. The building that stands there today was rebuilt in the imperial period. It is preserved to this day and can be visited. Sometimes, however, the Senate also met in temples. The sessions took place with the doors open.

abschnitte.titel: From republican council to imperial council
abschnitte.text: For a long time the Senate had about **300** members. The dictator **Sulla** doubled the number around 81 BC to about **600**. In the imperial period the Senate lost much power, for now the emperor decided. Nevertheless a seat in the Senate remained a great honour. Many countries still call a chamber of their parliament a senate today. In Switzerland the corresponding chamber is called the **Council of States**.

gewusst: The abbreviation SPQR still appears today on drain covers in Rome.
Julius Caesar was murdered in 44 BC during a session of the Senate.
The USA too has a senate, which is named after the Roman model.

teile.einleitung: Trajan was a Roman emperor from AD 98 to 117. Under him the Roman Empire reached its greatest extent. He was considered such a good ruler that the Senate called him the “best ruler”.
wichtigste: Trajan came from Italica in the province of Hispania.
He was the first Roman emperor who did not come from Italy.
Emperor Nerva adopted him in 97, and from 98 he ruled himself.
In two wars he conquered Dacia in present-day Romania.
The Senate gave him the title Optimus Princeps, “best ruler”.
He is counted among the adoptive emperors.
His successor in 117 was Hadrian.

abschnitte.text: Trajan was born in **Italica**, a Roman city near present-day **Seville** in Spain. This made him the **first Roman emperor** who did not come from Italy. He was a respected **general**. The old emperor **Nerva** needed the support of the army and therefore adopted him in **97**. After Nerva's death in **98**, Trajan took over the rule.

Trajan is counted among the **adoptive emperors**. These emperors usually did not choose their successor by descent. Instead they **adopted** a capable man. Trajan too is said to have adopted his relative **Hadrian** shortly before his death in **117**. The time of the adoptive emperors is regarded as a calm and successful period of the Roman Empire.

Trajan led two wars against King **Decebalus** of the **Dacians**, in the years **101 to 102** and **105 to 106**. After that, **Dacia** in present-day **Romania** became a Roman province. The land was rich in **gold**. For the war, the architect **Apollodorus of Damascus** built a great stone bridge over the **Danube**. It was over a kilometre long. Later Trajan also conquered areas in the east, and the empire became bigger than ever before.

In Rome, Trajan had a huge **forum** built with markets, libraries and a great hall, also designed by Apollodorus. **Trajan's Column** still stands there today. A band of pictures winds like a spiral around the column and tells of the **Dacian Wars**. At the top there originally stood a statue of the emperor. It was lost in the Middle Ages. In **1587**, Pope Sixtus V had a figure of the **Apostle Peter** put up.

The **Senate** gave Trajan the honorary title **Optimus Princeps**, “best ruler”. He was regarded as just and respected the Senate. For a long time afterwards, later emperors were greeted with the wish that they be **luckier than Augustus and better than Trajan**. Letters from his time with the governor **Pliny** also survive, which show how an emperor administered the provinces.

gewusst: Under Trajan the Roman Empire reached its greatest extent, from present-day Great Britain to Mesopotamia.
The pictures on Trajan's Column show about 2500 figures and are an important source on the Roman army.

teile.einleitung: The Rubicon is a small river in northern Italy. It became famous because Julius Caesar crossed it with soldiers in 49 BC. With that a civil war began, and to this day people know the expression “to cross the Rubicon”.
wichtigste: The Rubicon is a small river that flows into the Adriatic north of Rimini.
It formed the boundary between the province of Cisalpine Gaul and Italy.
A governor was not allowed to march into Italy with his army.
Caesar crossed the river in 49 BC with only one legion.
After that the civil war against Pompey began.
“To cross the Rubicon” means to take a decision that cannot be undone.

abschnitte.text: The **Rubicon** flows in the north-east of Italy and enters the **Adriatic** north of Rimini. In the time of the Roman Republic it was an important boundary. To the north lay the province of **Cisalpine Gaul**, which Caesar administered as governor. To the south began the Roman heartland of **Italy**. Where exactly the ancient Rubicon flowed was long disputed.

A governor was the administrator of a province and led an army there. At the boundary of his province, however, he had to leave the troops behind. Whoever marched into Italy under arms broke the law. He thereby practically declared **war** on the state. In this way people wanted to prevent a general from seizing power in Rome by force.

Caesar had fallen out with the **Senate** and with his former ally **Pompey**. He was supposed to give up his army and come to Rome as a private citizen. In January 49 BC he decided otherwise. With only one legion, the 13th, he crossed the Rubicon. According to the writer Suetonius he said as he did so “Alea iacta est”, which means “The die is cast”.

With the step across the river a **civil war** began. Pompey and many senators fled from Italy to Greece. In 48 BC Caesar defeated Pompey at the battle of **Pharsalus**. Pompey fled to Egypt and was murdered there. Caesar then became sole ruler until he himself was murdered in 44 BC.

gewusst: The expression “to cross the Rubicon” exists in many languages.
The present-day river that is regarded as the Rubicon is so small that one could easily overlook it.
The phrase “The die is cast” is also a well-known saying to this day.

teile.einleitung: Theodosius I was a Roman emperor in the 4th century AD. Under him, Christianity became the binding religion in the Roman Empire. He was the last emperor to rule over the whole empire.
wichtigste: Theodosius came from Hispania and ruled from 379.
With the Edict of Thessalonica in 380, he made Christianity in effect the state religion.
In 381 he summoned the First Council of Constantinople.
In 390, Bishop Ambrose of Milan forced him to do public penance.
In 391 and 392, his laws banned pagan sacrifices and cults.
In 394 he defeated Eugenius at the Battle of the Frigidus.
After his death in 395, the empire was divided between his two sons.

abschnitte.text: Theodosius came from **Hispania**, present-day Spain. In **379** he became emperor in the east of the empire. Shortly before, the **Goths** had heavily defeated a Roman army at Adrianople. Theodosius made a treaty with them and settled them within the empire. Later he was also called **the Great**.

In **380**, Theodosius and his co-emperors issued the **Edict of Thessalonica**. In it they demanded that all peoples adopt the Christian faith according to the creed of **Nicaea**. This made Christianity in effect the **state religion**. In 381 he summoned the **First Council of Constantinople**. It settled the dispute over the teaching of the priest Arius and also stressed the divinity of the Holy Spirit.

In **390**, after an uprising in **Thessalonica**, Theodosius had thousands of inhabitants killed. **Ambrose**, the Bishop of Milan, then refused him communion. The emperor had to do public **penance** before he was allowed to take part in church services again. This showed that the Church could now make demands even of an emperor.

In **391 and 392**, laws of Theodosius banned **pagan sacrifices** and visits to pagan temples. Many temples were closed or destroyed afterwards. According to tradition, the last **ancient Olympic Games** took place in **393**. As a festival in honour of Zeus, they no longer fitted the new religious policy.

In **394**, Theodosius defeated the rival emperor **Eugenius** at the Battle of the **Frigidus** river in present-day Slovenia. After that he briefly ruled over the whole empire. He died in Milan in January **395**. The empire was divided between his two sons: **Arcadius** received the east and **Honorius** the west. After that, the **Western and Eastern Roman Empires** developed separately.

gewusst: Theodosius was the last Roman emperor to rule over the whole empire from the Atlantic to the Euphrates.
The modern Olympic Games only began again in 1896, about 1500 years after the end of the ancient games.

teile.einleitung: The Trojan War is a famous legend of the ancient Greeks. It tells how a Greek army besieged the city of Troy for ten years. Whether this war really happened is still unclear today.
wichtigste: According to the legend, the war lasted ten years.
It was set off when the Trojan prince Paris carried off Helen.
Helen was the wife of **Menelaus**, the king of Sparta.
**Agamemnon** of Mycenae led the Greek army.
The king of Troy was the old **Priam**.
Troy lay on the strait of the **Dardanelles**.
The Trojan Aeneas was later regarded as the ancestor of the Romans.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the legend there is a **golden apple** with the inscription “for the fairest”. Three goddesses wanted it: Hera, Athena and Aphrodite. The Trojan prince **Paris** was to decide. He gave the apple to **Aphrodite**, because she promised him the most beautiful woman in the world. This story is called the **Judgement of Paris**. Hera and Athena therefore became enemies of Troy.

abschnitte.titel: Helen and the campaign of revenge
abschnitte.text: The most beautiful woman was **Helen**, the wife of King **Menelaus** of Sparta. Paris carried her off to Troy. Menelaus called on the Greek kings for a campaign of revenge. His brother **Agamemnon**, king of Mycenae, became commander-in-chief. With many ships, the Greeks sailed across the sea to Troy.

Troy lay on the strait of the **Dardanelles** and had strong walls. For ten years the Greeks besieged the city. Their strongest hero was **Achilles**. According to the legend he was almost invulnerable, except at the **heel**. That is why today we say “Achilles heel” for a weak spot. On the Trojan side fought Hector, a son of King **Priam**.

Only a **trick** brought the decision: the wooden Trojan Horse. Greek warriors got into the city inside it, and Troy fell. According to the legend, the Trojan **Aeneas** fled from the burning city. The Roman poet **Virgil** tells in the **Aeneid** how he came to Italy. In this way the Romans linked their own origins with Troy.

The most important source is the **Iliad** by the Greek poet **Homer**. But it describes only a few weeks in the last year of the war. Other parts of the legend come from later poems. Whether a real war lies behind the legend is still argued over by researchers.

gewusst: The expression “Achilles heel” for a vulnerable spot goes straight back to this legend.
According to the legend, the sea goddess Thetis dipped her son Achilles in a river of the underworld. The heel by which she held him stayed dry and was therefore vulnerable.

teile.einleitung: The Roman Imperial Period is the epoch in which the Roman Empire was ruled by emperors. It began in 27 BC with the first emperor Augustus. In this time the empire reached its greatest extent and enjoyed a long period of peace.
wichtigste: The imperial period began in 27 BC with Augustus.
In 64 AD, under Emperor Nero, a large part of Rome burned.
When Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, Pompeii was buried.
Under Emperor Trajan the empire reached its greatest extent around 117 AD.
Emperor Hadrian had a long frontier wall built in Britain.
Aqueducts carried water into the cities, and thermae were public baths.
Constantinople was inaugurated in 330 AD as the new capital in the east.

abschnitte.text: After many civil wars **Augustus** received a special position from the Senate in 27 BC. Officially Rome remained a republic, but in truth he held all the power. He ruled for over 40 years and provided order and peace. The month of August is named after him.

Under Emperor **Nero** a large part of Rome burned down in 64 AD. In 79 AD **Vesuvius** erupted and buried the cities of Pompeii and Herculaneum under ash. Under Emperor **Trajan** the empire was around 117 AD as large as never before, stretching from Britain to Mesopotamia. His successor **Hadrian** secured the frontiers, for example with Hadrian's Wall in Britain.

For about 200 years there was mostly peace inside the empire, the so-called **Pax Romana**. Trade and cities flourished, and one could travel from the Atlantic to Syria. In 212 AD almost all free inhabitants received **Roman citizenship**. Latin was understood everywhere in the west and Greek in the east.

The Romans built **aqueducts**, long water channels that brought fresh water into the cities. In the **thermae**, the public bathing complexes, there were warm and cold pools, sweating rooms and sports grounds. Thanks to underfloor heating rooms could be warmed. With concrete the Romans built great domes such as that of the Pantheon in Rome.

In the 3rd century the empire went through a severe crisis with attacks on the frontiers and many rapidly changing emperors. From 313 AD Emperor **Constantine** supported **Christianity**, which had often been persecuted before. In 330 he inaugurated **Constantinople**, present-day Istanbul, as the new capital in the east. In 395 the empire was finally divided into a western and an eastern part.

From the Latin of the Romans many languages arose, in Switzerland **French, Italian and Romansh**. Many German words such as Mauer (wall), Fenster (window) or Wein (wine) also come from Latin. In Switzerland ruins such as Augusta Raurica near Basel or the amphitheatre of Avenches bear witness to this time. Our calendar also goes back to the Romans.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sole ruler in the Roman Empire, the title goes back to the name Caesar.
Latin for “Roman peace”, a long period of peace in the empire.
A water channel that brings water over long distances into the cities.
A large public bathing complex of the Romans.

gewusst: The German word “Kaiser” comes from the name Caesar, and so does the Russian word “tsar”.
In Pompeii the city is so well preserved by the ash that one can still find loaves of bread and graffiti on walls.

teile.einleitung: The Nile is the great river that flows through Egypt, and one of the longest rivers in the world. Without it there would be hardly any life in the Egyptian desert, and the advanced civilisation of ancient Egypt would never have arisen. The Greek scholar Herodotus already called Egypt a “gift of the Nile”.
wichtigste: The Nile is one of the longest rivers in the world.
It flows from Africa northwards into the Mediterranean.
Before the sea it divides into many arms, the Nile Delta.
In ancient Egypt the Nile rose over its banks every year in late summer.
The flood left fertile black mud on the fields.
So the Egyptians called their land “Kemet”, the black land.
Most people lived on the banks of the Nile.
Crocodiles live in the Nile, and the hippopotamus bears its name.

abschnitte.text: The Nile is over 6,000 kilometres long and flows through about ten countries of Africa. It arises from two great source rivers: the **White Nile** comes from the region of Lake Victoria, the **Blue Nile** from Lake Tana in Ethiopia. In Khartoum, the capital of Sudan, the two flow together. North of Cairo the river divides into many arms, the **Nile Delta**, and flows into the Mediterranean.

Every summer it rains very heavily in the highlands of Ethiopia. This water made the Nile rise over its banks in late summer in ancient Egypt. When the water went down, fertile **Nile mud** was left lying on the fields. Because of this dark earth the Egyptians called their land **Kemet**, the black land, in contrast to the red desert.

Farmers led the Nile water onto their fields with **canals** and ditches and grew wheat, barley, flax and vegetables. With a water-lifting device, the **shaduf**, they raised water from the river. From papyrus, a plant on the bank, writing material and even boats were made. Almost all people lived in a narrow green strip along the river.

The Nile was the most important traffic route of Egypt. People travelled by **boat**, drifting downstream northwards with the current. Going south the boatmen set sail, because the wind mostly blows from the north. The huge stones for pyramids and temples were also transported on the river.

In the Nile live **Nile crocodiles**, which are among the largest crocodiles in the world and dangerous to people. The **hippopotamus** bears the name of the river and, despite its comfortable look, is a dangerous animal. On the bank live many birds such as herons and ibises. Below the Aswan Dam, however, there are hardly any crocodiles today, and hippopotamuses have disappeared from Egypt altogether.

Since 1970 the **Aswan High Dam** in the south of Egypt has held back the river into the huge Lake Nasser. Since then there has been no yearly flood in Egypt, but there is electricity and water all year. The fertile mud, however, now stays lying in the reservoir. Even so the great majority of Egyptians still live near the Nile.

begriffe.erklaerung: An area at a river's mouth where the river divides into many arms.
Ancient Egyptian name for Egypt, meaning “black land”.
A lifting beam with a bucket, used to draw water from the river.
A large wall that holds back a river.

gewusst: The Nile flows from south to north, so Lower Egypt lies at the top of the map and Upper Egypt at the bottom.
With measuring points, the nilometers, the ancient Egyptians measured the height of the flood and calculated the taxes accordingly.

teile.einleitung: The temples of Abu Simbel are two huge rock temples in the south of Egypt. Pharaoh Ramesses II had them cut into a mountain more than 3000 years ago. In the 1960s they were sawn into blocks and rebuilt in a higher place.
wichtigste: The temples were cut straight into a sandstone mountain.
In front of the great temple sit four statues of Pharaoh Ramesses II, each about 20 metres high.
The small temple is dedicated to the goddess Hathor and to Nefertari.
Abu Simbel lies at the very south of Egypt, in Nubia.
Because of the Aswan Dam, the temples would have sunk beneath the reservoir.
The temples were sawn into more than 1000 blocks and rebuilt higher up.
UNESCO called on many countries to help with the rescue.

abschnitte.text: Abu Simbel lies in the **far south of Egypt**, near the border with Sudan. The region is called **Nubia**. In the 13th century BC, Pharaoh **Ramesses II** had two temples built here. The workers chiselled the rooms and statues straight out of a **sandstone mountain**. That is why they are called **rock temples**. They were also meant to show how powerful the pharaoh was.

In front of the entrance of the great temple sit **four statues** of Ramesses II. Each is about **20 metres** high. The upper body of one statue already fell off in ancient times, probably because of an earthquake. The **small temple** next to it honours the goddess **Hathor** and **Nefertari**. Nefertari was the pharaoh's most important wife. She too can be seen as a large statue on the front of the temple.

Twice a year, in **February** and in **October**, something special happens. Then the morning light falls through the entrance deep into the great temple. It lights up the statues of the gods at the very back of the innermost room. The ancient builders lined up the temple exactly like this. Many people travel to Abu Simbel on these days to see it.

abschnitte.titel: A Swiss man finds the temples
abschnitte.text: Over time, the desert sand almost completely covered the temples. In **1813**, the explorer **Johann Ludwig Burckhardt** from Basel saw the heads of the great statues sticking out of the sand. He reported on it in Europe. A few years later, the entrance of the great temple was uncovered.

In the 1960s, Egypt built the **Aswan Dam**. Behind it, a huge lake formed that would have flooded the temples. **UNESCO** called on many countries for help. Workers sawed the temples into **more than 1000 large blocks** and put them back together exactly higher up and further from the water. An artificial mountain now surrounds them. The temples are a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: The rescue of Abu Simbel was one of the things that prompted UNESCO to create the World Heritage List later on.
Because of the move, the sunlight now reaches the inside about one day later than before.

teile.einleitung: The testudo was a fighting formation of the Roman army. The soldiers held their shields so close together that they looked like armour. That is why the formation is also called the tortoise.
wichtigste: “Testudo” is Latin and means tortoise.
The soldiers formed it with their shields.
On the outside they held the shields to the front and to the side, on the inside over their heads.
The formation protected against arrows, spears and stones.
It moved forward only slowly, because everyone had to stay close together.
The Romans liked to use it when attacking city walls.
It was formed by legionaries, who practised it often.

abschnitte.text: The Latin word **testudo** means **tortoise**. The formation is reminiscent of the hard shell of this animal. The soldiers stood close together in rows. The men on the outside held their shields **to the front and to the side**. The men on the inside held theirs like a **roof** over their heads. In this way a closed covering of shields was formed.

This was possible because of the special shields of the **legionaries**. That was the name for the well-trained foot soldiers of the Roman army. Their shield was called the **scutum**. It was large, rectangular and slightly curved. It was made of wood and leather and had a metal boss in the middle. Several such shields fitted well together, almost like tiles on a roof.

The tortoise protected the soldiers above all from **arrows, spears and stones** coming from above or from the front. That is why the Romans liked to use it when **attacking a city wall**. The defenders shot and threw things from the wall. Under the shields the soldiers could advance safely up to the wall or the gate and work there.

The formation also had disadvantages. All the soldiers had to **stay close together**, so the tortoise moved forward only **slowly**. In close combat with many enemies it was not very suitable, because the soldiers could hardly fight. It was therefore mainly a formation for protection and for advancing, not for open battle.

A good tortoise only worked with a lot of **practice**. The soldiers had to walk **in step**. Only if everyone was exactly the same speed did the shields stay close together. Otherwise **gaps** appeared, through which arrows could fly. The Roman army was famous for its **drill**, that is, for constantly practising such movements.

gewusst: Roman reliefs, for example on Marcus Aurelius's Column in Rome, show soldiers in the tortoise formation.
In demonstrations, soldiers are said to have stood so close together that people could walk over the shields.

teile.einleitung: Albrecht Dürer was one of the most important artists in Germany. He lived in Nuremberg from 1471 to 1528. He is famous for his paintings, drawings, woodcuts and engravings.
wichtigste: Dürer lived from 1471 to 1528 in **Nuremberg**.
He signed many works with a **monogram of A and D**.
In 1502 he painted a **hare** with almost every single hair.
He was one of the first artists to paint **self-portraits** several times.
The drawing **“Praying Hands”** is world famous.
“Melencolia I” of 1514 is an **engraving**.
From 1505 to 1507 he travelled to **Venice**.

abschnitte.text: **Albrecht Dürer** was born in **Nuremberg** in 1471. His father was a goldsmith. Albrecht first learnt from him, then from a painter. As a young man he went on his travels as a journeyman, as was usual for craftsmen at the time. On the way he also came to **Basel**, where he designed pictures for books for printers.

Dürer was very interested in the art of Italy. From **1505 to 1507** he lived in **Venice**. There he got to know the painters of the Italian **Renaissance**. He studied how to depict bodies correctly and how to paint spaces with perspective. He brought these ideas back to Germany.

Dürer observed nature very closely. In **1502** he painted a **hare** so finely that you can recognise almost every hair. Also famous is the drawing **“Praying Hands”**. He was also one of the first artists to paint himself several times. These **self-portraits** show him at different ages.

Dürer was a master of **printmaking**. With it, a picture could be printed many times and sold. In a **woodcut**, the picture is carved into a block of wood. In an **engraving**, it is scratched into a copper plate. The engraving **“Melencolia I”** of 1514 is among his most famous works. In this way his pictures spread all over Europe.

In **1515**, Dürer made a woodcut of a **rhinoceros**. He had never seen the animal himself. He knew only a description and a sketch from Lisbon, where a rhinoceros had been brought. That is why his rhinoceros looks as if it is wearing armour made of plates. Even so, the picture became very famous and was copied often.

gewusst: Dürer signed many works with a large A, under which stands a small D. This monogram became a kind of trademark.
Dürer's hare is kept in a museum in Vienna and is only rarely shown, because light could harm it.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Kadesh took place around 1274 BC in present-day Syria. There the army of the Egyptian pharaoh Ramesses II fought against the Hittites. It was probably the largest chariot battle in history.
wichtigste: The battle is usually dated to the year 1274 BC.
Ramesses II fought against the Hittite Great King Muwatalli II.
Kadesh lay on the River Orontes in the west of present-day Syria.
On both sides probably several thousand chariots fought.
Hittite chariots carried three men, Egyptian ones two.
Neither side could win decisively.
Ramesses II nevertheless had the battle shown as a great victory on temple walls.

abschnitte.text: In the 13th century BC **Egypt** and the empire of the **Hittites** in Asia Minor were two great powers. Both wanted to rule over the area of present-day Syria. The city of **Kadesh** on the River **Orontes** lay exactly in the border region. In the fifth year of the reign of **Ramesses II** the Egyptian army marched north. The Hittite Great King **Muwatalli II** with his allies faced it.

Muwatalli lured the Egyptians into a trap with **false information**. Two prisoners claimed that the Hittite army was still far away. In truth it waited hidden behind the city. The Egyptian army marched in several divisions that lay far apart. The Hittites attacked one of them by surprise, and Ramesses fell into great danger.

A **chariot** is a light two-wheeled cart that is drawn by horses. At Kadesh probably several thousand of them fought on each side. The Hittite chariots were heavier and carried **three men**: driver, fighter and shield bearer. The Egyptian chariots were lighter, faster and manned by **two men**. With the help of reinforcements the Egyptians were finally able to repel the attack.

Ramesses II celebrated the battle as a great **victory**. He had it shown in picture and text on temple walls at **Abu Simbel**, Karnak, Luxor and in the Ramesseum. There he appears as a hero who almost single-handedly defeats the enemies. Scholars see it differently today: Kadesh remained Hittite, and neither side prevailed. So people speak of a **draw**.

Some years later Ramesses II and the Hittite king **Hattusili III** made peace. This **peace treaty** is among the oldest known. It survives both in Egyptian script and on Hittite clay tablets. In it both empires promised not to attack each other any more and to help one another.

gewusst: A replica of the peace treaty hangs in the United Nations building in New York.
There are more accounts of the Battle of Kadesh than of almost any other battle of this period.
Later Ramesses II even married a Hittite king's daughter.

teile.einleitung: The Mycenaean civilisation was the first advanced civilisation on the Greek mainland. It flourished in the Late Bronze Age, from about 1600 to 1100 BC, and is named after the citadel of Mycenae on the Peloponnese.
wichtigste: The Mycenaean civilisation flourished from about 1600 to 1100 BC.
The citadel of Mycenae lies in the Argolis on the Peloponnese.
Its famous entrance gate is the Lion Gate.
The huge walls are called Cyclopean walls.
The Mycenaeans wrote in Linear B, an early form of Greek.
Michael Ventris deciphered Linear B in 1952.
Heinrich Schliemann dug at Mycenae from 1876.

abschnitte.text: The citadel of **Mycenae** lies in the region of the **Argolis** in the north-east of the **Peloponnese**. From there important routes were controlled. The Mycenaeans built mighty citadels with palaces, also at **Tiryns** and **Pylos**. In the palace of Pylos, the so-called “Palace of Nestor”, over a thousand clay tablets were found. According to the legend the wise King **Nestor** ruled there. The civilisation belongs to the **Late Bronze Age**.

The entrance of the citadel of Mycenae is the **Lion Gate**. Above the gate two stone lions can be seen flanking a column. It is regarded as one of the oldest large reliefs in Europe. The walls consist of huge blocks of stone. Later Greeks believed that only the one-eyed giants, the **Cyclopes**, could have piled them up. That is why they are called **Cyclopean walls**.

The merchant and archaeologist **Heinrich Schliemann**, who had dug at Troy before, found richly furnished **shaft graves** at Mycenae from **1876**. In them lay a golden funeral mask. Schliemann believed he had found the face of King **Agamemnon** from Homer's epics, hence the name **Mask of Agamemnon**. Today we know that it is about 300 years older than the supposed Trojan War. The so-called **“Treasury of Atreus”** is in reality a large **beehive tomb** made of rings of stone.

On clay tablets the Mycenaeans wrote mainly **lists** of stores, animals and dues. Their script is called **Linear B**. For a long time nobody could read it. In **1952** the Englishman **Michael Ventris** showed that it records an early form of **Greek**. That proved that the Mycenaeans were Greeks. Linear B contains the oldest known Greek. The tablets survived because they were hard-fired in fires in the palaces.

Around **1200 BC** many Mycenaean palaces were destroyed. Why is not certainly known. Researchers think of wars, uprisings, earthquakes, famines or a collapse of trade. After that the Mycenaean civilisation broke up, and the script too fell into oblivion. Only centuries later did the Greeks adopt a new alphabet. But the memory of the age of the palaces lived on in the **legends**, for example in Homer's Iliad.

gewusst: The clay tablets in Linear B survived only because fire baked them hard when the palaces were destroyed.
The citadels of Mycenae and Tiryns are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

teile.einleitung: The Palace of Aachen was a palace of Charlemagne in the city of Aachen. He spent many years of his reign here. What survives above all is the Palatine Chapel, which today is part of Aachen Cathedral.
wichtigste: A **palatinate** (Pfalz) was a palace in which a king lived with his court.
Among other things, the **warm springs** drew Charlemagne to Aachen.
The ground plan of the Palatine Chapel is an **octagon**.
Charlemagne died in Aachen in **814**.
In the chapel there is still a **marble throne** today.
His bones lie in the golden **Shrine of Charlemagne**.
In 1978, Aachen Cathedral became the first German monument on the World Heritage List.

abschnitte.text: In the early Middle Ages, the king had no fixed capital. He travelled through the empire with his court. In many places there were **palaces** (Pfalzen) for this, where he could live and govern. **Charlemagne** chose **Aachen** as his favourite place. In his later years he stayed almost only there.

One reason for Charlemagne's choice was the **warm springs** in Aachen. The Romans had already bathed there. Charlemagne liked to swim and often bathed in the warm water, together with family and guests. The palace included a great royal hall, living quarters and a church.

The **Palatine Chapel** was built around 800. Its ground plan is an **octagon**. A large dome arches over the space. Models were churches in Italy and in the Eastern Roman Empire. On the upper floor there is still a plain **marble throne** today. Later, many German kings were crowned here.

Charlemagne died in **814** in Aachen and was buried in the Palatine Chapel. Much later his bones were placed in a precious golden shrine, the **Shrine of Charlemagne**. It is decorated with figures of kings and with gemstones and still stands in the cathedral today.

In time, the Palatine Chapel became **Aachen Cathedral**. New parts were added, but the old octagon was preserved. In **1978**, Aachen Cathedral became the **first German monument** on UNESCO's World Heritage List. Of the rest of the palace only remains survive, and the town hall now stands on the walls of the old royal hall.

gewusst: For around 600 years, German kings were crowned in Aachen.
Aachen lies where Germany, Belgium and the Netherlands meet.

teile.einleitung: The New Kingdom is the time of the greatest power of ancient Egypt, roughly from 1550 to 1070 BC. Famous pharaohs such as Hatshepsut, Akhenaten, Tutankhamun and Ramesses II come from this time.
wichtigste: The New Kingdom lasted roughly from 1550 to 1070 BC.
It comprises the 18th to the 20th Dynasty.
Ahmose I drove out the foreign rulers and founded the New Kingdom.
Thutmose III won at Megiddo, and Ramesses III repelled the Sea Peoples.
The kings were buried in the Valley of the Kings near Thebes.
With Ramesses XI the New Kingdom ended.

abschnitte.text: Before the New Kingdom, foreign rulers, the **Hyksos**, ruled in the Nile Delta. King **Ahmose I** captured their capital **Avaris** around **1550 BC** and drove them out. With that the **18th Dynasty** and the **New Kingdom** began. It comprises the 18th to 20th Dynasties and was the time of Egypt's **greatest extent**. The empire stretched from Nubia in the south to Syria in the north.

**Thutmose III** defeated a group of Canaanite princes in the 15th century BC in the battle of **Megiddo**. With that Egyptian supremacy in the **Levant**, the area on the eastern Mediterranean, began. The campaign is described in the annals in the temple of **Karnak**. Before him his aunt and stepmother **Hatshepsut** ruled as pharaoh. Later **Ramesses II** fought the Hittites at Kadesh and made one of the oldest known peace treaties with them.

abschnitte.titel: The Amarna period and the return
abschnitte.text: **Amenhotep III** had many buildings erected. In front of his mortuary temple in Thebes West stand the **Colossi of Memnon**, two huge statues of him. Greeks later linked them with the hero Memnon. His son **Akhenaten** worshipped almost only the sun god **Aten** and founded the city of Amarna. After him people returned to the old gods. The former general **Horemheb**, as last king of the 18th Dynasty, completed this return and installed **Ramesses I** as his successor.

Around **1177 BC** **Ramesses III** repelled the attack of the **Sea Peoples**. These groups then threatened many kingdoms in the Mediterranean region. Ramesses III had the victory depicted on the walls of his mortuary temple **Medinet Habu**. After that the kingship lost power. Under **Ramesses XI**, the last king of the 20th Dynasty, high priests of the god Amun in Thebes ruled practically independently. Around 1070 BC the **Third Intermediate Period** began.

The kings of the New Kingdom no longer had themselves buried in pyramids but in rock tombs in the **Valley of the Kings** near Thebes. The tombs were dug deep into the mountain and painted in colour. Almost all of them were robbed already in antiquity. An exception is the tomb of the young king **Tutankhamun**, which **Howard Carter** found almost untouched in 1922. In it lay, among other things, the famous golden funeral mask.

gewusst: The peace treaty between Ramesses II and the Hittites is regarded as one of the oldest known peace treaties.
The tomb of Tutankhamun was discovered almost untouched in 1922.

teile.einleitung: The Abbasids were a ruling family who, as caliphs, governed a large Islamic empire for several centuries. Their capital Baghdad became one of the most important cities in the world.
wichtigste: The Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in **750**.
In **762** they founded the new capital **Baghdad**.
Because of its circular ground plan, Baghdad was called the **“Round City”**.
The caliph **Harun al-Rashid** ruled from 786 to 809.
Their flags were **black**.
In 751 they defeated a Chinese army at the Battle of **Talas**.
From the end of the 8th century, **paper** was made in Baghdad.

abschnitte.text: After the Prophet Muhammad, **caliphs** ruled the Islamic empire. At first the family of the **Umayyads** ruled. In **750** they were overthrown in the east by the **Abbasids**. The Abbasids traced their name back to al-Abbas, an uncle of Muhammad. Their colour was **black**, which is why their flags had this colour.

In **762**, the caliph al-Mansur founded a new capital on the river Tigris: **Baghdad**. The first layout was **perfectly circular**, with walls and gates all round. That is why it was called the **“Round City”**. In the middle stood the palace and the great mosque. Baghdad grew quickly and became a huge, rich trading city.

The best-known caliph is **Harun al-Rashid**. He ruled from **786 to 809**. He often appears in the stories of **“One Thousand and One Nights”**. He had contact with **Charlemagne** in the west. Around 800, a caliph even sent Charlemagne an **elephant** as a gift. The elephant was called Abul-Abbas.

In **751**, Abbasid troops defeated an army of the Chinese Tang dynasty at the Battle of **Talas** in Central Asia. After that, the art of making paper spread from China further west. From the end of the 8th century, **paper** was made in Baghdad. Scholars translated many books, for example from Greek, and carried out research in mathematics, medicine and astronomy.

In time the caliphs lost power. Other rulers governed in their name, and parts of the empire became independent. In **1258**, the **Mongols** conquered Baghdad. This ended the rule of the Abbasids in Baghdad. Their time is still regarded as a golden age of Islamic culture.

gewusst: The word “algebra” comes from the title of a mathematics book written in Baghdad at the time of the Abbasids.
The elephant Abul-Abbas travelled from Baghdad all the way to Aachen, to the court of Charlemagne.

teile.einleitung: Angkor Wat is a huge temple complex in Cambodia. It is regarded as the largest religious building in the world and is so important that it appears on the national flag.
wichtigste: Angkor Wat stands in Cambodia near the town of Siem Reap.
The Khmer people built the temple in the 12th century.
King Suryavarman II had it built.
The temple was originally dedicated to the god Vishnu.
In the middle stand five towers that recall lotus buds.
A broad moat surrounds the complex.
Unlike most Khmer temples, Angkor Wat faces west.

abschnitte.text: **Angkor Wat** stands in **Cambodia** in South-East Asia, near the town of Siem Reap. It is a huge **temple complex** and is regarded as the largest religious building in the world. It was built by the **Khmer** people, who then ruled a large empire. Building began about 900 years ago. Angkor Wat is so important to the country that it appears on the **flag of Cambodia**.

King **Suryavarman II** had the temple built in the first half of the **12th century**. Angkor Wat was originally a Hindu temple for the god **Vishnu**. It probably also served as the king's funerary temple. Later it became a **Buddhist** shrine and is still visited by monks today.

In the middle stand **five towers** that look like **lotus buds**. They represent the holy mountain of the gods, Meru. A broad **moat** runs around the whole complex, representing the ocean. Long galleries with **reliefs** show stories from the Indian world of the gods and pictures of battles.

Most Khmer temples open towards the **east**, to the rising sun. Angkor Wat, on the other hand, faces **west**. Researchers suspect that this has to do with the god Vishnu or with the death of the king. Many visitors come early in the morning to see the sunrise behind the towers.

Around the temples of Angkor grows tropical **jungle**. At some temples nearby, huge trees even grow on the walls, their roots wrapping around the stones. Angkor Wat itself was never completely abandoned and therefore stayed well preserved. Today it is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and is visited by very many tourists every year.

gewusst: Cambodia is one of the few countries that show a building on their flag.
The word “wat” means “temple” in the Khmer language.

teile.einleitung: The Minotaur is a monster from Greek legend, half man and half bull. He lived in a labyrinth on Crete until the hero Theseus of Athens defeated him.
wichtigste: The Minotaur was half man and half bull.
King Minos of Crete had him shut up in a labyrinth.
Athens had to send seven young men and seven young women to Crete.
Theseus of Athens defeated the Minotaur.
Ariadne, the daughter of Minos, gave him a thread for the way back.
According to the legend the Aegean is named after Theseus' father Aegeus.

abschnitte.text: According to the legend the **Minotaur** had the body of a man and the head of a bull. The name means “**bull of Minos**”. King **Minos** of Crete had the dangerous monster hidden away. The skilful builder **Daedalus** built a huge **labyrinth** for this. A labyrinth is a **maze** with many winding passages and dead ends. Whoever went in could not find the way out again.

The city of **Athens** had to send young people to King Minos regularly: according to the legend **seven young men and seven young women** each time. They were taken into the labyrinth and never came back. The ship therefore sailed to Crete with **black sails**. **Theseus**, the son of King Aegeus of Athens, wanted to put an end to this. He went along of his own free will and promised that if he won he would set a bright sail on the way home.

On Crete **Ariadne**, the daughter of King Minos, saw the young Theseus. She fell in love with him and wanted to help him. She gave him a **thread**. Theseus tied it at the entrance of the labyrinth and unwound it as he went. Inside he defeated the Minotaur. On the way back he simply had to follow the thread. So he found his way out of the maze and saved the other young people.

On the voyage home Theseus forgot to change the black sail for a bright one. His father **Aegeus** was waiting on the coast. When he saw the black sail he believed his son was dead and threw himself into the sea. Since then, according to the legend, this sea has been called the **Aegean**. Theseus then became king of Athens.

The legend has occupied people since antiquity. Many link the winding **palace of Knossos** with the labyrinth. The labyrinth became a popular symbol: it is found on coins from Knossos, on mosaics and in churches. Today there are labyrinths of hedges or maize fields, also in Switzerland, through which one can stroll.

gewusst: The expression “Ariadne's thread” still stands today for a help that leads out of a difficult situation.
On ancient coins from Knossos a labyrinth is shown.

teile.einleitung: The Vedic period is a stage in the early history of India. It is named after the Vedas, very old sacred texts. These texts are still important for Hinduism today.
wichtigste: The Vedic period lasted from about 1500 to 500 BC.
There are four Vedas, and the oldest is the **Rigveda**.
The Vedas are written in **Vedic Sanskrit**.
For a long time they were handed down **orally**, by learning them exactly by heart.
In the Rigveda, most of the hymns are dedicated to the god **Indra**.
At the end of the Vedic period, the **Upanishads** came into being.

abschnitte.text: The word **Veda** means “knowledge”. There are four Vedas: the **Rigveda**, the Samaveda, the Yajurveda and the Atharvaveda. The Rigveda is the oldest. It consists of over a thousand hymns, that is, solemn songs to the gods. The Vedas are written in **Vedic Sanskrit**, an ancient form of the Sanskrit language.

abschnitte.titel: Handed down by learning by heart
abschnitte.text: For many centuries, the Vedas were not written down. They were **handed down orally**. Pupils learnt the texts by heart word by word and sound by sound. There were special learning methods for this. In this way the hymns were preserved amazingly exactly, until they were also written down much later.

In the Rigveda, most of the hymns are dedicated to the god **Indra**. He was regarded as a strong warrior and lord over thunderstorms and rain. Also very important was **Agni**, the god of fire. He embodies the **sacrificial fire** and is seen as a messenger between humans and gods. Priests made offerings to the gods in the fire and sang the hymns as they did so.

In the Vedic texts, society is divided into four groups, the **varnas**. The priests belonged to the **Brahmins**. Then came the warriors and princes, the farmers and merchants, and the servants. From this model the caste system of India later developed. It is also viewed critically today.

At the end of the Vedic period, the **Upanishads** came into being. These writings ask about the deepest nature of the world. They deal with the relationship between **Atman**, the innermost self of a person, and **Brahman**, the ultimate ground of everything. The Upanishads have strongly shaped the philosophy of India.

gewusst: The Rigveda is one of the oldest religious texts in the world that are still used today.
UNESCO has recognised the tradition of reciting the Vedas as a cultural heritage of humanity.

teile.einleitung: A wax tablet was a kind of notepad in ancient times. You scratched letters into a layer of wax and could then smooth it over again. Roman children practised writing on it at school.
wichtigste: Roman children often wrote on **wax tablets** at school.
People wrote with a pointed **stylus**.
With the **flat end** of the stylus you could erase the writing.
The frame was usually made of **wood**.
Several tablets tied together were called a **codex**.
In **Windisch** in Aargau, many Roman writing tablets were found.

abschnitte.text: A wax tablet usually consisted of a small board of **wood**. In the middle was a shallow hollow filled with **wax**. A raised edge all round protected the writing. The wax was often dyed dark so that the light scratches could be seen well. In Latin the tablet was called tabula cerata.

For writing, a **stylus** was used, in Latin **stilus**. It was made of metal, bone or wood. With the point you scratched the letters into the wax. The other end was **flat** like a little spatula. With it you could smooth the wax flat again and so **erase** the writing.

Wax tablets were very practical for practising, because you could **use them again and again**. Papyrus was expensive, but wax could simply be smoothed over. That is why **Roman children** often wrote on wax tablets at school. Adults also used them for notes, letters, bills and contracts.

Often two or more tablets were **tied together** with cords. In this way they could be opened like a book. Such a collection was called a **codex**. Later, people also wrote on sheets of parchment bound in the same way. From this form our present-day **book** arose.

In **Windisch** in the canton of Aargau lay the Roman legionary camp of **Vindonissa**. There, very many remains of writing tablets made of wood were found. The wax has mostly vanished. But sometimes the stylus had scratched the wood underneath. In this way researchers can still decipher letters and notes by the soldiers today.

gewusst: Wax tablets were still used in the Middle Ages, for example in monastery schools.
The word “style” for the way someone writes comes from the Latin word stilus for the stylus.

teile.einleitung: Al-Andalus is the Arabic name for the parts of the Iberian Peninsula that were under Muslim rule in the Middle Ages. For almost 800 years, Muslims, Christians and Jews shaped culture and science there.
wichtigste: Al-Andalus means **Muslim Spain**.
In **711**, Muslim troops crossed from Africa to Spain.
The Rock of **Gibraltar** is named after the general Tariq ibn Ziyad.
In 929, **Abd al-Rahman III** proclaimed the Caliphate of Córdoba.
**Córdoba** was one of the biggest cities in Europe in the 10th century.
The Christian reconquest is called the **Reconquista**.
In 1492, **Granada**, the last Muslim kingdom, fell.

abschnitte.text: In **711**, Muslim troops crossed from North Africa to Spain. Their leader was the general **Tariq ibn Ziyad**. The Rock of **Gibraltar** is named after him: the name comes from “Jabal Tariq”, which means “Mountain of Tariq”. Within a few years, the troops conquered most of the Iberian Peninsula.

The capital of Al-Andalus became **Córdoba**. In **929**, the ruler **Abd al-Rahman III** proclaimed a **caliphate** of his own there. From 936 he had the magnificent palace city of **Medina Azahara** built outside the city gates. In the 10th century Córdoba was regarded as one of the **biggest cities in Europe**, with libraries, baths and markets.

The most famous building in Córdoba is the great mosque, the **Mezquita**. Inside there are hundreds of columns, joined by red and white striped arches. After the Christian conquest it was turned into a **cathedral**. Later a church was built right in the middle of the mosque.

In Al-Andalus, **Muslims, Christians and Jews** lived together, although not always peacefully and with equal rights. There were important scholars in medicine, mathematics and philosophy. One of the most famous was **Averroes** of Córdoba, a philosopher and doctor in the 12th century. He wrote commentaries on the works of the Greek Aristotle, which were later widely read in Europe.

In the north of the peninsula, Christian kingdoms remained. They gradually reconquered the Muslim territories. This is called the **Reconquista**, “reconquest”. In the end only the kingdom of **Granada** with the palace of the **Alhambra** was left. In **1492**, the Catholic Monarchs conquered Granada. This ended Al-Andalus.

gewusst: Many Spanish words come from Arabic, for example “aceite” for oil.
The name of the region of Andalusia in southern Spain goes back to Al-Andalus.

teile.einleitung: In 395, after the death of Emperor Theodosius I, the Roman Empire was finally divided into a western and an eastern part. His two sons each inherited one half. The two empires then went very different ways.
wichtigste: Theodosius I was the last emperor to rule over the whole Roman Empire.
After his death in 395 Arcadius received the east and Honorius the west.
The capital of the east was Constantinople.
From 402 the Western Roman emperors resided in Ravenna.
The Western Roman Empire ended in 476.
The Eastern Roman Empire, also called the Byzantine Empire, lasted until 1453.

abschnitte.text: Emperor **Theodosius I** at the end ruled alone over the huge empire. In 380 he declared **Christianity** the state religion. Later he also banned the old sacrificial cults. When he died in January 395, his sons divided the empire. The elder son **Arcadius** got the east, the younger son **Honorius** the west.

abschnitte.titel: Why two parts of the empire?
abschnitte.text: The empire was very large and threatened at many frontiers. Even earlier several emperors had often ruled at the same time. The division of 395 was really only a division of the administration. Legally the empire still counted as a single Roman Empire. But the two halves were never again permanently united under one emperor.

**Honorius** was only about ten years old at his father's death. At first the commander **Stilicho** ruled for him. From 402 **Ravenna** on the Adriatic became the residence of the Western Roman emperors. The city was surrounded by marshes and easy to defend. The area of present-day **Switzerland** belonged to the western part. The west grew weaker, and in 476 the Germanic leader Odoacer deposed the last emperor.

The east was ruled from **Constantinople**, present-day Istanbul. It was richer and lasted much longer. Today it is also called the **Byzantine Empire**, after Byzantion, the old Greek name of the capital. Its inhabitants, however, called themselves Romans. In the 6th century Emperor **Justinian** had the **Hagia Sophia** built, which was consecrated in 537. Only in 1453 did the Ottomans conquer Constantinople.

gewusst: After 395 the Eastern Roman Empire lasted for over a thousand years more.
In Ravenna famous mosaics from this period are preserved to this day.
The Hagia Sophia was the largest church in Christendom for almost a thousand years.

teile.einleitung: The theatre was invented in ancient Greece. People sat in the open air on stone steps on a hillside and watched tragedies and comedies. Many words to do with the theatre still come from Greek today.
wichtigste: Greek theatres were built into a hillside in the open air.
A funny play is called a comedy, a serious play a tragedy.
Only men acted, including the women's roles, and all wore masks.
The chorus sang, danced and explained the plot.
The round dancing area was called the orchestra.
In the theatre at Epidaurus you can hear very well even at the top.
Epidaurus had room for over 10,000 spectators.

abschnitte.text: The theatre arose in **Athens** at great festivals for the god **Dionysus**, the god of wine. At these festivals, poets competed against each other with their plays in a **contest**. Many citizens came to watch. Famous tragedy writers were **Aeschylus**, **Sophocles** and **Euripides**. The best-known comedy writer was **Aristophanes**.

A **tragedy** is a serious play that usually ends sadly. It is often about heroes from ancient legends who have to make hard decisions. A **comedy** is a funny play that makes people laugh. Greek comedies often poked fun at well-known politicians and thinkers. Both kinds of plays were invented by the Greeks.

Only **men** were allowed to act on the stage. They also played all the **women's roles**. They wore large **masks**, from which you could tell at once who a character was and whether they were happy or sad. In this way one actor could take on several roles in a play. In addition there was the **chorus**, a group that sang and danced together and explained to the audience what was happening in the story.

The spectators sat on **stone steps** that rose up a hillside in a semicircle. This seating area was called the **theatron**, which means “place for watching”. Below lay the round dancing area for the chorus, the **orchestra**. Our word **orchestra** comes from it. Behind it stood a stage building, the **skene**, from which our word **scene** comes.

Especially famous is the theatre at **Epidaurus** from the 4th century BC. After an extension it had room for up to about **14,000** people. It is built so cleverly that even quiet words can be heard right up in the **top rows**, entirely without technology. Even today **performances** take place there in summer. In Switzerland, too, at **Augusta Raurica** near Basel, there is a large ancient theatre, although from Roman times.

gewusst: Anyone in Athens who was too poor to pay for admission to the theatre was at times given money by the state for it.
The theatre at Epidaurus, together with the sanctuary there, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

teile.einleitung: Mesopotamia is an ancient region in the Near East whose Greek name means “land between the rivers”. Here, between the Euphrates and the Tigris, some of the first cities and the first script in the world arose more than 5,000 years ago. That is why Mesopotamia is often called a “cradle of civilisation”.
wichtigste: Mesopotamia lies between the rivers Euphrates and Tigris.
The greatest part of ancient Mesopotamia lies in present-day Iraq.
The region belongs to the Fertile Crescent, which stretches from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean.
Because it rained little, farmers watered their fields with canals.
Houses and temples were built mainly of mud bricks.
A stepped temple tower is called a ziggurat.
The Epic of Gilgamesh from Mesopotamia is one of the oldest poems in the world.
The sexagesimal system for hours, minutes and seconds comes from Mesopotamia.

abschnitte.text: Mesopotamia stretches from the highlands in the north to the **Persian Gulf** in the south. The greatest part lies in present-day **Iraq**, smaller parts belong to Syria and Turkey. The rivers **Euphrates and Tigris** rise in the mountains of present-day Turkey. In the south the land is flat, hot and dry, but the rivers bring fertile mud with them.

Mesopotamia belongs to the **Fertile Crescent**, an arc-shaped area in which people settled early. Because it hardly rained in the south, farmers dug **irrigation canals** and led the river water onto their fields. In this way they could grow barley, wheat, dates and vegetables. The canals had to be constantly maintained, which many people had to organise together.

In the south the **Sumerians** founded cities such as Uruk and Ur more than 5,000 years ago. Later various empires ruled there one after another, such as the Akkadians, the **Babylonians** and the **Assyrians**. The Assyrians had their capital for a time in **Nineveh** on the Tigris, in the north of Mesopotamia. Babylon on the Euphrates became one of the most magnificent cities in the world under King Nebuchadnezzar II.

Stone and wood were rare in Mesopotamia, but clay was found everywhere. So people built their houses, walls and temples of **mud bricks**, which were dried in the sun or fired in a kiln. The best-known building is the **ziggurat**, a stepped temple tower with a shrine at its top. The ziggurat of Ur partly survives to this day.

Around 3300 BC **cuneiform** arose in Mesopotamia, pressed with a reed into soft clay tablets. With it people first wrote accounts, later also laws, letters and stories. The **Epic of Gilgamesh** tells of King Gilgamesh, who searches for eternal life. The **sexagesimal system** also comes from here, which is why an hour has 60 minutes and a minute 60 seconds.

King **Hammurabi** of Babylon had a famous collection of laws written on a stone column around 1750 BC. This column stands today in the Louvre in Paris. The division of the circle into 360 degrees and the observation of the stars also go back to Mesopotamia. Many finds from Mesopotamia can be admired today in great museums in Baghdad, Berlin, London and Paris.

begriffe.erklaerung: A stepped temple tower of mud bricks in Mesopotamia.
One of the oldest scripts in the world, with wedge-shaped signs pressed into clay.
An arc-shaped, fertile region from the Persian Gulf to the Mediterranean.
Water is led artificially, for example through canals, onto the fields.

gewusst: When you look at the clock and count 60 minutes, you are using a number system from Mesopotamia that is over 4,000 years old.
The famous blue Ishtar Gate from Babylon was rebuilt and today stands in a museum in Berlin.

teile.einleitung: The Olmecs were one of the oldest advanced civilisations of the Americas. They lived about 3,000 years ago on the Gulf Coast of Mexico and are known above all for their giant stone heads.
wichtigste: The Olmecs lived about 3,000 years ago on the Gulf Coast of Mexico.
Their territory lies in the present-day states of Veracruz and Tabasco.
They carved giant colossal heads from volcanic rock.
To this day 17 such heads are known, and they weigh several tonnes.
The heads probably depict rulers.
The Olmecs are regarded as the mother culture of Mesoamerica.

abschnitte.text: The **Olmecs** lived in the humid lowlands on the **Gulf Coast of Mexico**, in the present-day states of **Veracruz** and **Tabasco**.
