Their culture flourished about **3,000 years ago**. So they are among the **oldest advanced civilisations of the Americas**. Important centres were **San Lorenzo** and **La Venta**. There were earth platforms, plazas and buildings for ceremonies there. What the Olmecs called themselves is not known.

Famous are the **colossal heads**, huge heads of stone. Some are almost three metres high and weigh **several tonnes**, as much as several cars together. To this day **17** such heads have been found. Each has its own facial features and wears a kind of helmet. Researchers believe that the heads show important **rulers**. They are carved from **basalt**, a hard **volcanic rock**.

The basalt blocks for the heads came from mountains that lay far from the cities, from the area of the **Tuxtla Mountains**. The Olmecs had no draught animals and did not use wheeled carts. How they moved the heavy stones is not certainly known. Perhaps many people dragged them overland and carried them on rafts over rivers. This shows that the rulers could deploy very many workers.

abschnitte.titel: The name and the mother culture
abschnitte.text: The name “**Olmecs**” comes from the language of the later Aztecs and means roughly “**people from the rubber land**”. In their area **rubber trees** grew, from whose sap rubber can be made. Many features such as the **ball game** with rubber balls, **calendars** and pictures of gods appear first among the Olmecs. That is why they are often called the **mother culture of Mesoamerica**. Later cultures such as the Maya and Aztecs took over some of it.

gewusst: The Olmecs were already making rubber balls about 3,000 years ago.
Each of the 17 colossal heads has its own face, and none is exactly like another.

teile.einleitung: The Romans wrote numbers with letters. These Roman numerals can still be seen today on clocks, on old buildings or in the names of kings. With a few simple rules they are easy to read.
wichtigste: The most important signs are I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500 and M = 1,000.
Identical signs next to each other are added together: XX is 20.
If a smaller sign stands after a larger one, it is added: XII is 12.
If a smaller sign stands before a larger one, it is subtracted: IV is 4.
The Romans had no sign for zero.
The year 2026 is written MMXXVI.

abschnitte.text: Roman numerals manage with seven signs: **I**, **V**, **X**, **L**, **C**, **D** and **M**. I means one, V five and X ten. L stands for 50, C for 100, D for 500 and M for 1,000. C fits the Latin word “centum” for hundred. M fits “mille”, the Latin word for thousand.

Mostly one simply adds the signs together. **III** is 1 + 1 + 1, that is, 3. **XX** is 10 + 10, that is, 20. **XII** is 10 + 2, that is, 12. Here the larger sign always stands first. A sign is normally written at most three times in a row.

If a smaller sign stands **before** a larger one, it is subtracted. **IV** is 5 minus 1, that is, 4. **IX** is 10 minus 1, that is, 9. **XIV** is 10 plus 4, that is, 14. So, for example, **MMXXVI** becomes the number 2,000 + 20 + 6, that is, 2026.

The Romans had **no sign for zero**. That made calculating with large numbers difficult. Our present-day digits 0 to 9 came from India by way of the Arab world to Europe. With them and the zero one can calculate much more easily. So they slowly became established in the Middle Ages and the early modern period.

Roman numerals can still be found in many places. On some **clocks** they stand instead of digits. With kings and popes they show which of that name someone was. Chapters in books or dates on old houses are also often written this way. In Switzerland they can be seen, for example, on churches and old town halls.

gewusst: On many clocks the four is shown as IIII instead of IV.
The largest number one can write with the simple rules is MMMCMXCIX, that is, 3,999.
The signs I, V and X probably go back to strokes, such as one makes when counting.

teile.einleitung: The Pax Romana was a long period of peace in the Roman Empire. It began with Emperor Augustus and lasted about 200 years. In this time trade, cities and roads flourished, also in the area of present-day Switzerland.
wichtigste: “Pax Romana” means “Roman Peace”.
It began with Emperor Augustus and lasted about 200 years.
It is usually taken to end with the death of Emperor Marcus Aurelius in 180.
In Rome the Altar of Peace, Ara Pacis, was dedicated in 9 BC.
When there was peace everywhere, the gates of the Temple of Janus were closed.
Thanks to the peace, trade flourished throughout the empire.

abschnitte.text: **Pax Romana** is Latin and means **Roman Peace**. It refers to the time in which there were hardly any great wars inside the huge Roman Empire. On the borders fighting did continue. But in most provinces people could live, travel and trade in safety. This time lasted about **200 years**.

The Pax Romana began with **Augustus**, the first Roman emperor. After many civil wars he provided calm and order. In honour of this peace the **Ara Pacis**, an altar of peace, was dedicated in Rome in 9 BC. An old sign of peace was the **Temple of Janus**: when there was peace throughout the empire, its gates were closed. Under Augustus that happened several times, which had been very rare before.

Because it was safe, **trade** flourished. Goods such as wine, olive oil, grain and pottery were transported over long distances. A dense network of **roads** linked the provinces. On the Mediterranean many merchant ships sailed. Everywhere cities arose with baths, theatres and aqueducts.

Later emperors ruled who chose their successor not by kinship but by ability. They adopted him, that is, took him as a son. That is why the emperors from **Nerva to Marcus Aurelius** are called the **adoptive emperors**. With the death of **Marcus Aurelius** in 180 the Pax Romana is usually taken to end. After that the empire became more unsettled.

The area of present-day Switzerland also belonged to the Roman Empire. On Lake Geneva near present-day **Nyon** lay the Roman colony **Colonia Iulia Equestris**. Other important places were **Aventicum**, present-day Avenches, and **Augusta Raurica** near Basel. In the time of peace these cities grew and were equipped with temples, theatres and baths.

gewusst: The Ara Pacis can still be visited in Rome today, and it stands in a modern museum building.
At Augusta Raurica near Basel one can visit a large Roman theatre.

teile.einleitung: The Parthenon is a temple on the Acropolis in Athens. It was built about 2,500 years ago for the goddess Athena. It is regarded as one of the most famous buildings in the world.
wichtigste: The Parthenon was dedicated to the goddess Athena, the patron goddess of Athens.
It was built about 2,500 years ago, between 447 and 432 BC.
The building material is white marble.
On the front there are 8 columns.
The figures on the temple were once painted in colour.
Many figures are today in the British Museum in London.

abschnitte.text: The Parthenon stands on the **Acropolis**, a rocky hill in the middle of Athens. It was dedicated to the goddess **Athena**, who was regarded as the patron goddess of the city. Inside stood a huge statue of the goddess made of gold and ivory. It was created by the sculptor **Phidias**. The name Parthenon comes from “Parthenos”, an epithet of Athena.

The temple was built of white **marble** from a quarry near Athens. The architects were called **Iktinos and Kallikrates**. On the front and the back there are **8 columns** each, on the long sides 17 each. The columns are in the **Doric style**, that is, plain and strong. The builders shaped many lines very slightly curved so that the building looks straight and harmonious from afar.

At the top of the temple there were many **reliefs and figures**. A long band shows a festive procession in honour of Athena. Today we see the marble white. In the past, however, the figures were **painted in colour**. Researchers have found tiny traces of paint that prove it.

The Parthenon later became a church and then a mosque. In **1687** gunpowder was stored in it. During an attack it exploded, and a large part of the temple was destroyed. Since then the Parthenon has stood as a ruin. Today it is carefully restored and is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

At the beginning of the 19th century the British diplomat **Lord Elgin** had many figures removed and brought to England. They are today displayed in the **British Museum in London**. Greece would like them back and shows its pieces in the **Acropolis Museum** in Athens. This question has been disputed for many years.

gewusst: Hardly a line on the Parthenon is quite straight, yet it looks perfectly regular.
Many buildings in the world, including banks and museums, imitate the columns of the Parthenon.

teile.einleitung: An abbot is the head of a monastery of monks. He leads the community and makes sure the monastic rules are kept. A convent of women is led by an abbess.
wichtigste: An **abbot** leads a men's monastery, an **abbess** a women's convent.
The word comes from **“Abba”**, which means **father**.
Usually the **monks** elect their abbot.
As a sign of his office, the abbot carries a **crozier**.
The monks owe the abbot **obedience**.
The abbot's deputy is called the **prior**.
The abbot of St Gallen was also a territorial ruler as a **prince-abbot**.

abschnitte.text: The word **abbot** comes from the Aramaic word **“Abba”**, which means **father**. The abbot is meant to be like a father to the monks. He leads the common life, the praying and the work in the monastery. Important for this was the **Rule of St Benedict**. It describes how an abbot should run his monastery.

Usually the abbot was elected by the **monks**. Often he stayed in office all his life. The monks owed him **obedience**, so they had to follow his instructions. But the abbot was meant to be just and to listen to the advice of the brothers. His deputy was called the **prior**.

As a sign of his office, an abbot carries a **crozier**, also called an abbot's staff. It is curved at the top like a shepherd's staff. This is meant to show that the abbot leads his community as a shepherd leads his flock. On special occasions many abbots also wear a tall hat, the **mitre**.

A women's convent is led by an **abbess**. In the Middle Ages, some abbesses were very powerful. In **Zurich**, an abbess ran the **Fraumünster**. The abbey owned a lot of land and had great influence on the city. The last abbess handed the convent over to the city of Zurich at the time of the Reformation.

Some abbots were not only spiritual leaders but also **territorial rulers**. They governed land and people like a prince. The abbot of **St Gallen** therefore bore the title **prince-abbot**. His territory covered large parts of present-day eastern Switzerland. Even today there are monasteries in Switzerland with an abbot, for example **Einsiedeln** and **Engelberg**.

gewusst: The Abbey Precinct of St Gallen with the famous Abbey Library is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The abbot of Einsiedeln leads a community of Benedictine monks that has existed for over a thousand years.

teile.einleitung: Paper is one of the most important materials of humankind. It was invented in China and took many centuries to reach Europe. Without paper there would be no cheap books, exercise books or newspapers.
wichtigste: Paper was invented in China.
The official Cai Lun improved its manufacture around the year 105 AD and is therefore regarded as the inventor.
The first paper consisted of plant fibres and old scraps of cloth, that is, rags.
Before that people in China often wrote on bamboo strips or on silk.
In papermaking the fibre pulp is scooped out of the water with a sieve.
The Arabs brought papermaking to Europe via Spain.
In Basel one can scoop paper oneself at the Basler Papiermühle, the Basel Paper Mill.

abschnitte.text: Before there was paper, people in China wrote on **bamboo strips**. The narrow strips were tied together with cords into books. Such books were heavy and took up a lot of space. One could also write on **silk**, but silk was very expensive. In Egypt people used **papyrus** from a marsh plant, and in Europe people later often wrote on **parchment** made of animal skin.

The inventor of paper is regarded as **Cai Lun**, an official at the Chinese imperial court. Around the year 105 AD he improved its manufacture so much that paper became good and cheap. Finds show, however, that there was simple paper in China even before. **Tree bark, hemp and rags** were boiled to a pulp. From it came thin, light sheets that were good to write on.

First the fibres are chopped up and stirred with a lot of water into a **fibre pulp**. Then a fine **sieve** is dipped into the pulp and lifted out. The water runs off, and a thin layer of fibres is left on the sieve. This layer is pressed and dried. Today large machines make paper mainly from **wood** and waste paper, but the principle has stayed the same.

The Chinese kept their knowledge secret for a long time. Later the **Arabs** learned papermaking and built paper mills in their cities. Via **Spain** the art reached Europe, where there was paper only in the Middle Ages. Gradually **paper mills** driven by water power also arose in other countries. When printing came into use, a great deal of paper was needed.

In **Basel** paper was already being made in the late Middle Ages. In the St Alban valley there stands today the **Basler Papiermühle**, a museum of paper, writing and printing. A water wheel still turns there. Visitors can scoop a sheet of paper themselves and see how printing was done in the past.

gewusst: Our word “paper” comes from the Egyptian papyrus, although papyrus is not really paper.
Rags from old clothes were for a long time the most important raw material for paper in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The Palace of Knossos on Crete is the largest building of the Minoan civilisation. It is about 3,500 years old and closely linked with the legend of the Labyrinth and the Minotaur.
wichtigste: Knossos lies on Crete, the largest island of Greece.
The Minoan civilisation is named after the legendary King Minos.
The palace's heyday was about 3,500 years ago.
The red wooden columns grow narrower towards the bottom.
Bulls can be seen in many wall paintings.
Arthur Evans excavated the palace from 1900.

abschnitte.text: **Knossos** lies on **Crete**, the largest island of Greece, near the present-day city of Heraklion. There in the **Bronze Age** lived the **Minoans**. The palace arose about 4,000 years ago and was rebuilt several times. Its **heyday** was about **3,500 years ago**. It had many storeys, stairways, courts, storerooms with huge clay jars and pipes for water. Around a great central court lay hundreds of rooms.

The **columns** in the Palace of Knossos are something special. They were made of **wood**, painted red and **wider at the top than at the bottom**. That is exactly the opposite of the later Greek temples. Also famous are the colourful **wall paintings**, the frescoes. They show dolphins, flowers, processions and people. In many pictures the **bull** can be seen. Young people leap over bulls there. The bull was an important animal on Crete.

The civilisation on Crete is called the **Minoan civilisation**, after the legendary **King Minos**. According to the legend Minos had the brilliant inventor **Daedalus** build a **labyrinth** in order to shut up the **Minotaur** in it. The hero **Theseus** defeated the monster. With a **woollen thread** that the king's daughter gave him, he found his way out again. Daedalus later fled from Crete with his son **Icarus** on wings.

From the year **1900** the Englishman **Arthur Evans** excavated the palace. He found wall paintings, clay tablets with written signs and many objects. Evans also rebuilt some parts, for example columns and stairways, partly with concrete. These reconstructions help visitors to imagine the palace. Experts criticise them, however, because it is not always known exactly what it looked like in the past.

gewusst: The columns of Knossos are wider at the top than at the bottom, so the reverse of Greek temples.
Some rooms of the palace already had water pipes of clay.

teile.einleitung: Thales of Miletus was a Greek thinker who lived around 2600 years ago. He is regarded as one of the first philosophers, because he wanted to explain the world through nature instead of stories about gods. His name is still well known in mathematics today, too.
wichtigste: Thales lived in Miletus in the 7th and 6th centuries BC.
He believed that everything had come from water.
He is said to have predicted the solar eclipse of 585 BC.
Thales's theorem is named after him: every angle in a semicircle measures 90 degrees.
He is said to have worked out the height of the pyramids from their shadows.
The Greeks counted him among the Seven Sages.
He is said to have studied amber, which attracts light things after being rubbed.

abschnitte.text: Thales lived in **Miletus**, a rich Greek port city on the west coast of present-day Turkey. He asked what the world is actually made of. His answer was: **water**. What mattered was not so much the answer as the way of asking. Thales was one of the first to look for a **natural** explanation instead of a story about gods. That is why he is regarded as one of the first **philosophers**.

According to the historian **Herodotus**, Thales predicted a **solar eclipse**. It took place on 28 May **585 BC** during a battle between the Lydians and the Medes. When it suddenly became dark, the fighters were so frightened that they made **peace**. We do not know exactly how Thales was able to predict the eclipse.

In mathematics we know **Thales's theorem**. It says: if one side of a triangle is the diameter of a circle and the third corner lies on the circle, then the angle at that corner is always **90 degrees**. This holds no matter where the corner lies on the semicircle. Pupils in Switzerland also learn this theorem in geometry lessons.

Thales is said to have travelled to **Egypt**. There he is said to have worked out the height of the **pyramids** from their **shadows**. He waited until his own shadow was exactly as long as he was tall. At that moment the shadow of the pyramid was also as long as its height. This idea is still used today to measure tall trees or towers.

Thales is also said to have studied **amber**. When you rub it, it attracts light things such as hair or feathers. The Greek word for amber is **elektron**. Our word **electricity** comes from it. The Greeks counted Thales among the **Seven Sages**, famous thinkers and statesmen of the early period. He is named in all the surviving lists.

gewusst: According to an anecdote, Thales fell into a well because he was only looking at the stars as he walked.
Not a single piece of writing by Thales himself survives, and everything we know comes from later accounts.

teile.einleitung: In Greek legend Poseidon was the god of the sea. He carried a trident and could cause storms and earthquakes. Among the Romans he was called Neptune.
wichtigste: Poseidon was the god of the sea.
His weapon was a trident.
His brother Zeus was king of the gods.
He was also the god of horses.
He could cause storms and earthquakes.
He lived in a palace in the sea, and his wife was called Amphitrite.
Among the Romans he was called Neptune.

abschnitte.text: **Poseidon** was one of the most important gods of the Greeks. He ruled over the **sea**, the lakes and the rivers. His weapon was a **trident**, a spear with three points. With it he could stir up the waves or calm the sea. Sailors and fishermen prayed to him for a good voyage.

Poseidon was a son of the Titan Cronus and of Rhea. His brothers were **Zeus** and **Hades**. According to the legend the three divided the world among themselves. Zeus became king of the gods and lord of the sky, Hades received the underworld and Poseidon the sea. Among the Romans Poseidon was called **Neptune**.

When Poseidon was angry, he sent **storms** over the sea. He could also shake the earth and cause **earthquakes**. That is why the Greeks also called him the “Earth-Shaker”. In a land with many coasts and frequent earthquakes he was therefore a much feared god. Odysseus had to feel his wrath on the long journey home.

Besides the sea, Poseidon was also the god of **horses**. According to one legend he created the first horse. People imagined that his chariot was drawn over the waves by horses with golden manes. He quarrelled with the goddess Athena over the city of Athens. She gave the Athenians an olive tree and won the contest.

According to the legend Poseidon lived in a magnificent **palace** deep **in the sea**. His wife was the sea goddess **Amphitrite**. Their son **Triton** is often shown half as a human, half as a fish. On a rock at Cape Sounion near Athens the columns of a temple to Poseidon still stand today.

gewusst: The planet Neptune is named after the Roman sea god, and its symbol is a trident.
In many cities there are Neptune fountains on which the god can be seen with his trident.

teile.einleitung: Persepolis was a magnificent residential city of the Persian kings. Its ruins lie in present-day Iran. They show how powerful and rich the ancient Persian Empire was.
wichtigste: King Darius I had building begun around 520 BC.
The ruins lie in present-day Iran.
The Greek name “Persepolis” means “City of the Persians”.
The great audience hall with tall columns is called the Apadana.
Xerxes I had the “Gate of All Nations” erected.
Alexander the Great had Persepolis set on fire in 330 BC.
Since 1979 Persepolis has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: Around **520 BC** King **Darius I** had building of Persepolis begun. The Persians called the place Parsa. The Greek name **Persepolis** means **City of the Persians**. The palaces stood on a huge **terrace** at the foot of a mountain. Here the kings held great festivals and received guests from the whole empire.

The most important building was the **Apadana**, a large audience hall. Its roof was carried by many very tall columns. Darius's son **Xerxes I** built further. He had the **“Gate of All Nations”** erected, through which visitors entered the terrace. Mighty bull figures with human heads guarded the entrance.

On the stairways of the Apadana long **reliefs** are carved in the stone. They show **delegations** from many peoples bringing **gifts** to the king. One sees, for example, animals, cloths, vessels and jewellery. Each people wears its own clothing. In this way the pictures show how large and varied the Persian Empire was.

In **330 BC** **Alexander the Great** conquered the Persian Empire. He had Persepolis plundered and **set on fire**. Why he did so is still not entirely certain. The wooden roofs burned, but many stone parts remained standing. Above the terrace the **tombs** of later Achaemenid kings are cut into the rock.

From **1931** the German archaeologist **Ernst Herzfeld** led the first large scientific excavations. In them many reliefs and clay tablets came to light. In **1979** Persepolis was inscribed as a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Today it is one of the most important sights in **Iran**, near the city of Shiraz.

gewusst: At Persepolis thousands of clay tablets were found on which, for example, wage payments to workers are recorded.
The fire baked and hardened some clay tablets and so preserved them for us.

teile.einleitung: The naval Battle of Salamis took place in autumn 480 BC off the coast near Athens. There the Greek fleet defeated the much larger fleet of the Persians. The victory was a turning point of the Persian Wars.
wichtigste: The naval Battle of Salamis took place in 480 BC.
Themistocles is regarded as the father of the victory.
The Greeks fought with triremes, ships with three rows of rowers.
Salamis is an island in the Saronic Gulf near Athens.
In the narrow strait the great Persian fleet could not deploy.
Athens paid for its fleet with silver from the mines of Laurium.
After the defeat the Persian king withdrew to Asia with part of the army.

abschnitte.text: At **Laurium** in Attica a rich vein of silver was found some years before 480 BC. The politician **Themistocles** pushed through that Athens should not distribute the silver. Instead the city used it to build about **200 triremes**. So Athens became a strong naval power. This decision was very important for the later victory.

A **trireme** was a fast warship with three rows of rowers one above another. About **170 rowers** drove it. At the front, at the bow, it had a bronze **ram**. With it one rammed enemy ships and sank them. In Athens it was mainly poorer citizens who rowed, and they thereby became more important to the city.

After the fall of **Thermopylae** the Persian army marched on Athens. Most inhabitants left their city. Women, children and the old were taken to **Salamis** and Troezen. The Persians occupied the empty city and laid it waste, including the temples on the Acropolis. The men meanwhile waited on the ships.

The island of **Salamis** lies in the **Saronic Gulf**, only a few kilometres from Piraeus, the harbour of Athens. Themistocles lured the Persians into the **narrow strait** between the island and the mainland. There the many Persian ships got in one another's way. The smaller Greek fleet could attack better and won. According to Herodotus the Persian king **Xerxes** watched the battle from a hill on the coast.

After the loss of many ships Xerxes returned with part of the army to **Asia Minor**. The rest of the Persian land army was defeated in 479 BC at **Plataea**. With that the danger to Greece was averted. Athens became very powerful in the following decades. Many see in Salamis a reason why Greek culture could develop freely.

gewusst: The poet Aeschylus later wrote the play “The Persians” about this battle.
A reconstruction of a trireme named Olympias was built and rowed in the 1980s.
The Battle of Salamis is handed down mainly by the historian Herodotus.

teile.einleitung: The Principate is the form of rule of the early Roman imperial period. Augustus ruled as sole ruler but outwardly left the old institutions of the Republic in place. The name comes from “princeps”, the “first citizen”.
wichtigste: The word Principate comes from “princeps”, which means “first citizen”.
After the naval battle of Actium in 31 BC Octavian was undisputed master of the empire.
From 27 BC he bore the honorary name Augustus.
The imperium proconsulare maius gave him control of the provinces with legions.
The tribunician power gave him the right of veto and inviolability.
The Praetorian Guard served as bodyguard.
Later the Dominate replaced the Principate.

abschnitte.text: After the death of Caesar several men fought for power in Rome. Caesar's adopted son **Octavian** defeated the fleet of Marcus Antonius and Cleopatra in **31 BC** in the **Battle of Actium**. After that he was the **undisputed master** of the Roman Empire. In 27 BC the Senate gave him the honorary name **Augustus**, the Revered One. With that the Principate begins.

Augustus did not call himself king, for kings were hated in Rome. He called himself **princeps**, **first citizen**. From this the word **Principate** derives. The Senate, the consuls and other offices of the **Republic** remained in place. In reality, however, power lay with the princeps. So people speak of rule with a republican façade.

The power of Augustus rested on special rights. The **imperium proconsulare maius** gave him the superior power of command over the **provinces with legions**. So he controlled the army. The **tribunician power** gave him the **right of veto** and made him **inviolable**, without his holding the office of a tribune of the people. In Rome the **Praetorian Guard**, the imperial bodyguard, protected him.

Shortly before his death in 14 AD Augustus summarised his achievements in a report. It is called **Res Gestae Divi Augusti**, the deeds of the divine Augustus. In it he lists his victories, buildings and gifts to the people. An almost complete copy survives on a temple in Ankara. Naturally Augustus presents himself very favourably in it.

The Principate lasted about three centuries. In the 3rd century AD the empire fell into a serious crisis. Under Emperor Diocletian rule changed greatly. The emperor now openly appeared as ruler over all. This late antique form of rule is called by scholars the **Dominate**, after the Latin word “dominus”, lord.

gewusst: The month of August is named after Emperor Augustus.
The English word “prince” goes back to the Latin term “princeps”.

teile.einleitung: The Persian Wars were wars between the huge Persian Empire and Greek city-states in the 5th century BC. Famous battles such as Marathon, Thermopylae and Salamis belong to them. In the end the Greeks were able to hold their own.
wichtigste: The trigger was the Ionian Revolt of Greek cities in Asia Minor.
In 490 BC a Persian army under Datis and Artaphernes landed in Attica and was defeated at Marathon.
From 481 Sparta led the Hellenic League against King Xerxes I.
At Thermopylae the Persians outflanked the Greeks by a mountain path.
In 480 Xerxes I saw the defeat of his fleet at Salamis.
In 479 the Greeks won at Plataea on land and at Mycale at sea.
Our most important narrator of these wars is Herodotus.

abschnitte.text: On the coast of Asia Minor, in present-day Turkey, lay many Greek cities. They belonged to the **Persian Empire**. Around 500 BC they rose against the Persians in the **Ionian Revolt**. Athens sent them ships to help. The Persians put down the revolt and now wanted to punish Athens.

In **490 BC** a Persian army under **Datis and Artaphernes** landed in Attica. According to Herodotus the runner **Pheidippides** had beforehand run from Athens to Sparta to fetch help. At **Marathon** the Athenians with their allies defeated the Persians. The memory of this battle lives on in the marathon race of today.

The Athenians sensed that the Persians would come back. With the yield of the silver mines of **Laurion** they greatly expanded their **war fleet**. The politician Themistocles had proposed this. In **481** many Greek cities joined together in the **Hellenic League**. **Sparta** took the leadership.

In 480 BC King **Xerxes I** marched into Greece with a huge army. At **Thermopylae**, a narrow pass, the Greeks under the Spartan king Leonidas held up the Persians. According to Herodotus a man named **Ephialtes** betrayed a **mountain path** to the Persians, so that they could outflank the Greeks. Shortly afterwards the Greeks lured the Persian fleet into the narrow strait at **Salamis** and defeated it. Xerxes watched the defeat from the shore.

In **479 BC** the Greeks finally defeated the Persian army at **Plataea**. Almost at the same time they destroyed the remains of the Persian fleet at **Mycale** on the coast of Asia Minor. With that the danger to Greece was over. Athens afterwards became a leading sea power. The historian **Herodotus** later told it all in detail.

gewusst: Herodotus is often called the “Father of History”.
The marathon race of today is a good 42 kilometres long and recalls the battle of Marathon.

teile.einleitung: Ramesses II was one of the most powerful pharaohs of ancient Egypt. He ruled for about 66 years and had huge temples and statues built. That is why he received the epithet “the Great”.
wichtigste: Ramesses II ruled for about 66 years, in the 13th century BC.
He received the epithet “the Great”.
Around 1274 BC he fought the Hittites at Kadesh in Syria.
Later he concluded a peace treaty with the Hittites.
Over 80 sons and daughters of his are known.
His mortuary temple in Thebes is called the Ramesseum, and he was buried in the Valley of the Kings.
He is estimated to have lived to about 90 years of age.

abschnitte.text: **Ramesses II** ruled in the 13th century BC for **about 66 years**. He is estimated to have lived to **about 90 years** of age. So he outlived many of his children. **Over 80 sons and daughters** of his are known. Because of his power and his many buildings he received the epithet **“the Great”**.

Around **1274 BC** Ramesses II marched against the **Hittites**, a powerful people from the north. At the city of **Kadesh** in present-day **Syria** a great battle with many chariots took place. Ramesses fell into great danger. Neither side could win clearly. Nevertheless Ramesses had the battle shown as a great victory on many temple walls.

Some years later Ramesses II concluded a **peace treaty** with the Hittites. It is regarded as one of the oldest known peace treaties in the world. Both empires promised not to attack each other any more and to help each other. A copy was found on clay tablets in the Hittite capital. A replica hangs today in the United Nations building in New York.

Ramesses II had building done throughout Egypt. Best known are the rock temples of **Abu Simbel** with four huge seated statues of the king. In **Thebes** he had his mortuary temple erected, the **Ramesseum**. He was buried in the **Valley of the Kings**. His mummy was later taken to a safe place and found only in the 19th century.

The Greeks called Ramesses II **Ozymandias**. Under this name the English poet Percy Shelley wrote a famous **poem**. It tells of a broken statue in the desert. On its pedestal a king boasts of his power, but all around there is nothing but sand. The poem shows that even the greatest power passes.

gewusst: The temples of Abu Simbel were taken apart in the 1960s and rebuilt higher up so that they would not sink beneath a reservoir.
The mummy of Ramesses II was flown to Paris for examination in 1976.

teile.einleitung: The Peloponnesian War was a long war in ancient Greece. From 431 to 404 BC Athens and Sparta, with their allies, fought against each other. In the end Sparta won, and Athens lost its leading position.
wichtigste: The war lasted from 431 to 404 BC.
The main opponents were Athens and Sparta with their allies.
Athens led the Delian League.
The first phase from 431 to 421 is called the Archidamian War.
In 413 BC Athens' expedition to Sicily ended in disaster.
The Persian Empire gave Sparta money for a fleet.
The Spartan Lysander destroyed the Athenian fleet in 405, and Sparta won the war.

abschnitte.text: **Athens** was a rich city with a large fleet. It led the **Delian League**, an alliance of many cities by the sea. **Sparta** had the strongest land army in Greece and led the Peloponnesian League. Both sides mistrusted each other more and more. In **431 BC** the war broke out.

The first phase from 431 to 421 is called the **Archidamian War**, after the Spartan king Archidamus. Every year the Spartans marched into Attica and laid waste the fields. The Athenians withdrew behind their city walls and attacked with their ships. In the overcrowded city a serious **plague** broke out, from which many died. In 421 both sides made a peace, which did not last long, however.

In 415 Athens sent a great fleet to **Sicily**. One of the leaders was the gifted politician **Alcibiades**. He was soon accused and defected to Sparta. Later he changed sides several more times. The expedition ended in **413 BC** with a heavy defeat in which Athens lost almost its whole army and many ships.

Towards the end of the war the **Persian Empire** supported Sparta with money. With it Sparta could build a fleet of its own. In **405 BC** the Spartan general **Lysander** destroyed the Athenian fleet at **Aegospotami**. Without ships Athens could no longer import grain. In 404 the city had to give up and tear down its walls.

We know a great deal about this war because **Thucydides** wrote it down. He was an Athenian and experienced the war himself as an **eyewitness**. Thucydides wanted to report exactly and to understand the causes. That is why he is regarded as one of the first true **historians**. His work, however, breaks off before the end of the war.

gewusst: The war lasted 27 years and shook almost the whole Greek world.
Thucydides was himself a general in the war and was banished from Athens after a defeat.

teile.einleitung: The vizier was the most important official after the pharaoh in ancient Egypt. He ran the administration of the country. Without him and his many scribes, the great empire on the Nile could not have worked.
wichtigste: The vizier was the **highest official after the pharaoh**.
In the New Kingdom there were **two** viziers at the same time.
Egypt was divided into districts, the **nomes**.
The backbone of the administration was the **scribes**.
With **Nilometers**, harvest and taxes were estimated.
In the tomb of the vizier **Rekhmire** there is a well-known set of instructions for his office.

abschnitte.text: The **pharaoh** was the king of Egypt. For the day-to-day work of government he had a **vizier**. He was the **highest official after the pharaoh**. The vizier was responsible for courts, taxes, building projects and stores. He reported to the king regularly on what was happening in the country. The word “vizier” comes from Arabic, and the ancient Egyptians used a title of their own.

In the **New Kingdom** there were at times **two viziers** at once. One was responsible for the south, that is, Upper Egypt. The other was responsible for the north, Lower Egypt. In this way the long land along the Nile could be administered better.

A famous vizier was **Rekhmire**. His tomb lies near **Thebes** in Upper Egypt. On its walls the best-known version of the **“Duties of the Vizier”** survives. It describes how the vizier should work and judge fairly. Pictures also show craftsmen, farmers and tribute from foreign lands.

Egypt was divided into administrative districts, the **nomes**. Each nome had its own officials. The **backbone** of the administration was the **scribes**. They could read and write hieroglyphs, which only a few people could do. They counted stores, wrote lists and recorded taxes.

Every year the Nile overflowed its banks and made the fields fertile. With a **Nilometer** people measured how high the water rose. From this the **harvest could be estimated**. The better the harvest, the higher the **taxes**. These taxes were usually paid in grain and other goods.

gewusst: The scribes in ancient Egypt were respected, because reading and writing was a rare skill.
In later Islamic empires too, the chief minister was called vizier. That is where the name for the Egyptian office comes from.

teile.einleitung: Thermae were large public bathhouses in ancient Rome. Many Romans bathed there almost every day, did sport and met friends. In Roman times there were baths like this in Switzerland too.
wichtigste: Thermae were large public bathhouses.
The caldarium was the hot room and the tepidarium the lukewarm one.
In the frigidarium there was a cold bath.
With a scraper, the strigil, people removed oil and dirt from the skin.
Admission cost only a little money.
Aqueducts brought the large amounts of water into the city.
In Baden in Aargau, the Romans already bathed in hot springs.

abschnitte.text: Thermae were **public baths**. Admission was very **cheap**, so even poor people could go bathing. Many Romans visited the baths almost every day, usually in the afternoon. In the city of Rome there were huge complexes, such as the **Baths of Caracalla** and the **Baths of Diocletian**. There were also many smaller baths in the city districts and in the provinces.

The bathers first undressed in a changing room. Then they went through different rooms. In the **tepidarium** it was pleasantly **lukewarm**. In the **caldarium** the water was hot and the air warm and humid. The word comes from the Latin “calidus”, meaning hot. Finally, you cooled off in the **frigidarium** in a **cold bath**. “Frigidus” means cold.

To make the rooms warm, the Romans had a clever invention: **underfloor heating**, the **hypocaust**. The floor stood on small pillars made of bricks. Hot air from a furnace flowed through underneath and warmed the floor and walls. The large amounts of water came into the city through **aqueducts**. These brought in fresh spring water on a gentle slope, often over many kilometres.

The Romans hardly used **soap** as we know it. Instead they rubbed themselves with **oil**. Then they scraped the oil off again together with the sweat and dirt. For this they used a curved metal **scraper**, the **strigil**. Many baths also had a sports ground. You could play ball, wrestle, chat and swap news.

In **Baden** in the canton of Aargau, warm water bubbles out of the ground. The Romans called the place **Aquae Helveticae** and built baths there. Baden is still a well-known spa town today. In other Roman places in present-day Switzerland too, for example in **Augusta Raurica** near Basel, archaeologists have found the remains of baths.

gewusst: The Baths of Caracalla in Rome were so big that thousands of people could bathe there at the same time.
Our word “thermometer” has the same Greek root as thermae: “thermos” means warm.

teile.einleitung: Purple is a red-violet dye that in antiquity was obtained from sea snails. It was so expensive that mainly kings and emperors wore it. The Phoenicians were especially famous for their purple.
wichtigste: Purple has a red-violet colour.
It was obtained from the juice of purple snails.
In light and air this juice changes its colour.
For a little dye one needed a great many snails, which is why purple was expensive.
The production smelled terrible.
The Phoenician city of Tyre was famous for its purple.
Kings and emperors wore clothes made of purple.

abschnitte.text: Purple comes from **purple snails**, which live in the Mediterranean. These sea snails have a small gland with a colourless or yellowish **juice**. When the juice comes into contact with **light and air**, **it changes its colour**. It turns first greenish and then **red-violet**. With this juice one could dye fabrics permanently.

A single snail yields only tiny amounts of dye. For a single gram one needed **a great many snails**, probably many thousands. That is why purple was extremely **expensive**, at times more expensive than gold. The production was also very unpleasant: the snails rotted in large basins, and it **smelled terrible**. Workshops were therefore often on the edge of towns.

The **Phoenicians** were especially famous for their purple. Their city **Tyre** on the coast of present-day Lebanon was known for the finest purple. The Phoenicians **dyed fabrics and clothes** with it and sold them throughout the Mediterranean. Their name probably comes from the Greek word for purple-red. So Phoenician probably means **“the Purple People”**.

Because purple was so precious, it was worn mainly by **kings and emperors**. Among the Romans senators had a purple stripe on the toga. Later only the emperor was allowed to wear a robe that was entirely purple. So purple became the colour of **power**. Even today cardinals of the Catholic Church wear red robes that are called purple.

gewusst: Since the 19th century dyes can be made artificially, which is why purple is quite ordinary and cheap today.
In excavations whole mountains of broken purple snail shells were found.

teile.einleitung: The Anglo-Saxons were Germanic peoples who came to Britain in the 5th century. They founded kingdoms there from which England later arose.
wichtigste: The Anglo-Saxons consisted mainly of Angles and Saxons, with Jutes as well.
Some of them came from the region of Angeln in present-day Schleswig-Holstein.
They came in the 5th century, after the Romans had left Britain around 410.
England means “land of the Angles”.
They spoke Old English, and the heroic poem “Beowulf” is famous.
Alfred the Great, king of Wessex, defended his kingdom against the Vikings.

abschnitte.text: Around the year 410, the **Romans** left Britain. Soon afterwards, in the **5th century**, Germanic groups sailed across the North Sea. They were mainly **Angles** and **Saxons**, with the **Jutes** as well. The Angles came from the region of **Angeln** on the Baltic Sea in present-day Schleswig-Holstein. In Britain these groups founded several kingdoms, for example Wessex, Mercia and Northumbria.

The word **England** means “land of the Angles”. The word **English** also comes from this people. The Anglo-Saxons spoke **Old English**. This language sounds foreign to us today, but present-day English developed from it. Many everyday English words come from this time.

At first the Anglo-Saxons believed in Germanic gods. In 597, Pope **Gregory the Great** sent the monk **Augustine** to Kent. Augustine baptised King Æthelberht and became the first **Archbishop of Canterbury**. Little by little the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms became Christian. Monasteries became places of learning and writing.

A famous work of the Anglo-Saxons is the heroic poem **“Beowulf”**. It tells of a hero who fights monsters and a dragon. At **Sutton Hoo** in the east of England, a royal grave with a whole **ship** was found. It included a magnificent helmet, gold jewellery and many other treasures. The find shows how rich Anglo-Saxon kings were.

In the 9th century, the **Vikings** attacked England and conquered large areas. **Alfred the Great**, king of **Wessex**, successfully defended his kingdom. He had fortified towns built and promoted education. His successors later united England into one kingdom. The Anglo-Saxon period ended in 1066 with the conquest by the Normans.

gewusst: The Sutton Hoo helmet can be seen in the British Museum in London today.
The English days of the week Wednesday and Thursday are named after the Germanic gods Woden and Thunor.

teile.einleitung: The statue of Zeus by Phidias stood in the Temple of Zeus at Olympia in Greece. It was made of gold and ivory and was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Today it is lost.
wichtigste: The sculptor **Phidias** created the statue of Zeus.
It stood in the **Temple of Zeus at Olympia** on the **Peloponnese** peninsula.
Zeus sat on a **throne**.
The statue was decorated with **gold and ivory**.
It was about **12 metres** high.
It counted as one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

abschnitte.text: **Olympia** lies on the Greek **Peloponnese** peninsula. In ancient times the place was a sanctuary of the god **Zeus**. Olympia was famous for the **Olympic Games**, which took place every four years in honour of Zeus. A large temple, the **Temple of Zeus**, was built for the statue of the god.

The statue was made by the famous Athenian sculptor **Phidias** around the middle of the 5th century BC. Earlier he had already made a great statue of the goddess Athena in Athens. Phidias was regarded as one of the best artists of his time. In Olympia he worked on his work for several years.

Zeus was shown **seated on a throne**. The statue was about **12 metres high** and filled the temple almost up to the ceiling. Skin and face were made of **ivory**, the robe of **gold**. The throne was richly decorated. Ancient writers wrote that anyone who saw the statue was deeply impressed.

Researchers found the **workshop of Phidias** in Olympia. There lay tools and moulds with which parts of the statue were made. They even found a small jug with the inscription “I belong to Phidias”. In this way the workshop could be assigned to the artist with certainty.

The statue of Zeus was one of the **Seven Wonders of the Ancient World**. These also included the Pyramids of Giza and the Colossus of Rhodes. The statue stayed in Olympia for about 800 years. Later it was taken to Constantinople and was probably lost there in a fire.

gewusst: Of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, only the Pyramids of Giza survive to this day.
What the statue of Zeus looked like we know, among other things, from ancient coins that depict it.

teile.einleitung: The Ziggurat of Ur is a stepped temple tower in the south of present-day Iraq. It was built more than 4000 years ago and is one of the best-preserved ziggurats of Mesopotamia.
wichtigste: A ziggurat is a **stepped temple tower**.
King **Ur-Nammu** had it built around 2100 BC.
The Neo-Babylonian king **Nabonidus** had it renovated in the 6th century BC.
Its core consists of **unbaked mud bricks**.
At the front, **three staircases** led up.
Its Sumerian name is **Etemenniguru**.
It lies in present-day **Iraq**.

abschnitte.text: The city of **Ur** was one of the most important cities of the **Sumerians**. It lay on the Euphrates in the south of Mesopotamia, in present-day **Iraq**. Above the city rose the **ziggurat**, a stepped temple tower. On its top stood a temple for the moon god, the protective god of the city.

King **Ur-Nammu** had the ziggurat built around **2100 BC**. Its Sumerian name is **Etemenniguru**. The core consists of **unbaked mud bricks**. On the outside it was covered with a thick layer of baked bricks joined with bitumen. On some bricks the king's name is written.

At the front, **three staircases** led up: one in the middle and two at the sides along the wall. They met at the top at a gate. From there you went on to the upper steps. Anyone who climbed up had a wide view over the city and the flat land.

More than a thousand years later, the ziggurat had fallen into ruin. The Neo-Babylonian king **Nabonidus** had it renovated in the **6th century BC**. After that it was forgotten again. In the 1920s and 1930s, the British archaeologist **Leonard Woolley** excavated Ur and uncovered the ziggurat.

In the **1980s**, the façade and the staircases of the lowest step were partly **reconstructed**. The upper steps and the temple have not survived. Even so, the Ziggurat of Ur is an impressive building. Together with the ruins of the city it is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: The walls of the ziggurat slope slightly inwards and are somewhat curved. This makes the building look even more massive from below.
Small openings were left in the brick casing so that moisture could escape from the mud core.

teile.einleitung: The Tetrarchy was a form of rule in the Roman Empire introduced by Emperor Diocletian. Instead of a single emperor, four rulers governed together. This was meant to protect the borders better and to prevent struggles over the throne.
wichtigste: Diocletian was proclaimed emperor by the army in AD 284.
He appointed Maximian as co-emperor for the west.
From 293 there were two Augusti and two Caesars.
Diocletian grouped provinces together into dioceses.
The Edict of 301 fixed maximum prices for goods and wages.
In 305 Diocletian resigned and lived in his palace near Split.
According to the legend, Maurice died at Agaunum, today's Saint-Maurice.

abschnitte.text: In the 3rd century AD, the Roman Empire was in a serious crisis. Many emperors were overthrown after a short time, which is why people speak of the **soldier emperors**. In November **284**, the army proclaimed **Diocletian** emperor near Nicomedia. He realised that a single ruler could hardly protect the huge empire with its many threatened borders.

Diocletian appointed **Maximian** as co-emperor. Maximian became Caesar in 285 and **Augustus** in 286 and ruled the west, while Diocletian ruled the east. From **293**, two **Caesars** were added, Constantius and Galerius. Each Augustus ruled with a Caesar as his assistant and later **successor**. This rule by four men is called the **Tetrarchy**, which means “rule of four”.

Diocletian reorganised the administration. He made the provinces smaller and grouped several together into **dioceses**. The word lives on in church administration to this day. In **301** he issued the **Edict on Maximum Prices**. It set upper limits for over a thousand goods and services and was meant to slow down **inflation**. But it had little success. From 303, Diocletian also had the **Christians** persecuted.

A legend from the **Valais** is linked to the time of Maximian. According to it, **Maurice** and his Christian soldiers of the **Theban Legion** refused at Agaunum to take part in persecutions of Christians, and died for it. The place is now named after him: **Saint-Maurice**. The **abbey** there has existed since the year 515 and is regarded as one of the oldest monasteries in the West that has existed without interruption.

In **305**, Diocletian and Maximian resigned of their own free will, which was quite unusual for Roman emperors. Diocletian retired to a **palace** built specially for him on the Dalmatian coast. The old town of **Split** in present-day Croatia is built into its walls. The Tetrarchy did not last long: soon several rulers were fighting for power, until **Constantine** finally ruled alone.

gewusst: In Venice, at St Mark's Basilica, there is a group of figures made of red porphyry showing the four tetrarchs in a close embrace.
Diocletian's Palace in Split is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and people still live in it today.

teile.einleitung: The Antikythera Mechanism is a device of bronze with many cogwheels that is over 2,000 years old. It was found in a shipwreck and is regarded as the oldest known analogue computer in the world.
wichtigste: Greek sponge divers found an ancient shipwreck off the island of Antikythera around 1900/1901.
Only in 1902 did people notice the cogwheels in a piece of bronze.
About 30 bronze cogwheels survive.
The device calculated the positions of the Sun, the Moon and probably also the planets.
It displayed the Saros cycle for predicting eclipses.
Today it is in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

abschnitte.text: Around 1900/1901 Greek **sponge divers** dived off the small island of **Antikythera** between the Peloponnese and Crete. There they came upon an **ancient shipwreck** with statues, coins and other treasures. Among the finds was also an unremarkable, encrusted lump. Only in **1902** did people notice **cogwheels** in it. The ship had sunk in antiquity, probably in the 1st century BC.

Today the mechanism is regarded as the **oldest known analogue computer**. An analogue computer does not calculate with digits but with movement. When one turned a crank, the about **30 bronze cogwheels** moved and showed on dials the positions of the **Sun** and the **Moon** and probably also of the **planets**. A similarly complicated device is not known again until the Middle Ages. Through the seawater the parts are badly corroded, that is, eaten away.

One display shows the **Saros cycle**. It comprises 223 lunar months, about 18 years and 11 days. After it, solar and lunar eclipses repeat in a similar sequence. So eclipses could be predicted. In **2008** researchers also discovered a scale with the names of contests, the **Panhellenic Games** such as the Olympic Games. So the device also served as a calendar.

For a long time nobody knew exactly how the device worked. The physicist and historian of science **Derek de Solla Price** examined the fragments with X-rays and published in **1974** the study “Gears from the Greeks”. He reconstructed the gear train. Later researchers made even finer pictures with modern computed tomography and were able to read tiny inscriptions. The fragments are displayed in the **National Archaeological Museum in Athens**.

gewusst: The mechanism survives only in fragments, and the whole device was about the size of a shoebox.
On the fragments there are tiny Greek inscriptions, a kind of instruction manual.

teile.einleitung: The Valley of the Kings is a desert valley in Egypt where pharaohs were buried for around 500 years. The tombs lie deep in the rock and are painted with colourful pictures. In 1922, the famous tomb of Tutankhamun was found here.
wichtigste: The Valley of the Kings contains the tombs of pharaohs.
It lies on the west bank of the Nile opposite Luxor, the ancient Thebes.
The tombs were cut deep into the rock to protect them from tomb robbers.
More than 60 tombs are known today, and they carry numbers with the letters KV.
Howard Carter found the tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922.
The workers lived in the village of Deir el-Medina.
In the neighbouring valley, the Valley of the Queens, queens and princes were buried.

abschnitte.titel: In the west, where the sun sets
abschnitte.text: The Valley of the Kings lies in the mountains on the **west bank of the Nile**, opposite the present-day city of **Luxor**. In ancient times the city was called **Thebes** and was the capital of Egypt. The sun sets in the west. For the ancient Egyptians, the west was therefore the **land of the dead**. Above the valley rises a mountain peak that looks a little like a pyramid.

Earlier pharaohs had themselves buried in **pyramids**. But these stood out at once and were often robbed. In the **New Kingdom**, the pharaohs therefore had their tombs cut deep into the **rock**. The entrances were well hidden. Even so, almost all the tombs were plundered by **tomb robbers** as early as ancient times. Today **more than 60 tombs** are known. They carry numbers with the letters **KV**.

The walls of many tombs are covered with **colourful paintings** and texts. They show gods and the dead person's journey through the underworld. The Egyptians believed that the pharaoh went on living after death. The pictures and spells were meant to help him reach the **afterlife** safely. The tombs also held furniture, jewellery, food and many other things for the life to come.

The British explorer **Howard Carter** searched the valley for many years. The search was paid for by **Lord Carnarvon**. In **1922**, Carter found the tomb of the young pharaoh **Tutankhamun**. It was almost untouched and full of treasures, including the famous golden **death mask**. The tomb carries the number KV62. The discovery made the valley famous all over the world.

abschnitte.titel: The workers and the neighbouring valley
abschnitte.text: The craftsmen who cut the tombs into the rock and painted them lived in the village of **Deir el-Medina**. There, many inscribed pottery fragments and notes were found about their daily lives, their work and even their quarrels. Only a few kilometres away lies the **Valley of the Queens**. There, mainly the wives and children of the pharaohs were buried. The whole area is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: In ancient times, the workers of Deir el-Medina held one of the first known strikes in history, because their pay did not arrive.
More than 5000 objects were found in the tomb of Tutankhamun.

teile.einleitung: Nero was emperor of Rome from 54 to 68 AD and is one of the best-known Roman emperors. He loved music and theatre, and in his time a large part of the city of Rome burned.
wichtigste: Nero was Roman emperor from 54 to 68 AD.
He became emperor at only 16 years old.
Emperor Claudius had adopted him and was his predecessor.
His teacher was the thinker Seneca.
In 64 a large part of Rome burned.
After that Nero had the palace Domus Aurea, the Golden House, built.
He held the Christians responsible for the fire.

abschnitte.text: **Nero** was born in 37 AD. Emperor **Claudius** adopted him in 50, although he had a son of his own. When Claudius died in **54**, Nero became emperor. He was then only **16 years** old. His teacher was **Seneca**, a well-known thinker and writer. Seneca advised the young emperor and in the first years, together with other advisers, steered many affairs of government.

Nero loved **music** and the **theatre**. For an emperor it was very unusual that he himself appeared before an audience as a **singer**. He played the cithara, a stringed instrument, and took part in competitions. On a journey to Greece he competed at several games and had himself celebrated as the winner. Many distinguished Romans found this unsuitable for a ruler.

In **64** a **great fire** broke out in Rome. The fire raged for several days and destroyed large parts of the city. An old story says that Nero **sang** and made music during the fire. Whether that is true is very uncertain, for he was not in Rome when the fire broke out. According to the historian **Tacitus**, Nero put the blame on the **Christians** to deflect rumours against himself, and had them persecuted.

After the fire Nero had a huge palace with park and lake built on cleared land. In Latin it was called **Domus Aurea**, the **Golden House**. It was very lavish, with gold, precious stones and painted ceilings. After Nero's death the palace was gradually built over. Where the artificial lake lay, the **Colosseum** later arose. Remains of the Golden House can still be visited underground in Rome today.

In time Nero became unpopular with many. He ruled more and more arbitrarily, and the army and the Senate turned against him. In **68** Nero died. He was the last emperor from the family of Augustus. After his death followed the **Year of the Four Emperors**, 69, in which four men in turn fought for power. Many ancient writers described Nero very negatively, so his image is still disputed today.

gewusst: The Colosseum arose where an artificial lake lay in the park of Nero's Golden House.
After Nero came the Year of the Four Emperors, 69, with four emperors in one year.

teile.einleitung: Ostracism, in German Scherbengericht, was a procedure in the democracy of ancient Athens. With it the citizens could banish a politician from the city for ten years if they thought him too powerful.
wichtigste: In ostracism citizens wrote a name on a clay potsherd.
The vote took place on the Agora, the marketplace of Athens.
According to tradition at least 6,000 votes were needed.
The banished man had to leave Attica for ten years.
The politician Themistocles was also banished around 471 BC.
Hyperbolus is regarded as the last man banished.

abschnitte.text: The name **ostracism** comes from the Greek word “**ostrakon**”, which means **potsherd**. Paper was expensive, and sherds of broken pots were to be found everywhere. In **ostracism** each citizen scratched on a sherd the name of the politician he wanted to banish. Archaeologists have found thousands of such sherds in Athens, often with well-known names on them. Only adult men with citizenship were allowed to vote.

First the Assembly decided whether an ostracism should take place at all that year. If so, an area of the **Agora**, the great square of Athens, was fenced off. The citizens cast their votes separated by **tribes**, which were districts of the citizen body. Ancient sources give a **quorum**, that is, a minimum number, of **6,000** votes. It is disputed whether this number had to be reached in total or for one single person.

Whoever received the most votes had to leave **Attica**, the territory of Athens, for **ten years**. Ostracism was not a punishment for a crime. The banished man kept his property and could return after ten years and exercise his rights again. The aim was to prevent a single man from becoming too powerful and threatening democracy.

Famous politicians were also hit by ostracism. **Themistocles** had promoted the expansion of the Athenian **fleet** and made Athens a sea power. Later he was felt to be too powerful and was banished around **471 BC**. He finally fled to the **Persian Empire**. As the last man banished is regarded **Hyperbolus**: around **417 BC** two rival politicians agreed with each other so that he himself was banished. After that the Athenians no longer used the procedure.

gewusst: In Athens thousands of inscribed sherds were found, including some with the name Themistocles.
Ostracism was not a punishment: the banished man kept his property.

teile.einleitung: Nineveh was one of the largest cities of antiquity and capital of the Assyrian Empire. The ruins lie on the Tigris opposite the present-day city of Mosul in Iraq.
wichtigste: Nineveh lies on the east bank of the Tigris, opposite the centre of Mosul in Iraq.
King Sennacherib made Nineveh the capital around 700 BC.
He built the Southwest Palace, which he called the “Palace Without a Rival”.
In 612 BC Babylonians and Medes captured the city.
According to the Bible the prophet Jonah was sent to Nineveh.
Austen Henry Layard dug at Nineveh in the 1840s.

abschnitte.text: **Nineveh** lies on the east bank of the **Tigris** in the north of present-day **Iraq**. The modern city of **Mosul** lies mainly on the other side of the river. Today the area of ruins belongs to the urban area of Mosul. Nineveh was already very old when the Assyrian king **Sennacherib** made the city the **capital** around **700 BC**. He expanded it magnificently, with new walls, canals and palaces.

Sennacherib had a huge palace built, the **Southwest Palace**. In his inscriptions he called it the “**Palace Without a Rival**”, that is, a palace that has no equal. The walls were decorated with **stone reliefs** that together were about three kilometres long. They show campaigns, building work and hunts. To bring water into the city, Sennacherib had long canals and an aqueduct built.

A later king, **Ashurbanipal**, collected a great **library** in Nineveh. It consisted of thousands of **clay tablets** in cuneiform. On them were letters, lists, prayers, knowledge about the stars and medicine, and famous stories. Among the finds is also the **Epic of Gilgamesh**, one of the oldest hero stories in the world. Many of these tablets are today in the **British Museum** in London.

At the end of the 7th century BC the Assyrian Empire grew weaker. The Babylonian king **Nabopolassar** allied himself with the **Medes** from Iran. Together they besieged Nineveh. After a long siege the city fell in **612 BC** and was destroyed. After that the **Assyrian Empire** collapsed within a few years. The city fell into oblivion, and its ruins became mounds.

Nineveh appears in the **Bible**. In the **Book of Jonah** the prophet **Jonah** is to call the inhabitants of Nineveh to repent. The story is well known because on the way Jonah is swallowed by a great fish. In the **1840s** the British researcher **Austen Henry Layard** dug at Nineveh. Among other things he uncovered parts of Sennacherib's palace and made the city known in Europe. Many finds went to the British Museum.

gewusst: In the library of Nineveh tablets with the Epic of Gilgamesh were found.
One of the ruin mounds of Nineveh is called Nebi Yunus, which means “Prophet Jonah”.

teile.einleitung: Nebuchadnezzar II was the most important king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. He ruled around 600 BC for over 40 years and made Babylon one of the most magnificent cities in the world.
wichtigste: Nebuchadnezzar II ruled from 605 to 562 BC.
His father Nabopolassar had founded the Neo-Babylonian Empire.
As crown prince he defeated the Egyptians at Carchemish in 605 BC.
In 587/586 BC he conquered Jerusalem and destroyed the Temple.
He built great temples for Marduk, the chief god of Babylon.
Verdi's opera “Nabucco” is named after him.

abschnitte.text: **Nebuchadnezzar II** was the son of **Nabopolassar**, who had made Babylon independent of the Assyrians and founded the **Neo-Babylonian Empire**. In **605 BC** Nebuchadnezzar followed his father on the throne. He ruled until **562 BC**, that is, for over 40 years. That is about 1,100 years after the famous King Hammurabi. Under Nebuchadnezzar **Babylon** experienced its greatest flowering.

Still as **crown prince**, Nebuchadnezzar defeated the army of the Egyptian pharaoh **Necho II** in 605 BC at **Carchemish** on the Euphrates. With that Babylon became the leading power in Syria and Palestine. After an uprising his army besieged **Jerusalem** and captured the city in **587/586 BC**. The Temple was destroyed, and the Kingdom of Judah lost its independence. Many people were taken to Babylon. This period is called the **Babylonian Exile**.

Nebuchadnezzar had Babylon magnificently expanded. The chief god of the city was **Marduk**, lord of the temple **Esagila**. For him the king had shrines expanded and the stepped tower **Etemenanki** completed. Famous is the **Ishtar Gate** with blue glazed bricks and pictures of lions, bulls and dragons. A large part of it stands today in a museum in **Berlin**. Whether the legendary **Hanging Gardens** really existed is disputed among researchers.

abschnitte.titel: Nebuchadnezzar in the Bible and opera
abschnitte.text: Nebuchadnezzar appears in the **Bible**, especially in the **Book of Daniel**. There the king dreams, among other things, of a great **statue** made of different metals, and the prophet **Daniel** interprets this dream for him. He lives on in music too: Giuseppe **Verdi** wrote the opera **“Nabucco”**. “Nabucco” is the Italian short form of Nebuchadnezzar. Especially famous from it is the **Chorus of the Hebrew Slaves**.

gewusst: Many bricks from Babylon bear a stamp with the name of Nebuchadnezzar.
The Ishtar Gate can be admired today in Berlin, rebuilt from the original bricks.

teile.einleitung: Romulus and Remus are twin brothers from an old Roman legend. It tells how the city of Rome was founded. The story is not real historical writing, but it was very important to the Romans.
wichtigste: Romulus and Remus are the founders of Rome in a legend.
Their mother was called Rhea Silvia, and their father is said to have been the god of war Mars.
As babies they were abandoned in a basket on the Tiber.
A she-wolf suckled them, and the shepherd Faustulus raised them.
According to the legend Rome was founded in 753 BC.
Romulus killed his brother in a quarrel and became the first king of Rome.

abschnitte.text: The mother of the twins was **Rhea Silvia**, a king's daughter from the city of Alba Longa. Their father was held to be the god of war **Mars**. Their uncle **Amulius** had seized the throne and feared for his power. So he had the babies put in a basket on the river **Tiber**. The basket, however, caught on the bank.

A **she-wolf** found the crying children and suckled them. Then the shepherd **Faustulus** discovered the twins. He and his wife took the boys home and raised them. Romulus and Remus grew strong and brave. Later they learned who they really were and helped their grandfather Numitor to become king again.

The brothers wanted to found a city where they had been found. But they quarrelled over who should be the founder. So they stood on two hills and watched **birds**. Remus saw six vultures, but Romulus twelve. Romulus began building the city wall on the **Palatine**. When Remus mockingly jumped over the wall, Romulus killed him.

The city was named **Rome** after Romulus, and he became its first king. The Romans counted **753 BC** as the founding year. The day was held to be 21 April. Archaeologists have indeed found remains of very old huts on the Palatine. The legend itself, however, is a tale and not an exact account.

gewusst: Because of the legend the Romans liked to call themselves children of Mars.
On the famous bronze figure of the Capitoline Wolf in Rome the twins were added only much later.
The she-wolf with the twins is still an emblem of the city of Rome today.

teile.einleitung: Roman religion was the belief of the ancient Romans in many gods and goddesses. For almost every area of life there was a deity, from war through the sea to the hearth fire. Many names of these gods we still know today, for example from the planets.
wichtigste: The Romans worshipped many gods, which is called polytheism.
The chief god was Jupiter, and his wife was Juno.
Mars was the god of war, Neptune the god of the sea.
Venus was the goddess of love and beauty.
Mercury was the swift messenger of the gods, and Janus had two faces.
Vesta guarded the hearth fire.
The Romans worshipped their gods in temples.
Later Christianity became the most important religion in the empire.

abschnitte.text: At the head stood **Jupiter**, the god of the sky and of thunder, with his wife **Juno**, the protector of women and of marriage. **Mars** was the god of war and was regarded as the father of Romulus. **Neptune** ruled over the sea, and **Venus** was the goddess of love and beauty. **Mercury** was the swift messenger of the gods and protector of merchants.

The Romans took over many stories from the **Greeks** and equated their own gods with the Greek ones. So Jupiter corresponds to the Greek Zeus, Juno to Hera and Venus to Aphrodite. Neptune is the Greek Poseidon, and Mercury is Hermes. Some gods, however, were typically Roman, for example **Janus** with his two faces.

The Romans worshipped their gods in **temples**, in which stood a statue of the deity. In front of the temple lay the altar on which one made **sacrifices**, for example fruit, wine, incense or animals. People believed in an exchange: whoever gave to the gods could hope for their help. Priests also interpreted the flight of birds in order to learn the will of the gods.

In every house too there was a small altar for the **household gods**, the Lares and Penates. The family prayed there and brought small gifts. **Vesta** was the goddess of the hearth fire, and in her temple in Rome priestesses, the **Vestals**, tended a sacred fire that was never allowed to go out. Their fire was regarded as a sign of the continuing existence of Rome.

In the imperial period deceased emperors were often worshipped as gods, which is called the **imperial cult**. Christians refused to sacrifice to the emperors and were therefore persecuted at times. From 313 AD under Emperor Constantine they were allowed to practise their faith freely. Towards the end of the 4th century **Christianity** became the state religion, and the old cults were banned.

The planets **Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Neptune** bear the names of Roman gods. The month of January is named after Janus, March after Mars. In French Tuesday is called “mardi” after Mars and Wednesday “mercredi” after Mercury. The Pope still bears the title Pontifex Maximus, which formerly belonged to the chief Roman priest.

begriffe.erklaerung: The belief in many gods.
A gift to the gods in order to put them in a kindly mood.
A priestess of the goddess Vesta who tended the sacred fire.
Roman protective gods of the house and the family.

gewusst: Janus was shown with two faces because he could look forwards and backwards at the same time, like the end and beginning of a year.
The doors of the temple of Janus in Rome were closed only when there was peace throughout the empire, which happened very rarely.

teile.einleitung: For rich Romans the banquet was an important event. One reclined on couches, ate several courses and talked for a long time. The hosts thereby also showed their wealth.
wichtigste: Rich Romans ate reclining at a banquet.
The guests propped themselves on the left elbow.
People ate mainly with their fingers.
The dining room was called the triclinium, because three couches stood around the table.
The salty fish sauce garum was very popular.
Slaves carried in the food and brought water for washing hands.
A feast often began with eggs and ended with fruit.

abschnitte.text: At a fine meal the guests lay on broad **couches**. That was considered refined. One propped oneself on the **left elbow**, so that one had the right hand free. The dining room was called the **triclinium**. The word shows that three couches stood around a table, and on each there was usually room for three people.

The Romans ate mainly **with their fingers**. Spoons and knives existed, but forks for eating hardly did. Many dishes were already cut small in the kitchen. Between the courses **slaves** handed round water for washing hands. They also carried in the dishes and cleared away.

A feast had several courses. The starter often consisted of **eggs**, olives or salad. After that came main dishes with meat, fish or poultry. At the end there was often **fruit** and something sweet. The poet Horace therefore spoke of “ab ovo usque ad mala”, that is, from the egg to the apples.

Very popular was **garum**, a salty sauce made from fermented fish. With it the Romans seasoned many dishes, much as we use salt today. Pepper, honey and vinegar were also important. The Romans liked sweet and sour together. The main drink was **wine**, which was usually mixed with water.

A banquet often lasted many hours. People talked about politics, books and news. Sometimes musicians played, or someone recited poems. For most people in Rome, however, the meal looked quite different. They ate plain grain porridge, bread and vegetables, often sitting down.

gewusst: An old cookery book by a Roman named Apicius has come down to us.
Garum was produced in large factories on the Mediterranean and shipped far afield.
In Roman settlements in Switzerland too, amphorae were found in which fish sauce was transported.

teile.einleitung: Plato was one of the most important philosophers in the world. He lived in ancient Athens and was a pupil of Socrates. His thoughts on justice, the state and truth are still read today.
wichtigste: Plato was a pupil of the philosopher Socrates.
Around 387 BC he founded the Academy in Athens.
Most of his works he wrote as conversations, so-called dialogues.
In the “Apology” he describes the defence speech of Socrates.
In the “Republic” he describes the just state that philosophers should rule.
His Theory of Forms says that behind visible things stand eternal archetypes.
Plato tells of Atlantis in the dialogues Timaeus and Critias.

abschnitte.text: Plato lived from about 428 to 348 BC in **Athens**. As a young man he became a pupil of **Socrates**. Socrates asked people many questions in order to come closer to the truth together. In 399 Socrates was accused and sentenced to death. That shook Plato deeply. In his work the **“Apology”** he describes the defence speech that Socrates gave in court.

Around **387 BC** Plato founded a school in Athens, the **Academy**. It lay in a grove that was named after the hero Academus. There pupils learned and discussed mathematics, nature and philosophy. His most famous pupil was **Aristotle**. Even today some universities and learned societies are called academies.

Plato wrote most of his works as **conversations**, so-called **dialogues**. Usually Socrates is the main figure and asks questions. The **“Republic”** is about the **just state**. Plato thought that **philosophers** should rule because they recognise the good best. According to his teaching the human **soul** also has three parts: **reason, courage and desire**.

According to Plato's **Theory of Forms**, behind visible things stand eternal, perfect **archetypes**, the Forms. A drawn circle is never quite round, but the Form of the circle is. Plato explains this in the Republic with the **allegory of the cave**. In it people sit chained in a cave and see only shadows on the wall. They take the shadows for reality until one goes outside and sees the real world in sunlight.

In the dialogues **Timaeus and Critias** Plato tells of **Atlantis**. It is said to have been a powerful island city that sank into the sea. Many people have later searched for Atlantis. Most experts, however, regard the story as an invention of Plato. With it he probably wanted to show what happens to an arrogant state.

gewusst: All the works of Plato survive to this day, which is rare among ancient writers.
A famous mural by the painter Raphael shows Plato and Aristotle in the middle of many scholars.

teile.einleitung: The Phoenicians were a people of seafarers and traders who lived about 3,000 years ago on the coast of the eastern Mediterranean. With their ships they sailed as far as Spain and North Africa. Their most important invention still accompanies us today: an alphabet from which our letters later arose.
wichtigste: The Phoenicians lived on the eastern Mediterranean, in the area of present-day Lebanon.
They were famous for seafaring and trade.
