Their most important cities were Tyre, Sidon and Byblos.
They developed an alphabet of 22 consonants.
From sea snails they obtained the precious dye purple.
They sold, among other things, cedar wood to Egypt.
In North Africa they founded the city of Carthage.

abschnitte.text: The Phoenicians lived on a narrow coastal strip between sea and mountains, mainly in present-day **Lebanon**. They did not form a large empire but independent **city-states** with kings of their own. The most important were **Tyre, Sidon and Byblos**. Their heyday lay roughly between 1200 and 500 BC.

Because land was scarce, the Phoenicians turned to the sea. They built manoeuvrable **merchant ships** and steered by the stars at night. They sold cedar wood, glass, cloth, metalwork and carved ivory. According to a report by the Greek Herodotus, Phoenician sailors are even said to have sailed right around Africa.

From the mountains of their homeland the Phoenicians fetched the valuable **cedar wood**, which was in demand in Egypt for ships, coffins and temples. Also famous was **purple**, a red to violet dye from sea snails. For a little dye thousands of snails were needed, so purple was as expensive as gold. Purple-dyed clothes were later worn above all by kings and Roman emperors.

The Phoenicians developed a script with only **22 signs**, all of which stood for consonants. That was much simpler than cuneiform or hieroglyphs with hundreds of signs. The **Greeks** took over these letters and added vowels. From it later arose the Latin **alphabet**, which we use today, and many other scripts.

Along their trade routes the Phoenicians founded **trading posts** and colonies, for example on Cyprus, Sicily and Sardinia. Gadir, present-day Cádiz in Spain, was also a Phoenician foundation. The best-known colony was **Carthage** in present-day Tunisia, which according to legend was founded in 814 BC. Carthage became so powerful that it later fought a war against Rome.

Later the Phoenician cities came under the rule of the Assyrians, Babylonians and Persians. In 332 BC **Alexander the Great** captured the island city of Tyre after a long siege. The word **“Bible”** probably comes from the name of the city of Byblos, through which papyrus was traded to Greece. The cedar is still the emblem on the flag of Lebanon today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A script in which each sign stands for a sound.
A very expensive red to violet dye from sea snails.
A settlement that people found far from their homeland.
A city that with its surrounding land forms a state of its own.

gewusst: The name “Phoenicians” probably comes from the Greek word for purple-red.
The letter A goes back to a Phoenician sign that represented the head of an ox, and the word alphabet comes from the first Greek letters, alpha and beta.

teile.einleitung: Turicum was a small settlement from Roman times on the Limmat. The present-day city of Zurich grew out of it. Traces of the Romans can still be found in the old town today.
wichtigste: Turicum is the Roman name for **Zurich**.
The settlement lay on the **Limmat**, where it flows out of Lake Zurich.
In Turicum there was a Roman **customs post**.
The name Turicum was first found on a **gravestone**.
A Roman fort later stood on the **Lindenhof**.
Near the **Weinplatz**, remains of a public bath were found.

abschnitte.text: Turicum lay where the **Limmat** flows out of Lake Zurich. In Roman times the lake lay **about 2.5 metres lower** than today. That is why the shore was different from now. Goods were transported by ship over the lake and the Limmat. The settlement was a small place, a so-called **vicus**.

In Turicum there was a Roman **customs post**. Here merchants had to pay a duty on their goods. The place lay on the border between two Roman provinces. Traffic on the waterway brought money and trade to the settlement.

The name Turicum was first found on a **gravestone**. It came to light in the 18th century on the **Lindenhof**. Parents had put it up for their little son. The father worked at the customs post. The name of the place is on the stone, and so we know what Zurich was called by the Romans.

In late Roman times, the Romans built a **fort**, a small fortress with walls, on the **Lindenhof** hill. It was meant to protect the area **against the Alemanni**, Germanic groups from the north. Today the Lindenhof is a quiet square with trees and a lovely view over the old town.

Near the **Weinplatz** in Zurich's old town, archaeologists found the remains of a **public bath** from Roman times. Baths like this were very popular with the Romans. People met there, washed and relaxed in the warm water. Some finds from Turicum can be seen in the museum today.

gewusst: Without the gravestone from the Lindenhof, we might not know that Zurich was called Turicum in Roman times.
Because Lake Zurich lay lower then, part of today's old town stood on dry land at the shore.

teile.einleitung: In the 3rd century AD the Roman Empire fell into a severe crisis. Emperors changed very quickly, enemies attacked at the frontiers, and money lost its value. People speak of the imperial crisis or the age of the soldier emperors.
wichtigste: The age of the soldier emperors lasted from 235 to 284 AD.
It began with the murder of Emperor Severus Alexander.
Many emperors were raised up by the army and ruled only briefly.
Emperor Decius fell in 251 fighting the Goths.
Emperor Valerian fell into Persian captivity in 260.
In the west and in the east separate partial realms arose for a time.
Emperor Aurelian reunited the empire and had Rome protected with a wall.

abschnitte.text: In 235 mutinous soldiers killed Emperor **Severus Alexander** near Mainz. The troops then proclaimed their commander Maximinus Thrax emperor. So began the age of the **soldier emperors**. In the following fifty years armies again and again raised their leaders to emperor. Many of these rulers reigned only a few years or months and died violently.

At the same time the frontiers were severely threatened. In the north Germanic groups such as Goths, Franks and **Alemanni** pushed into the empire. Emperor **Decius** fell in 251 at Abritus in present-day Bulgaria against the Goths. He was the first emperor to die in battle against an external enemy. In the east the Persian **Sasanians** attacked. Their king Shapur I took Emperor **Valerian** prisoner in 260.

Because the emperor could not protect the frontiers everywhere, others founded realms of their own. In the west **Postumus** began the **Gallic Empire** from 260. It included Gaul, Germania, Britain and for a time Hispania. In the east **Zenobia**, the ruler of **Palmyra**, extended her power as far as Egypt and Asia Minor. Emperor **Aurelian** defeated Zenobia in 272 and in 274 won back the west as well.

The emperors needed a great deal of money to pay the soldiers. So they mixed less and less silver into the silver coin, the **antoninianus**. In the end it was almost only silver-plated copper. People noticed this, and prices rose sharply. This **inflation**, that is, loss in the value of money, made life hard for many.

From 271 Emperor Aurelian had a new city wall built around Rome, the **Aurelian Wall**. It is largely preserved to this day. In the area of present-day **Switzerland** too the crisis was felt: around 260 the limes, the border fortification in Germania, was abandoned, and Alemanni pushed as far as the Swiss Plateau. Later strong fortresses arose, such as the fort at **Kaiseraugst**. With Emperor **Diocletian** the age of the soldier emperors ended in 284.

gewusst: In about fifty years there were over twenty recognised emperors.
A rock relief at Naqsh-e Rostam in present-day Iran celebrates Shapur's victory over Valerian.
The Aurelian Wall was about 19 kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: Pythagoras was a Greek thinker who lived about 2,500 years ago. The famous Pythagorean theorem, which one learns at school, is named after him. For him and his pupils numbers were the origin of everything.
wichtigste: Pythagoras was born on the Greek island of Samos.
He lived about 2,500 years ago.
He founded a school in southern Italy.
His pupils and followers are called Pythagoreans.
For them numbers were the origin of everything.
He also concerned himself with music and notes.
The Pythagorean theorem applies to right-angled triangles: a² + b² = c².

abschnitte.text: **Pythagoras** was born around 570 BC on the Greek island of **Samos**. So he lived **about 2,500 years ago**. Later he moved to **southern Italy**, where many Greeks lived at the time. In the city of Croton he founded a school. His pupils and followers are called **Pythagoreans**. They lived by strict rules and kept much secret.

For Pythagoras and his pupils **numbers were the origin of everything**. They believed that the whole world can be explained with numbers and their ratios. They studied, for example, even and odd numbers. Some numbers also had a special meaning for them. What Pythagoras himself discovered and what his pupils did can often no longer be separated today.

Pythagoras also concerned himself with **music and notes**. It is said that he examined notes on strings of different lengths. If one halves a string, the note sounds an **octave** higher. Pleasing harmonies arise when the lengths stand in simple ratios. For the Pythagoreans that confirmed that numbers order the world.

The famous theorem applies to **right-angled triangles**. The two short sides at the right angle are called the **legs** a and b, and the long side is called the **hypotenuse** c. The theorem states: **a² + b² = c²**. A well-known example is the numbers **3, 4 and 5**, because 9 + 16 = 25. If the hypotenuse is 13 cm long and one leg is 5 cm long, one calculates 169 minus 25 equals 144. So the other leg is **12 cm** long.

The knowledge behind the theorem was known even before Pythagoras. The **Babylonians** knew numbers that fit the theorem many centuries earlier. Such ratios were also used for marking out right angles in the field. The Greeks, however, were probably the first to **prove** the theorem in general. The name Pythagoras is still linked with it today.

gewusst: With a rope with 12 equal intervals one can lay out a 3-4-5 triangle and so build a right angle.
Today there are hundreds of different proofs of the Pythagorean theorem.

teile.einleitung: The Kingdom of Aksum was a powerful kingdom in the area of present-day Ethiopia and Eritrea. It flourished in the first centuries AD through trade on the Red Sea. Aksum became Christian early and is famous for its huge stone stelae.
wichtigste: Aksum lay in the north of present-day Ethiopia and in Eritrea.
The Greek trade handbook “Periplus of the Erythraean Sea” from the 1st century mentions the kingdom.
In the 4th century campaigns by Aksum decisively weakened the Nubian kingdom of Meroe.
Frumentius is regarded as the first bishop of Aksum.
The city of Aksum is famous for huge decorated stone stelae.
Around 525 King Kaleb marched against the South Arabian kingdom of Himyar.
Around 615 early followers of Muhammad found refuge with the Negus of Aksum.

abschnitte.titel: A trading kingdom on the Red Sea
abschnitte.text: The **Kingdom of Aksum** lay in the highlands of present-day **Ethiopia** and in **Eritrea**. Through the port of Adulis on the **Red Sea** it traded with the Roman Empire, Arabia and India. Sold were, for example, ivory, gold and frankincense. The Greek trade handbook **Periplus of the Erythraean Sea** from the 1st century AD mentions the kingdom. Aksum even minted its own **coins** of gold, silver and bronze.

Archaeologically the city of Aksum is famous for its **huge decorated stone stelae**. These are tall, narrow stone pillars made from a single piece. Some are decorated so that they look like tall buildings with windows and doors. They probably stood at the tombs of rulers. One stele had been taken to Rome in the 20th century and was returned to Aksum in **2005**.

In the 4th century Aksum became **Christian**. An important role was played by **Frumentius**, a Christian from the city of Tyre. He advised the royal court and is regarded as the **first bishop of Aksum**. King Ezana adopted the Christian faith. Aksum is thus one of the first kingdoms in the world to become Christian.

Aksum was also strong militarily. In the 4th century the Nubian kingdom of **Meroe** was decisively weakened by campaigns of Aksum. Around **525 AD** **King Kaleb** crossed the Red Sea against the South Arabian kingdom of **Himyar** in present-day Yemen. For some time South Arabia thus stood under the influence of Aksum.

Around **615** early followers of the Prophet **Muhammad** fled from Mecca. They found **refuge with the Negus**, the king of Aksum. This story is still well known in Islam today. According to Ethiopian tradition the church of **Mary of Zion** in Aksum is said to house the **Ark of the Covenant**, a sacred chest from the Bible. Only a single monk is allowed to see it, so this cannot be checked.

gewusst: The ruins of Aksum have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980.
The Ethiopian Church still uses the old language Ge'ez in worship, which was already used in Aksum.

teile.einleitung: In ancient Egypt many people wore wigs. They were practical against heat and lice and at the same time a sign of wealth. Especially distinguished people had large and elaborate wigs.
wichtigste: Many Egyptian men and women shaved their heads or wore their hair very short.
That helped against lice and against the great heat.
Over it they wore wigs.
Good wigs were made of real human hair.
Rich and distinguished people wore especially large and elaborate wigs.

abschnitte.text: In Egypt it is very hot. So many people **shaved their heads** or wore their hair very short. In this way **lice** had hardly a chance, and the head stayed cooler. Over the short hair they wore **wigs**. The wig also protected against the sun.

Good wigs were made of **real human hair**. Simpler wigs consisted of **plant fibres**. The strands of hair were knotted onto a net and often shaped into fine plaits or curls. With **beeswax** and resin the hairstyle was held in shape. Some wigs were even decorated with jewellery.

A large wig was expensive and showed who one was. Especially **rich and distinguished people** wore large and elaborate wigs, above all at festivals. Pharaohs and queens too were shown with magnificent wigs. Some wigs were given to the dead to take with them into the **tomb**. That is why some survive to this day and can be seen in museums.

gewusst: Archaeologists have found wigs in Egyptian tombs that are over 3,000 years old.

teile.einleitung: The alpaca is an animal from the Andes in South America. For the Incas and other peoples of the Andes it was very important, above all because of its soft wool.
wichtigste: Alpacas come from the high mountains of the Andes.
They are smaller than llamas and have shorter, rounded ears.
Alpacas were kept mainly for their fine wool.
Llamas, on the other hand, often carried loads.
People burnt the dried dung of the animals for cooking and heating.

abschnitte.text: The **alpaca** is related to the **llama**. Both belong to the camel family, but have no hump. Alpacas are **smaller** than llamas and have shorter, rounded ears. They live in herds on the high grasslands of the **Andes**. The people there have kept them as domestic animals for thousands of years.

For the **Incas**, the alpaca was valuable above all for its **wool**. It is soft, warm and fine. People wove clothes, blankets and precious fabrics from it. Llamas, on the other hand, were often used as **pack animals** and carried goods over the mountain paths.

In the high Andes hardly any trees grow, so there is little **wood**. People therefore collected the **dried dung** of llamas and alpacas. It burns well and was used for **cooking and heating**. In this way they made use of almost everything the animals gave them.

gewusst: Alpacas often leave their droppings together in a few fixed places, which makes collecting them easy.
Today alpacas are also kept in Switzerland, for example for treks and for their wool.

teile.einleitung: Petra is an ancient rock city in present-day Jordan. The Nabataeans carved their buildings directly into the reddish rock. A researcher from Basel made Petra known in Europe.
wichtigste: Petra was built by the people of the Nabataeans.
The buildings were carved directly into the rock.
The rock is reddish, so people speak of the “rose-red city”.
The most famous building is the “Treasury of the Pharaoh”.
On foot one reaches the city through a narrow gorge.
The Basel researcher Johann Ludwig Burckhardt made Petra known in Europe in 1812.
In 2007 Petra was chosen as one of the new Seven Wonders of the World.

abschnitte.text: The **Nabataeans** were an Arab people of traders. They controlled important **trade routes** for incense and spices. Their capital **Petra** lay well protected between mountains. Through trade the Nabataeans became rich. Later, in the year 106 AD, Petra came under Roman rule.

The buildings of Petra were not built of masonry but **carved into the rock**. The builders worked their way into the rock face from top to bottom. The sandstone is **reddish** and, depending on the light, shimmers pink, red or orange. Many of the buildings were **tombs**. With cisterns and channels the Nabataeans skilfully collected the scarce rainwater.

The most famous building is called the **“Treasury of the Pharaoh”**, in Arabic Al-Khazneh. Its magnificent façade is about 40 metres high. The name comes from an old legend according to which a treasure was hidden at the top in a stone urn. Probably, however, the building was the tomb of a king. Another great rock building is called the Monastery.

On foot one reaches the city through a **narrow gorge**, the **Siq**. It is over a kilometre long, and the rock walls are very high in some places. At the end of the gorge the Treasury suddenly appears. This sight is among the most impressive moments of a visit.

abschnitte.titel: A man from Basel discovers Petra
abschnitte.text: After many centuries Petra was almost forgotten in Europe. In **1812** the researcher **Johann Ludwig Burckhardt** from **Basel** travelled to the area. He was disguised as an Arab trader and called himself Sheikh Ibrahim. In this way he could see the ruins and report on them. Today Petra is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and was chosen in **2007** as one of the **new Seven Wonders of the World**.

gewusst: Petra comes from Greek and means “rock”.
Johann Ludwig Burckhardt was also one of the first Europeans to visit the temples of Abu Simbel in Egypt.

teile.einleitung: Already thousands of years ago people in ancient Egypt wore make-up. Especially the eyes were emphasised with dark and green colours. The make-up was beautiful but was also meant to protect.
wichtigste: The ancient Egyptians made up mainly the eyes.
The black eye make-up is called kohl.
Green eye make-up was made from the stone malachite.
The dark colour helped against the glaring sunlight.
Men and women wore make-up, and so did the pharaohs.

abschnitte.text: In pictures and statues from Egypt one often sees thick **dark lines** around the eyes. This was typical of Egypt. The black eye make-up is called **kohl**. It was made from a dark mineral that was ground finely to powder. With a small stick it was applied around the eyes.

There was also **green** eye make-up. For this people took **malachite**, a green stone. It was ground to powder on a flat stone slab, a **cosmetic palette**. Then the powder was mixed with fat so that it stuck well. The make-up was kept in small vessels and pots.

In Egypt the **sun** shines very strongly. The dark colour around the eyes dazzled less in the glaring light. The Egyptians also believed that the make-up protected against **eye diseases**. It also had a religious meaning. It was meant to guard against misfortune and evil powers.

In ancient Egypt **men and women** wore make-up. The **pharaohs** too wore eye make-up. Make-up and cosmetic palettes were even placed in the tomb. In this way the dead were to look beautiful in the afterlife as well. Many of these objects can be found today in museums.

gewusst: We still use the word kohl today for black eye pencils.
Some cosmetic palettes from Egypt are over 5,000 years old.

teile.einleitung: Polyphemus is a one-eyed giant from Greek legend. In Homer's “Odyssey” he holds Odysseus and his men captive in his cave. With a trick they manage to escape.
wichtigste: Polyphemus was a Cyclops, that is, a one-eyed giant.
His father was the sea god Poseidon.
He held Odysseus and his men captive in his cave.
Odysseus told him his name was “Nobody”.
He gave Polyphemus strong wine to drink and blinded him with a glowing stake.
The men escaped under the bellies of sheep.

abschnitte.text: **Polyphemus** is one of the **Cyclopes**. These are huge creatures with only **one eye** in the middle of the forehead. Polyphemus lived as a shepherd on an island and tended sheep and goats. His father was the sea god **Poseidon**. The story is in the **“Odyssey”**, a famous work by the poet Homer.

On his journey home from Troy **Odysseus** came with some men to the island of the Cyclopes. They went into a **cave** to look for food. Then Polyphemus came home with his flock. He rolled a huge stone in front of the entrance. Now the men were trapped, and the giant did not want to let them go. Some companions lost their lives.

Odysseus gave Polyphemus **strong wine** to drink. When the giant asked for his name, Odysseus answered: **“Nobody”**. Polyphemus fell asleep drunk. Then the men thrust a **glowing stake** into his single eye and blinded him. Polyphemus screamed for help. But when the other Cyclopes asked who was harming him, he cried: “Nobody!” So nobody came to his aid.

In the morning the blind Polyphemus opened the cave to let his sheep out. He felt each animal on the back. But Odysseus and his men clung **beneath the bellies of the sheep**. In this way they got out unnoticed. On the ship Odysseus called his real name to the giant. Polyphemus then asked his father Poseidon to punish Odysseus. That is why the journey home took many years.

gewusst: The word “Cyclops” comes from Greek and means roughly “round-eye”.
The legend of Polyphemus was often painted on vases already in antiquity.

teile.einleitung: The Maya had a simple and clever number script made of dots, bars and a sign for zero. They did not count in tens as we do but in twenties.
wichtigste: A dot means 1, a horizontal bar means 5.
At most 4 dots stand side by side; five dots are replaced by a bar.
The Maya drew zero as a shell.
Two bars and a dot mean 11, three bars mean 15.
The Maya counted in groups of twenty, probably because of fingers and toes.
Larger numbers they wrote in levels one above another.

abschnitte.text: For the numbers from 1 to 19 the Maya needed only two signs. A **dot** means **1**, a horizontal **bar** means **5**. Three dots are therefore 3. Two bars and a dot are 5 plus 5 plus 1, which makes **11**. Three bars are **15**. Because five dots are replaced by a bar, **at most 4 dots** stand side by side. The largest number in one level is 19: three bars and four dots.

For **zero** the Maya drew a sign that looks like a **shell**. That was a great achievement, because many other peoples at that time did not yet know zero. The Maya needed zero to show that a level is empty, just as with us the zero in the number 105 shows the empty tens place. Without zero a place-value script would hardly be possible.

We calculate in the **decimal system**, the Maya calculated in the **vigesimal system**, which is base twenty. This probably has to do with the body: a person has 10 fingers and 10 toes, together **20**. The Maya calendars too are full of twenties, for example the 20 days of a month. In French some traces of it remain: “quatre-vingts” literally means “four times twenty” and means 80.

Larger numbers the Maya wrote in **levels one above another**, and the lowest level counts the ones. The next level above counts twenties. A dot in the second level and a shell below therefore means 20. In this way the Maya could write very large numbers with few signs. They needed this for their calendars, which counted over many centuries, and for calculations on the course of the stars.

gewusst: With only three signs, dot, bar and shell, the Maya could write any number.
In the French word “quatre-vingts” for 80 there is still a trace of counting in twenties.

teile.einleitung: The Sumerians were a people who lived in southern Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq, more than 5000 years ago. They built some of the first great cities in the world and invented one of the oldest scripts. Many things that we take for granted today began with them.
wichtigste: The Sumerians lived in southern Mesopotamia between the Euphrates and the Tigris.
Uruk is regarded as one of the first big cities in the world.
The Sumerians were organised in independent city-states.
Each city had a city god as its lord and protector.
They developed cuneiform, one of the oldest scripts in the world.
Around 2300 BC, Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian cities.
The Sumerian language is not related to any known language.

abschnitte.text: The Sumerians lived in southern **Mesopotamia**, on the flat plain between the Euphrates and the Tigris near the Persian Gulf. Around 3500 BC, **Uruk** grew there into one of the first big cities in the world, with perhaps several tens of thousands of inhabitants. Other important cities were Ur, Lagash, Nippur and Eridu. They built their houses and temples from mud bricks, because there was hardly any stone or wood in the region.

The Sumerians had no shared empire, but lived in independent **city-states**. Each city had its own ruler, and the cities often quarrelled over water and fields. Around 2300 BC, **Sargon of Akkad** conquered the Sumerian cities and founded the first great empire of Mesopotamia. Later, the city of Ur enjoyed another golden age under its kings.

The Sumerians believed in many gods. According to their belief, every city belonged to a **city god**, who was its lord and protector, in Ur for example the moon god Nanna. In the centre of the cities stood temples on stepped towers called **ziggurats**. The ziggurat of Ur is partly preserved to this day and has been partly rebuilt.

Around 3300 BC, the people of Uruk began to press signs into damp **clay tablets**. At first they used them to record supplies such as grain and cattle. From this developed **cuneiform**, whose signs look like little wedges because they were pressed in with a reed pen. Later it was also used to write laws, letters, prayers and stories, for example about King Gilgamesh of Uruk.

The Sumerians counted in a **base-60 system**, which is why an hour still has 60 minutes today. They watered their fields with canals and knew the plough. The wheel used to be often credited to the Sumerians, but similarly old finds also exist from Europe. The Sumerian language is particularly difficult for researchers because it is not related to any known language.

begriffe.erklaerung: An ancient script made of wedge-shaped signs that were pressed into soft clay.
A city with the land around it, governed like a small state of its own.
A stepped temple tower made of mud bricks in Mesopotamia.
A way of counting in steps of sixty, as we still do with minutes and seconds.

gewusst: Many thousands of Sumerian clay tablets have survived, because baked and dried clay lasts a very long time.
In the Bible, the Sumerian city of Ur is named as the place where Abraham came from.
The Sumerians did not call themselves Sumerians. The name comes from the language of their neighbours, the Akkadians.

teile.einleitung: Tutankhamun was a pharaoh in ancient Egypt who ruled more than 3300 years ago. He became king as a child and died young. He is famous mainly because his tomb was found in 1922 almost untouched and full of treasures.
wichtigste: Tutankhamun became pharaoh at about the age of 9.
He died at about the age of 19.
His tomb lies in the Valley of the Kings.
Howard Carter discovered the tomb in 1922, so around 100 years ago.
The wealthy Englishman Lord Carnarvon paid for the search.
The famous death mask is made of gold.
The “curse of the pharaoh” is a legend with no proof.

abschnitte.text: Tutankhamun lived in the time of the **New Kingdom** and ruled from about 1332 to 1323 BC. He became pharaoh at about the age of 9, so experienced advisers such as the high official Ay helped him. At first he was called Tutankhaten, because his father, probably Pharaoh Akhenaten, allowed only the sun god Aten to be worshipped. Under Tutankhamun, Egypt returned to the old gods, especially to **Amun**, and so he also changed his name.

Tutankhamun died at about the age of 19. What he died of has still not been settled for certain. Examinations of his **mummy** showed that he had an injured foot and had been ill with malaria. Because he died so suddenly, he was probably buried in a smaller tomb than was actually usual for a pharaoh.

The British archaeologist **Howard Carter** searched for years in the **Valley of the Kings** for the tomb, paid for by Lord Carnarvon. In November 1922 he found a staircase that led to a sealed door. When he looked in and was asked whether he could see anything, he is said to have answered: “Yes, wonderful things.” It was the first almost untouched pharaoh's tomb ever found.

In the tomb lay over 5000 objects, including furniture, jewellery, games, clothes, weapons and several **chariots**. The mummy lay in three human-shaped coffins that fitted inside one another, and the innermost is made of solid gold. On the face of the mummy lay the famous **death mask** of gold, which weighs about 10 kilograms. The treasures are now on display in Egypt, mainly in the Grand Egyptian Museum near Giza.

Lord Carnarvon died a few months after the opening of the tomb of blood poisoning. Newspapers then invented the **curse of the pharaoh**, which was supposed to strike everyone who disturbed the tomb. But Howard Carter himself lived for about another 16 years. Today we know that this curse is only a legend with no proof at all.

begriffe.erklaerung: The king in ancient Egypt, who was also worshipped as a son of the gods.
A researcher who digs up and studies ancient traces of people.
A large stone coffin in which the coffins with the mummy were placed.
A valley in the desert near the present-day city of Luxor, where many pharaohs were buried.

gewusst: Tutankhamun's mummy still lies in his tomb in the Valley of the Kings today.
The tomb even held board games, so that the young pharaoh would not be bored in the afterlife.
That the tomb stayed undiscovered for so long is also because workmen building a later tomb had covered the entrance with rubble.

teile.einleitung: The Migration Period is the name given to the time when many Germanic and other peoples moved into the Roman Empire. It lasted from about the late 4th century to the 6th century. In this time the Western Roman Empire fell.
wichtigste: The trigger is considered to be the advance of the **Huns** westwards around 375.
In 378, Emperor **Valens** fell at the Battle of Adrianople against the Goths.
In 406/407, Vandals, Alans and Suebi crossed the **Rhine**.
In 410, the Visigoth **Alaric** plundered the city of Rome.
In 439, the Vandals conquered **Carthage** in North Africa.
In 451, the battle on the **Catalaunian Plains** took place.
Burgundians and **Alemanni** shaped the area of present-day Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: Around **375**, the **Huns**, a people of horsemen from Asia, pushed westwards. Many peoples fled from them. The **Goths** asked to be admitted to the Roman Empire. But a quarrel broke out. In **378**, the Goths defeated the Romans at the Battle of **Adrianople**. The eastern Roman emperor **Valens** fell there.

Around the turn of the year **406/407**, **Vandals, Alans and Suebi** crossed the Rhine into Gaul. The border could no longer be held. In **410**, the Visigothic leader **Alaric** captured the city of **Rome** and plundered it. For many people this was a shock, because Rome had not been captured by enemies for centuries.

The **Vandals** moved as far as North Africa. In **439** they conquered **Carthage** and made it their centre. The Huns under **Attila** moved further west. In **451**, a Roman-Germanic army under **Aetius** stood against them on the **Catalaunian Plains** in Gaul. Attila had to withdraw.

In **443**, the Romans settled the **Burgundians** in the region of **Sapaudia** around Lake Geneva. In the north came the **Alemanni**. From the 5th century they settled large parts of present-day **German-speaking Switzerland**. In the west, the Burgundians adopted the Latin language of the population. That is why people speak French in western Switzerland and German in German-speaking Switzerland today.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the Western Empire
abschnitte.text: The Western Roman Empire grew weaker and weaker. In **476**, the Germanic general **Odoacer** deposed the last western Roman emperor. This year is often seen as the end of antiquity in the west. The Eastern Roman Empire with its capital Constantinople lasted for almost a thousand years more. On the soil of the Western Empire, new Germanic kingdoms arose.

gewusst: The name Savoy goes back to the region of Sapaudia, where the Burgundians were settled.
The word “vandalism” for wilful destruction arose only much later and, in the opinion of many researchers, does the Vandals an injustice.

tplmrqv.t: Fall of the Western Roman Empire

teile.einleitung: The fall of the Western Roman Empire was a long process that dragged on over many decades. In AD 476, the Germanic general Odoacer deposed the last western Roman emperor. This ended antiquity in the west, and the Middle Ages began.
wichtigste: In AD 395, the Roman Empire was finally divided into the Western and the Eastern Empire.
The Migration Period weakened the Western Roman Empire greatly.
In AD 410, the Visigoths under King Alaric plundered the city of Rome.
The last western Roman emperor was called Romulus Augustulus.
The Germanic leader Odoacer deposed him in AD 476.
In northern and eastern Switzerland, the Alemanni settled afterwards.
The Eastern Roman Empire lasted until 1453.

abschnitte.text: The Roman Empire was so huge that a single emperor could hardly govern it any more. After the death of Emperor Theodosius in AD 395, it was finally divided between his two sons. This created the **Western Empire** with Italy, Gaul, Spain and North Africa, and the **Eastern Empire** with its capital Constantinople. The east was richer and better protected than the west.

There were many reasons for the fall, all at once. There were frequent **civil wars**, because generals wanted to become emperor themselves. Taxes were high, trade declined and money lost its value. At the same time, more and more foreign peoples pressed across the borders, and the army consisted increasingly of Germanic **mercenaries**.

Around AD 375, the **Huns** pushed from Asia into Europe and drove out other peoples. Many Germanic peoples such as the Goths, Vandals and Franks therefore moved into the Roman Empire. In AD 410, the **Visigoths** under King Alaric plundered the city of Rome, which deeply shocked people at the time. In AD 455, the Vandals also plundered the city.

In the end, the western Roman emperors had hardly any power, and the real rulers were the generals. The last emperor was **Romulus Augustulus**, a boy who ruled for barely a year. In AD 476, the Germanic general **Odoacer** deposed him and sent him to southern Italy with a pension. Odoacer did not appoint a new emperor, but ruled Italy himself as king.

In the area of present-day Switzerland too, the Romans withdrew. In western Switzerland, the **Burgundians** settled, who soon adopted the Latin language of their neighbours. In northern and eastern Switzerland, the **Alemanni** settled, who spoke a Germanic dialect. From this the language border between German and French gradually arose, which still exists today.

While the west broke up into many Germanic kingdoms, the **Eastern Roman Empire** lasted for almost 1000 more years. Today it is often called the Byzantine Empire. Only in 1453 did the **Ottomans** conquer Constantinople, present-day Istanbul. Much knowledge of antiquity was preserved there and in the monasteries of the west.

begriffe.erklaerung: The great movements of Germanic and other peoples in late antiquity, which weakened the Roman Empire.
A soldier who fights for a foreign state in return for payment.
A collective name for many peoples who lived north and east of the Roman borders.
Another name for the Eastern Roman Empire with its capital Constantinople.

gewusst: The name of the last western Roman emperor recalls two founders: Romulus, according to legend, founded Rome, and Augustus was the first emperor.
The word “vandalism” for wilful destruction recalls the plundering of Rome by the Vandals in AD 455.
In the end, the capital of the west was no longer Rome at all, but the well-protected city of Ravenna.

teile.einleitung: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was a huge sanctuary of the Greek goddess Artemis. It counted as one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Today, only a single column remains of the magnificent marble building.
wichtigste: The temple was dedicated to the goddess Artemis and was therefore called the Artemision.
Artemis was the goddess of hunting and wild animals.
Ephesus lies on the west coast of present-day Turkey.
The temple was one of the first great buildings made entirely of marble.
King Croesus of Lydia helped with the building of the first great temple.
In 356 BC, Herostratus set fire to the temple in order to become famous.
Today only one re-erected column still stands.

abschnitte.text: **Artemis** was the Greek goddess of **hunting** and wild animals. She is often shown with a bow and arrow. She was the twin sister of the god Apollo. The Romans called her **Diana**. In **Ephesus**, Artemis was especially honoured. Her huge temple was therefore also called the **Artemision**.

Ephesus was a rich Greek port city on the west coast of present-day **Turkey**. Many merchants and pilgrims came there. Later the city became part of the Roman Empire and was one of the biggest cities in the east. The ruins of Ephesus lie near the present-day town of Selçuk and are a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

The first great temple was built in the 6th century BC. King **Croesus** of Lydia, who was famous for his wealth, donated columns for it. The temple was one of the first great buildings made entirely of **marble**. It had **more than a hundred columns** and was much bigger than most other temples. That is why the Greeks counted it among the **Seven Wonders**.

In **356 BC**, a man named **Herostratus** set fire to the temple, and the great building burnt down. He did it because he wanted to become **famous**. The people of Ephesus then forbade anyone to say his name, but it was handed down all the same. To this day, an act by which someone wants to become known at any price is called a **Herostratic act**.

After the fire, the people of Ephesus rebuilt the temple even more magnificently. In Roman times it was plundered and damaged. Later its stones were used for other buildings. In this way the temple almost completely disappeared. Of the many columns, only **a single one** stands today, put back together from fragments. A stork often sits on top of it.

gewusst: According to a legend, the temple burnt down on the very night when Alexander the Great was born.
Some parts of the temple's columns are on display in the British Museum in London.

teile.einleitung: The Roman Empire was one of the largest and most powerful empires in history. From the capital Rome the Romans ruled all the lands around the Mediterranean. The language, law, buildings and script of the Romans shape Europe to this day.
wichtigste: The capital of the Roman Empire was Rome.
The empire lay around the Mediterranean.
It was divided into regions called provinces.
From Augustus on an emperor ruled the empire.
Egypt with its pyramids also belonged to the Roman Empire.
Distinguished men wore a toga.
The large bathhouses were called thermae.
In Roman numerals V means the number 5 and X the number 10.

abschnitte.text: From the small city of **Rome** a world empire grew over many centuries. The Romans ruled all the lands around the **Mediterranean**, which they called “mare nostrum”, our sea. At the time of its greatest extent around 117 AD the empire stretched from Britain to Mesopotamia and from Spain to Egypt. In it lived an estimated 50 to 60 million people.

For a long time Rome was a **republic** in which elected officials and the Senate governed. In 27 BC **Augustus** became the first emperor. After that an **emperor** ruled the empire, and many emperors followed one another. In 395 AD the empire was divided into a western and an eastern part.

The empire was divided into **provinces**, which were administered by governors. **Egypt** too became a Roman province in 30 BC after the death of Queen Cleopatra and supplied a great deal of grain. Good roads and a strong army held the empire together. **Roman law** with its statutes is to this day the foundation of many legal systems.

Distinguished Roman citizens wore a **toga**, a large, artfully wrapped cloth of white wool. In the cities there were markets, theatres and **thermae**, large bathhouses with warm and cold pools. Rich families lived in houses with a courtyard, mosaics and wall paintings. Many poor people, by contrast, lived in cramped apartment blocks.

The Romans wrote with the **Latin alphabet**, which we still use today. For numbers they used letters: I is 1, V is 5, X is 10, L is 50, C is 100, D is 500 and M is 1,000. **Roman numerals** can still be seen today on clocks, on buildings or in the names of kings. The Romans did not know a zero.

From **Latin** arose languages such as Italian, French, Spanish, Portuguese, Romanian and Romansh. Our calendar goes back to the **Julian calendar** introduced by Julius Caesar, and the months July and August are named after Caesar and Augustus. Throughout Europe bridges, aqueducts and theatres from Roman times still stand. In Switzerland too one can visit Roman ruins at Augusta Raurica and Avenches.

begriffe.erklaerung: An administrative region of the Roman Empire outside Italy.
The sole ruler of the Roman Empire.
A large white woollen cloth worn by distinguished Romans.
A large public bathing complex.
The language of the Romans, from which many present-day languages arose.

gewusst: The number 4 is written IV in Roman numerals, but on many clocks it nevertheless appears as IIII.
After the end of the Western Roman Empire the Eastern Roman Empire with its capital Constantinople continued for almost 1,000 years more.

teile.einleitung: The Alhambra is a magnificent complex of fortress and palaces in Granada in the south of Spain. It was built by Muslim rulers and is regarded as one of the most beautiful buildings of Islamic art in Europe.
wichtigste: The Alhambra stands on a hill above the city of Granada in Andalusia, Spain.
The name comes from Arabic and means “the red one”.
Above all the Nasrid dynasty extended the complex in the 13th and 14th centuries.
In the Court of the Lions, twelve stone lions carry a fountain.
Everywhere there are fountains, pools and channels.
The walls are decorated with fine patterns and lettering in stucco.
The Alhambra includes magnificent gardens, for example the Generalife.

abschnitte.titel: A red castle on the hill
abschnitte.text: The Alhambra lies on a hill high above **Granada**. From there you can see over the city as far as the mountains of the Sierra Nevada. The name comes from Arabic and means **“the red one”**. The walls of clay and bricks shimmer reddish in the sunlight. The complex consists of a fortress, several palaces, towers and gardens.

From the 8th century onwards, **Muslim rulers** governed large parts of Spain for many centuries. The region was called **al-Andalus**. The last Muslim ruling family was the **Nasrid** dynasty. It ruled the Emirate of Granada from the 13th to the 15th century and extended the Alhambra into a magnificent palace city. In 1492 the Catholic Monarchs conquered Granada, and after that Christian rulers lived in the Alhambra.

The most famous place in the Alhambra is the **Court of the Lions**. In its middle stands a fountain whose basin is carried by **twelve stone lions**. Water flows from the lions' mouths. Around the court stand slender columns that look like a forest of stone. From here, water channels lead into the surrounding halls.

Water was very important to the builders. In the Alhambra there are many **fountains**, **pools** and narrow channels. The water cools the air in the summer heat and splashes soothingly. The complex also includes magnificent **gardens** with flowers, hedges and watercourses. The best-known garden lies by the summer palace, the **Generalife**.

The walls and ceilings of the palaces are decorated with very fine **patterns**. Many of them were carved in **stucco**, a soft mass of plaster that then hardens. You can see tendrils, stars and geometric shapes. In addition there are Arabic **lettering** with poems and pious sayings. Some domes look like stalactite caves made of stucco.

gewusst: The Alhambra has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1984.
On many walls the same Arabic motto of the Nasrids appears again and again: “There is no victor but God”.

teile.einleitung: Rome is a city on the River Tiber in Italy and about 2,000 years ago was the centre of a huge world empire. According to legend it was founded by Romulus and built on seven hills. Because of its long history Rome is called the “Eternal City”.
wichtigste: Rome lies in present-day Italy on the River Tiber.
According to legend Romulus founded the city in 753 BC.
A she-wolf is said to have suckled the twins Romulus and Remus.
Rome was built on seven hills.
In the Colosseum gladiators fought.
The Roman Forum was the great marketplace in the centre.
In the Circus Maximus chariot races took place.
Rome bears the nickname “Eternal City”.

abschnitte.text: According to legend the twins **Romulus and Remus** were abandoned as babies in a basket in the Tiber. A **she-wolf** found them and suckled them until a shepherd raised them. As adults they wanted to found a city but fell into a quarrel, and Romulus killed Remus. Romulus became the first king, and the city received his name. The year of founding is given as **753 BC**.

Rome lies in central Italy on the River **Tiber**, not far from the Mediterranean. The city arose on **seven hills**, among them the Palatine and the Capitoline. On the Palatine the emperors later lived, which is why the word **palace** comes from this hill. Its position at a ford across the river made Rome an important trading place.

The **Roman Forum** was the heart of ancient Rome. Here stood temples, law courts, triumphal arches and the building of the Senate. People came to shop, to hear speeches and to attend elections and festivals. Today many ruins can be seen there, through which one can stroll.

The **Colosseum** is a huge oval amphitheatre that opened in 80 AD. It had room for about 50,000 spectators, who watched gladiator fights and animal hunts. Even bigger was the **Circus Maximus**, a long racetrack for chariot races with room for far more than 100,000 people. The charioteers belonged to teams with colours such as red, white, green and blue.

In the time of the emperors probably about a million people lived in Rome, more than in any other city of Europe. Many lived in cramped, multi-storey apartment blocks, the **insulae**. **Aqueducts** brought fresh water from the mountains into the city to fountains and baths. The **Pantheon**, a temple with a huge dome, is almost completely preserved to this day.

Today Rome is the **capital of Italy** and has about 2.8 million inhabitants (as of 2024). In the middle of Rome lies **Vatican City**, the smallest state in the world and seat of the Pope. Every year millions of tourists visit the ancient buildings, churches and fountains. According to custom, whoever throws a coin backwards into the Trevi Fountain will one day return to Rome.

begriffe.erklaerung: An old tale that is not certainly true.
A central marketplace and meeting place in a Roman city.
A round or oval building with rows of seats around a combat arena.
A water channel, often on high arches, that brings water into the city.

gewusst: The bronze figure of the Capitoline Wolf with the twins is the emblem of Rome.
The word palace comes from the Palatine, the hill on which the Roman emperors lived.

teile.einleitung: “Roman Switzerland” is the term for the time when the area of present-day Switzerland belonged to the Roman Empire, from about 15 BC to around 400 AD. In this time cities, roads, country estates and baths arose. Many traces of this time are still visible today, even in our language.
wichtigste: Before the Romans, the Celtic Helvetii lived mainly on the Swiss Plateau.
In 58 BC Julius Caesar defeated the emigrating Helvetii at Bibracte.
Around 15 BC the Romans also conquered the Alpine region.
Important places were Augusta Raurica, Aventicum and the legionary fortress Vindonissa.
A large Roman farm in the countryside is called a country estate.
French, Italian and Romansh descend from the Latin of the Romans.
German words such as Ziegel (tile) also come from Latin.

abschnitte.text: Before the Roman period the Celtic **Helvetii** lived on the Swiss Plateau. In 58 BC they wanted to emigrate to Gaul but were defeated by **Julius Caesar** at Bibracte in present-day France and sent back. Around **15 BC** the Romans under Drusus and Tiberius also conquered the Alps. After that the whole area of present-day Switzerland belonged to the Roman Empire.

Around 44 BC **Augusta Raurica** was founded at present-day Augst near Basel. There one can today visit a large theatre, temples and baths. **Aventicum**, present-day Avenches in the canton of Vaud, was the capital of the Helvetii and had an amphitheatre that still stands. Geneva, Lausanne, Chur, Solothurn and Zurich also go back to Roman settlements, and Zurich was then called **Turicum**.

At present-day Windisch in Aargau lay the legionary fortress **Vindonissa**. Here in the 1st century AD several thousand soldiers were stationed to protect the frontier on the Rhine. The fortress also had an amphitheatre. Finds from Vindonissa show how the soldiers lived, ate and wrote.

In the countryside many **country estates** arose, large Roman farms that are called villa rustica in Latin. They had a manor house with mosaic floors, underfloor heating and its own bath, as well as stables and workshops. The estates supplied the cities and soldiers with grain, meat and wine. Remains of such estates have been found in many places on the Swiss Plateau, for example at Orbe in the canton of Vaud with magnificent mosaics.

Roman roads connected the cities with one another and led over Alpine passes such as the **Great St Bernard** and the Julier Pass. On lakes and rivers goods were transported by ship. From Italy came wine, olive oil and tableware, from the region cheese, timber and cattle. People paid with **Roman coins**.

abschnitte.titel: The end and traces in language
abschnitte.text: From about 260 AD the **Alemanni** invaded again and again across the Rhine, and around 400 the Roman troops withdrew. The language of the Romans, however, remained: from **Latin** arose French, Italian and Romansh. Many German words also come from Latin, for example Ziegel (tile) from tegula, Mauer (wall) from murus, Fenster (window) from fenestra and Keller (cellar) from cellarium. The Romans also brought viticulture and new plants such as cherries and walnuts to our region.

begriffe.erklaerung: A Celtic people that lived on the Swiss Plateau before the Romans.
A large Roman farm, in Latin villa rustica.
A fortified camp in which a Roman legion lived.
The language of the ancient Romans.

gewusst: In Augusta Raurica in 1961 a large Roman silver treasure with plates, bowls and coins was discovered during building work.
The Latin name of Switzerland, Confoederatio Helvetica, still recalls the Helvetii today, hence the car sticker CH.

teile.einleitung: In 221 BC Qin Shi Huangdi united China and became its first emperor. With harsh laws and many standardisations he built a tightly run state. His dynasty, however, collapsed soon after his death.
wichtigste: The capital of the Qin Empire was Xianyang.
His chancellor Li Si put the state doctrine of Legalism into practice.
The empire was divided into commanderies under appointed officials.
Among other things, the script, coins, measures and the axle widths of carts were standardised.
Older border walls in the north were joined into a longer line of defence.
In 227 BC Jing Ke tried to kill him on behalf of the state of Yan.
After his death the eunuch Zhao Gao manipulated the succession.

abschnitte.text: In the 3rd century BC China was divided into several states that fought one another. The king of the state of **Qin** conquered one after another. In **227 BC** the assassin **Jing Ke** tried to kill him on behalf of the state of **Yan**. The attack failed. By **221 BC** the king had united all of China and called himself **Qin Shi Huangdi**, First Emperor of Qin.

Qin Shi Huangdi ruled according to the state doctrine of **Legalism**. This doctrine relied on strict **laws**, harsh punishments and rewards. It was put into practice above all by his chancellor **Li Si**. Other teachings, such as those of Confucius, were suppressed. The emperor had many books burned.

The capital of the empire was **Xianyang**. The emperor abolished the old principalities and divided the empire into **commanderies**. These were run by **appointed officials**, not by nobles. In addition, **script, coins, measures and weights** were standardised. Even the **axle widths of carts** had to be the same everywhere so that they fitted the same ruts.

In the north the emperor had **older border walls** joined into a **longer line of defence**. It is regarded as a forerunner of the later Great Wall of China. Roads and canals were added. For the works a great many people had to perform forced labour. Near his huge tomb at Xi'an the famous **Terracotta Army** was found in 1974.

Qin Shi Huangdi died in **210 BC** on a journey. Afterwards the eunuch **Zhao Gao** together with Li Si manipulated the **succession**. Instead of the eldest son, a younger son came to the throne. Soon uprisings broke out everywhere. By **206 BC** the Qin dynasty was finished, and the Han dynasty took power.

gewusst: The Terracotta Army consists of thousands of life-size warriors made of fired clay, and almost every face looks different.
Many institutions of the Qin, such as administration by officials, were taken over by later emperors for many centuries.

teile.einleitung: The pyramids are huge structures with a square base and four triangular sides that run up to a point. The ancient Egyptians built them over 4,500 years ago as tombs for their kings, the pharaohs. The Great Pyramid of Khufu at Giza is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World that still stands.
wichtigste: The great pyramids were built as tombs for pharaohs.
Most pyramids stand west of the Nile, where the sun sets.
At Giza three great pyramids stand side by side.
The base of an Egyptian pyramid is a square.
The Great Pyramid of Khufu is about 140 metres high.
The pyramids were built by many Egyptian workers.
The heavy blocks of stone were moved on wooden sledges.
Inside a pyramid lay a burial chamber.

abschnitte.text: The Egyptians believed that the **pharaoh** rose to the gods after his death. The pyramid was meant to protect his body and ease his way to heaven. Inside lay a **burial chamber** with the sarcophagus, reached by narrow passages. Beside the pyramid stood temples in which priests made offerings.

abschnitte.titel: On the west bank of the Nile
abschnitte.text: Most pyramids and tombs were built by the Egyptians in the **west** of the Nile. There the sun sets, and the west was regarded as the realm of the dead. In all, over 100 pyramids are known in Egypt. Many of them are today badly decayed or only heaps of rubble.

One of the oldest pyramids is the **Step Pyramid of Djoser** at Saqqara, built around 2650 BC. Its architect **Imhotep** stacked several ever smaller steps on top of one another. Later the Egyptians learned to build pyramids with smooth sides. The pyramids of Giza were covered on the outside with smooth, white **limestone slabs** that gleamed in the sun.

At Giza, on the edge of today's capital Cairo, stand **three great pyramids** of the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure. The **Great Pyramid of Khufu** is the largest. It was originally about 146 metres high and is today about 139 metres high. Each side of its square base is about 230 metres long. In front of it keeps watch the famous **Sphinx**, a huge figure with the body of a lion and the head of a human.

According to present knowledge, the pyramids were built not by slaves but by many thousands of Egyptian **workers**. Researchers have found their settlements, bakeries and tombs nearby. The blocks of stone were cut in quarries, transported on the Nile and pulled up ramps on **wooden sledges**. Probably wet sand was poured in front of the sledges so that they slid more easily.

The Great Pyramid of Khufu was the tallest structure in the world for thousands of years. It is the only one of the **Seven Wonders** of the Ancient World that is still preserved. The pyramids of Giza belong to the **UNESCO World Heritage** and are visited by millions of people every year. In present-day Sudan too there are many smaller, steep pyramids from the Kingdom of Kush.

begriffe.erklaerung: A structure with a square base and triangular sides that meet at the top.
The king in ancient Egypt.
The room inside where the dead person lay with his coffin.
A pyramid made of several steps placed on top of one another.

gewusst: For the Great Pyramid of Khufu over two million blocks of stone were used, many of them heavier than a car.
The sides of the Great Pyramid of Khufu are aligned very precisely with the four cardinal directions.

teile.einleitung: Thucydides was a historian from Athens in the 5th century BC. He described the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta. Because he examined causes carefully and checked his sources, he is regarded as the founder of critical history writing.
wichtigste: Thucydides was an Athenian and lived in the 5th century BC.
He wrote about the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta.
After the loss of Amphipolis in 424 BC, he was banished.
As the “truest cause” of the war he named Sparta's fear of Athens's power.
He called his work a “possession for all time”.
The work breaks off in the middle of the year 411 BC, and Xenophon continued it.
Today, in politics, people speak of the Thucydides Trap.

abschnitte.titel: A war between Athens and Sparta
abschnitte.text: From **431 to 404 BC**, the two most powerful Greek cities, **Athens** and **Sparta**, fought against each other with their allies. This long war is called the **Peloponnesian War**. Thucydides lived through it himself. He began collecting material right at the start, because he sensed that this war would become more important than all earlier ones.

In **424 BC**, Thucydides was a **strategos**, that is, a general, for Athens. But he arrived too late to save the important city of **Amphipolis** from the Spartan **Brasidas**. He was then **banished** from Athens. He used the twenty years of exile to gather information from both sides. Even earlier he had lived through and survived the terrible **plague** in Athens.

Thucydides distinguished between the outward **occasions** of a war and its deeper **cause**. He saw the “truest cause” in the growth of Athens, which put **Sparta** in fear. He did not want to tell stories about gods, but examined reports critically. Also famous are the **speeches** in his work, for example the funeral speech of Pericles. He called his work not a showpiece for the moment, but a “**possession for all time**”.

The history is divided into **eight books**. It breaks off in the middle of the account of the events of **411 BC**. The rest of the war was described by other authors. The Athenian **Xenophon** took up exactly where Thucydides had stopped in his “Hellenica”. His account extends to 362 BC.

Thucydides is still read today, including by politicians and experts in international relations. The American political scientist **Graham Allison** coined the term **Thucydides Trap**. It describes the danger of war when a **rising** power challenges an **established** power. The term is often applied to the relationship between the **USA** and **China**. Whether the comparison fits is disputed among experts.

gewusst: Thucydides described the plague in Athens so precisely that experts still puzzle over which disease it was.
His work is regarded as one of the first to explain history without the gods intervening.

teile.einleitung: The Odyssey is one of the oldest hero stories of Europe and is attributed to the Greek poet Homer. It tells of the long, adventurous journey home of Odysseus after the Trojan War.
wichtigste: Odysseus was king of the Greek island of Ithaca.
After the Trojan War he wandered for ten years over the sea.
His wife Penelope and his son Telemachus waited for him.
He met monsters such as Scylla and sorceresses such as Circe.
With the nymph Calypso he had to stay for seven years.
At home he proved with his bow who he was.

abschnitte.text: The **Odyssey** is a long poem, an **epic**, attributed to the poet **Homer**. It probably arose in the 8th or 7th century BC and is divided into 24 books. The hero is **Odysseus**, king of the small island of **Ithaca**. He had fought for ten years in the **Trojan War** and afterwards needed another ten years for the journey home. From his name comes our word “odyssey” for a long wandering.

On the journey many dangers lay in wait. In a narrow **strait** waited the monster **Scylla** with six heads, and opposite threatened the whirlpool **Charybdis**. The **Sirens** lured sailors to their doom with their singing. His companions put **wax** in their ears. Odysseus had himself **tied to the mast**, so that he could hear the singing without following it. The one-eyed giant Polyphemus he outwitted by calling himself “Nobody”.

The wind god **Aeolus** gave Odysseus a **bag full of winds**. But the curious companions opened it, and a storm drove the ship far away. The sorceress **Circe** turned the companions into **pigs** with a magic potion. Odysseus forced her to change the men back. The nymph **Calypso** held him on her island for **seven years** because she wanted to marry him. Only on the orders of the gods did she let him go.

At home his wife **Penelope** waited faithfully for him for many years. Many men wanted to marry her and hoped to become king. Penelope said she would decide only when a cloth was finished weaving. But at night she secretly unpicked what she had woven by day. Her son **Telemachus** was a baby when his father went to war. When Odysseus came home, he was a young man.

After **20 years** Odysseus came to Ithaca disguised as a **beggar**, and nobody recognised him. Only his old **dog Argos** wagged his tail. Penelope had a contest held: whoever could string the old **bow** of Odysseus was to marry her. Nobody managed it except the beggar. He even shot the arrow through **twelve axe heads**. So Odysseus proved who he really was and defeated the men who had occupied his house.

gewusst: The word “odyssey” still stands today for a long, arduous journey.
Odysseus outwitted the giant Polyphemus by calling himself “Nobody”.

teile.einleitung: The tribune of the plebs was a special office in the Roman Republic. He was meant to protect the ordinary citizens, the plebeians, from unfair decisions by the powerful. For this he had very special rights.
wichtigste: Tribunes protected the **plebeians**, the ordinary citizens of Rome.
Later, **ten** tribunes were elected every year.
A **patrician** was not allowed to become a tribune.
With the word **“veto”**, “I forbid”, they could stop decisions.
During their term of office they were **inviolable**.
They led the assembly of the plebeians.
The emperors later had the authority of a tribune conferred on themselves.

abschnitte.text: In ancient Rome there were two classes. The **patricians** were the old, noble families. The **plebeians** were the other citizens, for example farmers and craftsmen. For a long time the patricians had almost all the power. The plebeians therefore fought for more rights. One result of these struggles was the office of **tribune of the plebs**, in Latin tribunus plebis.

A tribune could stop decisions by officials and even resolutions of the Senate. To do so he said **“veto”**, which means **“I forbid”**. Even today we speak of a veto when someone can block a decision. In addition, the tribune was allowed to help citizens who were threatened by an official.

During their term of office, tribunes enjoyed special protection: they were **inviolable**. Anyone who attacked a tribune or stopped him from doing his work was severely punished. So that he could be there for everyone, a tribune had to **leave his front door open day and night**. In this way people seeking help could come to him at any time.

Only plebeians could become tribunes, not a **patrician**. At the beginning there were probably only a few tribunes, but later **ten** were elected every year. The tribunes led the **assembly of the plebeians**. There, resolutions could be passed that later applied to all Romans.

When Rome was ruled by emperors, the office lost importance. But the **emperors** had the **authority of a tribune** conferred on themselves, without being tribunes themselves. In this way they too were inviolable and could use any veto. This shows how powerful this office had once been.

gewusst: The word “veto” comes straight from ancient Rome and is still used today, for example in the Security Council of the United Nations.
During his term of office, a tribune was not allowed to leave the city of Rome for any length of time.

teile.einleitung: Troy was an ancient city in the north-west of present-day Turkey. It is famous for the legend of the Trojan War, which the poet Homer tells. Archaeologists have found and studied its ruins on a hill.
wichtigste: The ruins of Troy lie in the north-west of Turkey.
The hill with the ruins is called Hisarlik.
The Greek poet Homer told of the war over Troy in the **Iliad**.
Another name for Troy is “Ilion”.
In the hill lie the remains of many cities one above another.
According to the legend, Paris, a prince of Troy, set off the war.

abschnitte.text: Troy lay on a hill in the north-west of present-day **Turkey**, not far from the strait of the **Dardanelles**. Today the hill is called **Hisarlik**. From there you could keep a good watch on the route between the Mediterranean and the Black Sea. This position made the city important and perhaps also rich.

The Greek poet **Homer** told of the war over Troy. His work is called the **Iliad**, after “Ilion”, another name for Troy. The Iliad is a very long poem and almost 3000 years old. It describes only one part of the war. A second work, the **Odyssey**, tells of the journey home of the hero Odysseus.

According to the legend, **Paris** was a prince of Troy, a son of King **Priam**. He carried off Helen, the wife of a Greek king. The Greeks then marched against Troy with a great army. After a long siege, the city fell through a trick with a wooden horse. Whether this war really happened like this is not known exactly by researchers.

In the 19th century, the German merchant **Heinrich Schliemann** dug on the hill of Hisarlik. He wanted to find the Troy of Homer's legend. The researchers discovered that the remains of **many cities lie one above another** in the hill. Again and again, new buildings were put up on the ruins of an old settlement. These layers are counted with numbers, for example Troy I to Troy IX.

The ruins of Troy are now a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Visitors see walls, gates and remains of houses from very different periods. Many finds are in museums. The story of Troy has inspired poets, painters and film-makers again and again to this day.

gewusst: In Troy, Schliemann found a treasure of gold and called it “Priam's Treasure”. It later turned out to be much older than the time in which Priam is supposed to have lived.
For a long time, many scholars thought Troy was pure invention, until the ruins were excavated.

teile.einleitung: The Trojan Horse is one of the best-known tricks from the Greek legends. With a huge wooden horse, the Greeks are said to have captured the city of Troy after ten years of war.
wichtigste: The Trojan Horse was built of **wood**.
The idea came from the clever **Odysseus**.
Greek warriors hid in the belly of the horse.
The other Greeks sailed away so that Troy would believe they had left.
The Trojans themselves pulled the horse into the city.
In the night, the warriors opened the city gates.
The king's daughter **Cassandra** warned them in vain.

abschnitte.text: For ten years the Greeks had besieged Troy, but the walls held. Then **Odysseus** had an idea. The Greeks built a huge, hollow **wooden horse**. In its belly hid the best **Greek warriors**. The horse looked like a gift to the gods.

The other Greeks burnt their camp and **sailed away**. In reality they hid with their ships behind a nearby island. The Trojans were meant to believe the war was over. Only the big wooden horse was left behind on the beach.

The Trojans argued about what to do with the horse. **Cassandra**, a daughter of King Priam, warned of a trap. According to the legend she could see the future, but no one ever believed her. The priest **Laocoön** also warned them. Even so, **the Trojans pulled the horse into the city** and celebrated their supposed victory.

In the night the warriors climbed out of the horse. They **opened the city gates**, and the Greek army, which had meanwhile come back, poured into the city. This is how Troy fell. The Roman poet **Virgil** tells this story in detail in the **Aeneid**. Homer mentions the horse in the **Odyssey**.

The story is so well known that it lives on in our language to this day. A **“Trojan”** is a harmful computer program that disguises itself as a useful program. Someone who is given a gift with a hidden catch sometimes speaks of a “Trojan horse”.

gewusst: In the Iliad, the best-known work about the war, the wooden horse does not appear at all. The Iliad ends before the fall of Troy.
Someone who predicts misfortune but is not believed by anyone is still called a “Cassandra” today.

teile.einleitung: Papyrus is a marsh plant that grows on the Nile. The ancient Egyptians made from it a writing material that was used throughout the ancient world. From its name comes our word “paper”.
wichtigste: Papyrus is a marsh plant that grew in Egypt on the banks of the Nile and in the Nile Delta.
The stem of the plant was needed for the writing sheets.
Strips from the pith of the stem were laid crosswise and pressed.
Long texts were glued together into lengths and rolled up.
From papyrus the Egyptians also made sandals, baskets, ropes and boats.
Many old papyri have survived thanks to the dry air in Egypt.
The word “paper” comes from the Greek “papyros”.

abschnitte.text: The **papyrus plant** is a sedge that grows in water and in marshes. It needs a lot of water and therefore used to grow close to the **Nile** and in the **Nile Delta**. Its stems grow several metres high. At the top they carry a bushy tuft of thin stalks. Today the plant has become rare in Egypt.

For a writing sheet the **stem** was cut into pieces and the rind peeled off. The soft **pith** inside was cut into thin strips. The strips were laid side by side and over them a second layer **crosswise**. Then everything was pressed and beaten until the strips held firmly together. After drying, the sheet was smoothed so that it could be written on well.

A single sheet was not very large. For long texts many sheets were glued together into a **length**. These lengths were wound into **rolls** and kept like that. People wrote with a rush or a reed pen and black or red ink. The Greeks and Romans also took over papyrus and wrote their books as rolls.

The Egyptians used papyrus for many things. They plaited from it **sandals**, mats, baskets and ropes. From bundled stems they even built light **boats**. So papyrus was an important everyday raw material. It was also a trade good that Egypt sold to other countries.

Papyrus decays over time in damp air. In Egypt, however, the air is very **dry**. So many old **papyri** have survived there to this day, and some are several thousand years old. They contain letters, bills, poems and religious texts. Researchers learn a great deal from them about life in antiquity.

gewusst: The plural of papyrus is papyri.
The words “Bible” and “bibliography” are also linked through Greek with the trade in papyrus.

teile.einleitung: The Oracle of Delphi was the most famous oracle of the ancient Greeks. People from many cities travelled to Delphi to ask the god Apollo about the future.
wichtigste: The Oracle of Delphi was dedicated to the god Apollo.
The priestess who gave the answers was called the Pythia.
She sat on a tripod while prophesying.
The answers were often mysterious and ambiguous.
The Greeks regarded Delphi as the centre of the world.
On the temple stood the saying “Know thyself”.

abschnitte.text: **Delphi** lies on a steep slope of the mountain range **Parnassus** in central Greece. There stood a great temple of the god **Apollo**. Through the oracle Apollo was to speak to people. The Greeks regarded Delphi as the **centre of the world**, the “navel of the world”. A special stone called the **omphalos** marked this centre. Today the ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The answers were given by a priestess, the **Pythia**. She sat on a high stool with three legs, a **tripod**. That is also how she is shown on old vases. The name recalls a legend: according to it Apollo defeated the dragon-like serpent **Python** at Delphi. Whoever wanted to consult the oracle had first to make offerings and wait until it was his turn. Kings and whole cities also sent messengers.

The answers of the oracle were often **mysterious** and **ambiguous**. They could be understood in different ways. Famous is a story from the historian Herodotus: King Croesus of Lydia asked whether he should wage war against the Persians. The oracle said he would destroy a great empire. Croesus attacked and lost. The great empire that was destroyed was his own.

Many Greek cities built their own **treasury** along the **Sacred Way**. In it they kept their **votive offerings** for the god. The **Treasury of the Athenians** has been rebuilt. At Delphi the **Pythian Games** also took place, with contests in sport and music. In **1896** the famous bronze statue of the **Charioteer** was found. It dates from around 470 BC and recalls a victory in a chariot race.

On the temple of Apollo stood the saying “**Know thyself**”. It means that one should think about oneself and know one's limits. The saying is still famous today and often quoted. The oracle was important for many centuries. It ended only in the 4th century AD, when Christianity prevailed in the Roman Empire.

gewusst: A stone called the omphalos, “navel”, marked the centre of the world at Delphi.
The bronze statue of the Charioteer is one of the few surviving large bronzes from ancient Greece.

teile.einleitung: Pericles was the most important politician in ancient Athens. He expanded democracy and had magnificent buildings such as the Parthenon erected. His time is regarded as the golden age of Athens.
wichtigste: Pericles was the leading politician in Athens.
For years he was elected strategos again and again.
He developed democracy further.
He introduced a daily allowance so that poor citizens could also serve as jurors.
Under him the Parthenon was built from 447 BC.
The golden age of Athens is named after him the Age of Pericles.
He died in 429 BC of a plague.

abschnitte.text: Pericles lived in the 5th century BC in **Athens**. He came from a distinguished family and was a good speaker. The citizens elected him **strategos** for many years in a row. A strategos was a military commander who also had great influence in politics. So Pericles became the leading man of the city.

Pericles developed **democracy** further. Many offices were given by lot to ordinary citizens. For the jurors of the **people's courts** he introduced a **daily allowance**. In this way poor citizens could also serve as jurors without losing a day's wage. However, only adult men with citizenship were allowed to take part in decisions, not women, slaves and foreigners.

Under the leadership of Pericles the **Parthenon** on the Acropolis arose from **447 BC**. Further buildings were added such as the magnificent entrance gate, the Propylaea. Much was paid for with **funds of the League**. These funds had actually been paid by the allied cities for common defence. Critics therefore accused Pericles of wasting the allies' money.

The time around the middle of the 5th century BC is called the **Age of Pericles**. Athens was rich and powerful. Artists, builders, poets and thinkers came to the city. Plays were performed that are still staged today. Athens became the intellectual centre of Greece.

In 431 the **Peloponnesian War** against Sparta began. For the first dead Pericles gave the famous **Funeral Oration**, which the historian **Thucydides** has handed down. In it he praises democracy and the freedom of Athens. Soon afterwards a **plague** broke out in the overcrowded city. Pericles died of it in **429 BC**.

gewusst: Pericles was almost always depicted with a helmet, probably as a sign of his office as strategos.
His partner Aspasia was known for her intelligence, which was very unusual for a woman in Athens at that time.

teile.einleitung: Angkor was the capital of the Khmer Empire in Cambodia. Today hundreds of temples survive there, including Angkor Wat and the small temple of Banteay Srei.
wichtigste: From the 9th to the 15th century, Angkor was the centre of the Khmer Empire.
The five towers of Angkor Wat represent the mountain of the gods, Mount Meru.
The most famous relief shows the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
Banteay Srei was consecrated in 967 and is known for its reliefs in pink sandstone.
The Chinese envoy Zhou Daguan described everyday life in Angkor in 1296 to 1297.
According to inscriptions, King Jayavarman VII had over a hundred hospitals built.
Since 1992, Angkor has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

abschnitte.text: **Angkor** lies in the north of **Cambodia** near the town of Siem Reap. From the 9th to the 15th century it was the capital of the **Khmer Empire**. The kings had huge temples, water basins and canals built there. The dwelling houses were of wood and have vanished, while the temples of stone remained. The best known is **Angkor Wat**.
